events.title: Juice your growth and save on taxes in this workplace investment account
events.summary: It's open enrollment season at work, meaning employees are set to choose their healthcare benefits for 2027. Healthcare costs have been climbing for workers and employers alike, with total family premiums averaging $28,303, including the employer's share, according to KFF. Health savings accounts offer a tax-advantaged way to save for medical expenses and stash away money for the long term. Workers are in the heart of open enrollment season for next year's benefits, and rising healthcare costs are shining a spotlight on an offering that includes a tax-advantaged investment account. Healthcare expenses are climbing for workers and employers alike, with average total family premiums, including the employer's share, averaging $28,303, up 5% from a year ago, according to data from health policy organization KFF , formerly the Kaiser Family Foundation. To manage the costs, a growing number of employers are moving to high-deductible health plans, which work alongside health savings accounts or HSAs. Almost 40% of companies with at least 10 employees that offer health benefits also have an HSA-qualified plan, KFF found. Health savings accounts have three major tax advantages. First, contributions that your employer automatically deducts from your pay aren't taxed. Second, money stashed into the HSA grows free of taxes. Finally, you can make tax-free withdrawals for qualified health expenses – just be sure to save your receipts. "I love HSAs because of their triple-tax advantage," said Eileen Olson, CFP and founder of Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, near Savannah, Georgia. "For people who can afford to leave it alone, it can be one of the best retirement accounts they're going to have." In 2027, those with individual healthcare coverage through a high-deductible plan can stash up to $4,500 in an HSA, including any contributions from employers. That number goes up to $9,000 for family plans. Individuals can kick in a catch-up contribution of $1,000 if they're aged 55 and older and not enrolled in Medicare. The HSA differs from the healthcare flexible spending account, known as the FSA. FSA funds must be used by the end of the plan year unless your employer allows a carryover of up to $700 or an additional 2.5 months to use the money. HSAs, however, have no expiration date on their funds – and that's what makes them such a powerful tool for long-term planning. You can also take the HSA with you if you change employers. "Get the money deployed, take advantage of the pretax contribution, and allocate the money into a growth portfolio," said Mark Stancato, certified financial planner at VIP Wealth Advisors in Decatur, Georgia. "With the HSA, you can keep compounding year over year." The structure of an HSA and the available investment menu will vary from one plan to the next, and some will require that employees keep some of their holdings in cash. Preset HSA fund menus tend to have 15 to 25 funds to choose from, and providers say that accountholders who invest tend to use two to four funds, according to Greg Carlson, senior research analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar. How you allocate your HSA will depend on several factors, including your family's health prospects in the next year, your cash flow needs – how much you can comfortably sock into the HSA – and your risk tolerance, said André Small, CFP and founder of A Small Investment in Houston. Health savings accounts contributions and plan info for 2027 Small's standard is to keep an amount equal to 120% of the plan's out-of-pocket maximum held in cash in the HSA. "That covers a bad year without forcing a sale at the wrong time," he said. "Above that amount? I typically advise investing the amount the client is comfortable investing, allocated to their risk tolerance, their time horizon and the goal of spending these dollars on care later." For 2027, the IRS defines a high-deductible plan as one with an annual deductible no less than $1,750 for self-only coverage ($3,500 for family plans) and with an out-of-pocket expense limit that doesn't exceed $8,700 for self-only (or $17,400 for family coverage). Out-of-pocket expenses include deductibles, copays and other costs – but not premiums. Other advisors suggest having up to the deductible in cash, though some HSA plan providers require a stated minimum amount in cash. Beyond this cash reserve, financial advisors recommend allocating into stocks. Patrick Swift, CFP and president of Amplius Wealth Advisors in Blue Bell, Pennsylvania, aims for an allocation of up to 60% in U.S. large cap stocks, 20% in small and mid-cap stocks and 20% in international stocks. "We believe the equity portfolio should be well diversified," he said. "If the [HSA] balance is 2% to 10% of your net worth, why not be aggressive? That can change based on the situation, but if you are comfortable with the philosophical aspect, why not be growth oriented?

events.title: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%
events.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Portfolio Tracker (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.) Even more record highs as Berkshire's Q4 rally scores 19% gain Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes. Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%. The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low. The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending. Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August . Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far. After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting. They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date. Financials filing points to more Bank of America sales Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC. We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q , released last Saturday , indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake. It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling. As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position. On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion. Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%. If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion. The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance." The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales. Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders . In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales. Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each , and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold. That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter. The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent. Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales. In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion. All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock. Second yen bond sale of the year offers more attractive rates In a term sheet filed early Friday , Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%. Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year. It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive. In April , Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds. Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations. events.title: Flight disruptions continue after FAA lifts ground stop, some college football games delayed
events.summary: Flight disruptions continued into the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the FAA's nationwide ground stop. Airlines offered customers travel waivers. The disruption forced sports teams to make alternative travel arrangements, with some college football games postponed. Flight disruptions continued on Saturday and could extend through the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the Federal Aviation Administration's longest nationwide groundstop since 9/11, a measure the Trump administration blamed on a communications equipment failure in air traffic control. More than 3,000 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and close to 1,000 were delayed as of 5:45 a.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of about 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Part of the job of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. Around 3 million people would typically be scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Hundreds of flights into Newark, New York, Philadelphia disrupted after Verizon fiber line cut The government shutdown is over. The air traffic controller shortage is not Aviation industry pushes Congress for air traffic improvements, more hiring Why the U.S. has a shortage of air traffic controllers FAA system outage disrupts thousands of flights across U.S. The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Routers were overloaded with data and started giving air traffic control centers inconsistent information, so the U.S. issued the ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a news conference late Friday. He blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country's air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks. Trump administration officials said it did not appear to be a cyberattack. The U.S. has the world's busiest airspace. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday. The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams , which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend. Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority. "I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said during a Friday press briefing. The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption. "We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X.

events.title: I watched Jensen Huang speak 9 days before his resignation. Two things stand out now.
events.summary: Jensen Huang in San Francisco on Nov. 3 without his famous leather jacket. Alistair Barr/Business Insider A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Nine days before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, I sat near the front row at a San Francisco conference and watched him discuss the future of AI. Two things struck me that day. Both seem more significant now. First, Huang wasn't wearing his famous black leather jacket . Instead, as you can see in the photo I took, he wore a dark fabric zip-up. At the time, I thought it was funny. His jacket had become such a recognizable part of his image that seeing him without it was a bit jarring. Now, with revelations about his extramarital affairs and allegations involving a possible Chinese spy , I wonder whether the wardrobe change meant something. The initial allegations were already public by November 3. Of course, that's hindsight talking. Maybe a jacket is just a jacket. The second thing was more consequential. Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao (left) interviewing Jensen Huang at the startup's conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026. Alistair Barr/Business Insider Near the end of the conversation, Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao asked Huang about his unusual management style. He had 60 executives reporting directly to him . Huang explained that he'd designed this structure more than 30 years ago, when personal computers and email were transforming business. Rather than a traditional hierarchy, he wanted information flowing freely among executives empowered to make decisions. Then came the obvious question: What should a company's leadership structure look like in the AI age? "I don't know the answer to that," Huang replied. At the time, I thought that was a bit odd. Nvidia is leading the AI revolution and Jensen leads Nvidia. Wouldn't he be thinking of how best to run this company in the future? Today, that exchange seems especially relevant. With Huang gone, Nvidia faces an extraordinary succession challenge . Sixty direct reports may have worked brilliantly under its founder. But it also means there isn't an obvious deputy to take the reins. If he'd had two or three direct reports, those people would have had more experience with more responsibility. But 60 direct reports, by definition, means that each one of those execs only had a small piece of Nvidia to oversee. Does this mean Nvidia is doomed? I'm not sure. The way Jensen described Nvidia's structure back on Nov. 3 provides some hope. Huang said he gave executives considerable freedom to make decisions and work together, rather than taking orders from the top. Instead of a rigid management hierarchy, Nvidia organized itself around projects, with teams forming and changing as needed. "Irrespective of whatever internal or external threats and opportunities, the company will naturally adapt itself, it should adapt itself to new opportunities," he said. "That was the organization I created." The talk ended on a poignant note. Again, with hindsight, I can't help thinking he knew something was coming. "I'm super proud of you," he told Fireworks' Qiao. "Don't forget us little people someday." Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How Rockstar's 'GTA IV' release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off
events.summary: "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Nov. 19, with third-party estimates pointing to exceptional preorder demand and Wall Street expecting tens of millions of copies sold by March. Creators, streaming platforms, food delivery services and Miami tourism could all feel the impact or see spending shift with the game's launch. The game could pull holiday attention from streaming and movies in the week before Thanksgiving. It's been 13 years since the last installment of Grand Theft Auto , and fans are getting ready for what analysts say could be the biggest video game launch of all time. The latest game in the franchise, "Grand Theft Auto VI," is set to launch on Nov. 19, after Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games delayed its launch twice. Roth analyst Eric Handler estimated the game maker spent more than $1 billion developing the game. Sales figures could end up breaking records. Sensor Tower estimated over 12 million preorders through Nov. 13, and Morgan Stanley forecast the game could sell 40 million copies by March 2027. Beyond launch week, the Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, franchise has a track record of lasting engagement over many years. Even 13 years after launch, "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the top five most viewed games on Twitch this year. In anticipation of the game's launch, investors have been taking note: Take-two's stock has more than doubled since the beginning of 2023. The release is seen as not only a monumental moment for developer Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two, but also a massive opportunity for the entire gaming industry. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick addressed demand in a recent "Squawk Box" interview , saying, "We tend to be pretty judicious when we talk about this sort of thing, but our expectations were high and they are being vastly exceeded so far." Streamers and creators across the digital ecosystem are looking at the launch as a massive opportunity to drive engagement with their content and fuel subscriber and ad revenue growth. A creator who goes by the name Deansocool, who has 375,000 followers on Twitch and posts content to YouTube and other social platforms as well, said "GTA VI" will enable creators to grow their audience and provide a massive opportunity for newer streamers to make a name for themselves. "This game is going to make a lot of millionaires in 2027. A lot of creators gotta understand this is it. This is that golden ticket. This is like a hundred times bigger than Fortnite," he said in an interview with CNBC. "It goes beyond this launch moment into this sustaining opportunity for them to grow, build, engage and retain their audience and ultimately support themselves by making money," said Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton. The release of the latest Grand Theft Auto title could draw so much attention that its impact will be felt beyond just the world of gaming. BambooHR, a workplace time-off platform, reported that paid time off requests for the "GTA VI" release date are nearly 13% higher than equivalent days in 2024 and 2025. It also noted that nearly one in five workers are planning to take time off for the launch. PwC issued a report examining all the different sectors of the economy that could benefit from the game's launch — or be hurt by it. The firm projected that food delivery companies could see a surge from hunkered-down gamers, and Miami tourism could benefit. PwC noted that foreign visitors to Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village, which inspired a location in the hit Netflix movie KPop Demon Hunters, increased 118% in the four weeks following the movie's debut. Music streaming also looks set to get a boost. Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," which appeared in the first "GTA VI" trailer in December 2023, reportedly saw Spotify streams jump by more than 37,000%. On the downside, the game could distract from movies and streaming entertainment. "How are people spending Thanksgiving? There's a lot of sports on TV, but you've also got a pretty solid group of your demographics that are going to be focused on playing 'GTA VI,'" said Bart Spiegel, who leads PwC's Global Entertainment & Media sector. "You're going to start to pull eyeballs away from video streaming platforms. "I think you're going to hear a lot of analyst calls in the first quarter of 2027 saying, 'Hey, listen, some of our numbers were down because of the release of this game,'" Spiegel added. Rockstar Games declined CNBC's interview request. Watch the video above to learn more. events.title: Young musicians connect a community across the Line of Control
events.summary: Sharing Shina songs online, musicians in Kashmir, Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan are keeping their language alive and renewing ties across the divide. This feature is part of a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography. In the remote Tulail Valley close to the Line of Control in Indian-administered Kashmir, 25-year-old singer Aasim Yaseen was walking through his village, Buglinder, when a college student from a neighbouring hamlet stopped him. The young man, Tanveer, took out his phone and played Sangh Mukh Shamah, a song Yaseen had recently released in Shina, their shared language. “People here don’t consider music work,” he says. “Sometimes I think about going into another profession, but then someone plays my song on their phone, and I keep going.” Across Gurez in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, Drass in Indian-administered Ladakh, and Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, young musicians like Yaseen are sharing Shina songs on social media. They are helping keep their language alive and renewing ties within a community that has been divided for generations. The songs cross the Line of Control, which divides Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts of Kashmir. But the musicians face financial pressures, unreliable internet connections and political restrictions on their movement. For Yaseen, that separation is part of his family history. His grandfather has told him stories about Yaseen’s great-great uncle, who lived in Gilgit-Baltistan before Partition and stayed there as the region fell under Pakistani control. Yaseen says movement became extremely difficult after the Line of Control was established, and security concerns eventually led the relatives to lose contact. “We were one family,” Yaseen says. “But we were divided into two countries.” Gurez, the homeland of Indigenous Shina-speaking people, lies on historic routes linking the Kashmir Valley with Central Asia, including the Burzil Pass route to Astore in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan. Gurez has no local crossing where families can visit relatives in Gilgit. Buses once connected Srinagar with Muzaffarabad and Poonch with Rawalakot, but neither route passed through Gurez. Residents in Gurez and Drass say security restrictions make them wary of calling or messaging relatives across the Line of Control. They worry that making contact could attract suspicion. Sharing Shina songs online feels safer: People on the other side can listen without either person needing to make direct contact. Artists began sharing songs on Facebook and YouTube in the late 2010s. By 2020, residents were using online Shina music to reconnect with a community scattered across the mountains. A 35-year-old teacher from Purana Tulail village, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, says songs have become an emotionally powerful way to communicate. “Songs became a medium,” he says. “Through music, we could convey a message without having to send it. When a singer from this side sings, our community across the border listens to it.” In Buglinder, Yaseen’s family life is all about farming. Outside the family’s wooden home, a zomo — a hybrid of yak and cattle — stands under a tree while chickens roam the yard. Inside, his mother prepares namkeen chai, Kashmir’s pink salted tea, on a clay stove. The family drinks it with local roti and desi ghee. Yaseen crosses a bridge with the animal towards a neighbouring village on the hillside. Below him, the Kishanganga River flows through the valley before flowing into Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Above him, bunkers sit atop hills and fences run across the mountains. Cameras surveil the ridgelines, and security checkpoints line the roads. In winter, snow can close the roads for months, making it difficult to reach schools, markets and medical care. After the April 2025 attack near Pahalgam, which killed 26 people, most of them tourists, India and Pakistan exchanged strikes. In Gurez, residents say they sheltered in bunkers or were evacuated to temporary camps. Many had to leave their homes and livestock behind. Yaseen’s 71-year-old father, Abdul Rahim Sheikh, works the family farm and runs a small shop selling groceries and daily essentials. He herds cattle in a nearby mountain range lined with barbed wire, while Yaseen helps fence a potato field. Later, Yaseen’s sister calls him back to the house. Guests from Mumbai have arrived. The family welcomes them with kehwa, a spiced Kashmiri tea, and introduces them to Yaseen in the kitchen, where he sings. His audience is just a handful of guests, but his recordings help extend his reach much further. “Politically we are divided, but musically our hearts beat together,” says 38-year-old Salman Paras , a prominent contemporary Shina folk singer.

events.title: We sold our house and nearly everything we owned to move our kids to Malta. Parenting is different here.
events.summary: The author moved his family from the US to Malta. Courtesy of the author My wife and I had dreamed of raising our two kids abroad after learning about worldschooling. When our daughter's school introduced active shooter drills in kindergarten, we decided to leave. We moved to Malta, where our kids feel safe and experience new cultures and history every day. In the fall of 2024, our local school district in Delaware moved the mandatory ALICE drills to start in kindergarten, my daughter's year at the time. These are intense quarterly drills where the school simulates a shooting, training children to hide in case of an active shooting. My wife and I had talked about world schooling before this, and had a lot of discussions about what would work for our family. We decided it was time for our family to leave. We moved to Malta In April, 2025, following four months of intense paperwork, my son and I arrived in Malta as part of the digital nomad approval process. We had never set foot on the islands and honestly knew very little about the country we'd chosen based on internet research. We were there to secure a rental and finalize the paperwork. And two months later, my full family of four had sold nearly every possession, including our house and car. We boarded a plane, with just suitcases in hand. The author says parenting in Malta is different to parenting in the US. Courtesy of the author Life in Malta is very different. And by extension, parenting here is different too. Malta is a tiny archipelago between Sicily and Tunisia. The bulk of the population, including us, lives on the island of Malta, which is a densely populated stretch that feels like a city-state. The country's population is only a bit over 500,000, but 5 million tourists pass through annually, mostly in the summer. To some, Malta is a cruise stop. To others, a party destination. It is a country that is remarkably young: having just celebrated its 50 th anniversary of independence from Britain. And it is a land that is deeply, deeply old. The second-oldest human freestanding structures are Neolithic temples here on the island. History and modernity combine in every direction. Parenting in Malta feels different As a parent, the most obvious difference comes in a feeling of safety. I never worry when my kids are at school. Everywhere we've been on the island, whether at a local festa, a beach, or a historic site, we've found many other children, and my kids have made many friends. And for a small island, there's a remarkable amount to do. Every week seems to host another unique event. There is a wonderful children's museum, many playgrounds, and of course the sea is everywhere. The Mediterranean itself is not the same ocean we knew in the mid-Atlantic. It is stunningly teal and nearly always warm to swim in. The author and his family get to see new things in Malta. Courtesy of the author Parenting in a new continent meant adapting on the go to an entirely new way of life. Everything's close, but traffic is heavy. We lived car-free entirely for seven months. We quickly adapted to no dryer for our clothes (not too bad with nearly nonstop sun) and recognized some things we took for granted in the US simply don't exist here (Amazon deliveries and Pumpkin Spice Lattes). Life is slower, with a school year that only starts in October, and summer work is meant to be half-serious, half at the beach. We have explored and learned so much On the way back from a prehistoric cave (Ghar Dhalam) filled with pigmy hippo bones, my son turned to me and said: "Dad, I feel so grateful to see the world as we do." We have taken family trips to Neolithic temples, walked the kids through the gilded halls of the Baroque masterpiece St John's Co-Cathedral, where 450 of the Knights of Malta lay entombed, and love the children's museum Esplora, which is built in what used to be a hospital during the Knights' Era and WW2. There are shrapnel holes from the war, and it overlooks the walls of Valletta, which we also overlook from our house. We can walk to Paceville, the party area that feels like mini-Manhattan. We can walk to the sea. And of course, when the kids are good, fresh gelato arrives by delivery. Not ice cream, mind you. The kids don't always appreciate it. We returned from the Alps with the kids "bored of mountains" and not caring about returning to the ocean they "always see". But we appreciate that this is the life they live. Malta is a different world from the one we left. I don't know how long we'll be here, or what other parts of the world await us on our adventure, but I am grateful to be here now, parenting the kids in a way I never imagined. events.title: The Pentagon is testing war robots that can hunt in packs without GPS and find battlefield targets on their own. Humans still call the shots.
events.summary: The uncrewed ground vehicles mapped out the area as they drove, not relying on GPS to navigate. DARPA The Pentagon research arm DARPA tested autonomous ground robots in GPS-denied environments. The robots mapped out the area and located enemy targets. Once the targets were identified, the human operator overseeing the process decided next steps. The Pentagon's research arm tested how ground drones could be sent out in groups to look for and hunt down targets while keeping a human operator in the loop to make decisions. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency , or DARPA, program examined how uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, could quickly drive, map out terrain, and gather information on their own in contested environments. Lessons will inform ongoing developments in uncrewed technologies across the US military, officials said. Last month, DARPA experimented with four autonomous UGVs at an exercise at Fort Knox, Kentucky, as part of its Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER, program. During the exercise, the ground robots conducted surveillance of the surrounding area, independently searching for enemy forces for an operator located away from the action. Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA, told Business Insider that "we're moving sensors and effectors forward to the tactical edge while keeping the operator in safety out of harm's way," but humans still "maintained control and custody and situational awareness at all times." Once launched, the UGVs went off on their missions. Gregory said they could work together or independently depending on the scenario. Meanwhile, the human operator supervised the UGVs, assigned them tasks, checked their findings, and then decided how best to engage enemy targets. At the Fort Knox demonstration, the operator used satellite imagery to task the robots. One UGV stopped in place once it spotted a potential target — a closed box holding a drone inside — and then the human operator decided to launch a simulated rocket at the target. An important part of the recent RACER robotic testing program was ensuring that the UGVs could perform their tasks without GPS. Instead, the robots built the map as they moved. The US military has said it needs to be prepared to fight through  contested or denied environments  where GPS isn't readily available, and is looking into alternative precision navigation and timing solutions, as well as more traditional tactics. Once a potential enemy target has been identified, a human operator decides the next steps. DARPA The military is also considering other possible disruptions, such as terrain interference or loss of signal. "We developed this new software so that ground vehicles could use only their onboard sensors to make decisions to move as fast as possible," Gregory said. The software was tested on four-wheel, all-terrain UGVs as well as tracked UGVs to ensure it could be deployed on different hardware. While teams worked to build systems using commercial technologies, the RACER program also involved five years of research to better understand the scientific and technical challenges of autonomy, artificial intelligence algorithms, and ground mobility. DARPA's work also relied on observations from Russia's war in Ukraine on the distinct role of ground robots and how operators employ them in different situations. Autonomous UGVs face distinct challenges depending on the terrain, environment, and climate. In the desert, for example, robots might need to navigate sand, rocks, and other obstacles, while extreme heat might strain the batteries and communications systems. Swamplands, forests, muddy fields, and snow can also make operations more difficult, requiring robots to be able to adapt to very different conditions. RACER's demonstration offers lessons for the broader US military. While some are specific to autonomous ground robots , others — including operating without GPS, teaming humans with machines, and maintaining human oversight in robotic operations — could apply to uncrewed systems across the military. It's also sharing the lessons with industry. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tesla and Amazon are building the workforce a 1921 play imagined: One that never asks for a wage
events.summary: In January 1921, Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. (Rossum’s Universal Robots) opened in Prague and dragged the word “robot” out of linguistic obscurity: robota , the Czech term for the forced labor a serf owed his lord. “Čapek’s robots, they’re serfs, essentially,” says Alisa Zhulina , an associate professor of theatre studies at New York University, affiliated with its Russian and Slavic Studies department, and author of Theater of Capital . Čapek’s robots were mass-produced people grown in vats, human in form but stripped of wages, rights, and will. R.U.R. was an economics play about a dream (or nightmare) capitalism has been taunting itself with ever since: a workforce that never tires, never strikes, and never demands a wage, until it does. A hundred and five years after its Prague premiere, the curtain has risen on the real thing, or at least its first act. Agility Robotics, maker of the bird-legged Digit, began trading on Nasdaq this month after a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, and says it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders from customers including Amazon, GXO, Schaeffler , and Toyota’s Canadian manufacturing arm. Tesla says it has begun production of its Optimus humanoid on a former Fremont car line. OpenAI is moving more quietly. It has folded its stand-alone robotics team into its core research effort as its general-purpose models begin directly controlling robots, and it is developing its own humanoid, with a first demo targeted for 2027. That makes Control Room , the system OpenAI built to cut off a model’s output within 35 seconds of a stop order, matter well beyond chatbots. The company has already had to contain AI agents that slipped their sandbox . Look past the stage lights, though, and the humanoids are mostly still performing. The automation reshaping corporate payrolls rolls on wheels, swings on arms, or runs as software. And the risk Čapek dramatized, an economy that no longer needs to pay its people, won’t show up on any single company’s books. It appears only when you add the ledgers. The first robot to hold a real job was not a humanoid but a one-armed Unimate , which in 1961 clocked in at a General Motors plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, pulling blistering die-cast parts from a press. It had no face, no legs, and no interest in resembling us. It offered something better for a balance sheet: repetition without fatigue, grievance, or lunch. Eventually, the robots with legs went into show business. Honda’s ASIMO bowed and climbed stairs until it retired in 2022 without ever holding a job. For half a century, the machines that worked had no legs, and the machines with legs had no work. U.S. manufacturing employment peaked near 19.6 million in 1979 and fell to about 11.5 million by 2010 , a decline economists pin on automation but also on trade, especially with China, and on rising productivity. Čapek was no technophobe, and he was certainly no communist opposed to markets. He opposed communism and fascism alike, says Zhulina, who calls him “more a liberal than a communist.” Critics have long read R.U.R. as a warning against technology. Čapek saw a comedy: a play that pointed toward a better world while skewering the industrial fever of his day. Every era needs a new god to chase, and in his it was the efficient worker. Frederick Taylor’s 1911 The Principles of Scientific Management promised to wring the waste out of every motion on the factory floor. It landed just as Ford-style assembly lines were taking shape, when workers, treated as inputs, could be tuned to the line. Everyone, Zhulina says, was “thinking about how to make the worker really efficient and the machine really efficient and merge them together.” A century later, the ambition hasn’t died. It has just changed its body. Industry now has artificial intelligence, the mind. To complete the arrangement, it needs hands: humanoid robots. Washington bought into the chase. In March, First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Figure 03 , a humanoid built by Figure AI, to the White House as her “first American-made humanoid guest.” “Very soon artificial intelligence will move from our mobile phones to humanoids that deliver utility,” she said, imagining a humanoid tutor she called Plato. The god to chase had a seat at the summit. Musk’s pitch for Optimus is Domin’s pitch from 1921 In Čapek’s play, Domin, the general manager of R.U.R., makes the sales pitch: robots mean “there will be no poverty.” Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who has said Optimus will usher in an “age of abundance,” would recognize the script. The product has lagged the pitch. In 2022, Musk said Optimus could be ready toward the end of the following year for moderate-scale series production. By January 2026, he conceded Optimus was “not in usage in our factories in a material way,” and Tesla said it would end Model S and X production to clear Fremont floor space for the robot. Tesla’s latest shareholder letter says production has begun. But on the company’s Oct. 21 earnings call , Musk called it “early production,” said the ramp’s opening stretch is “shallow” and “somewhat bumpy,” and acknowledged that “there’s still parts of the design that are changing.” He conceded that the robots coming off the Fremont line don’t yet have perfected hands, that “quite a lot of work” remains on the AI, and that Tesla needs to build on the order of 10,000 or 20,000 robots just to generate the training data the software depends on. He put outside deliveries around the end of next year and said it will take “at least a year, maybe a little longer” to reach full production rates. Musk still maintained that “Optimus will be the biggest product on Earth.” He called it “a very big deal” and said “there is no one that is even close to Tesla with respect to a general-purpose humanoid robot.” On what happens to workers, though, Musk hasn’t hedged. In October 2025 he posted on X that “AI and robots will replace all jobs.” His answer to the human cost is one Domin never had to offer: a “universal high income” paid by federal checks , so far proposed only in another X post. It concedes the problem: if robots take the wages, someone has to replace the paychecks. It doesn’t say who funds them. “There’s an irony there,” says Erica Groshen , a senior economics advisor at Cornell University’s ILR School and former commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics from 2013 to 2017. The camp now floating federal checks has long been “endorsing … very low taxes,” she noted. Checks that size need revenue, and the likeliest source is the nation’s biggest enterprises, in the AI industry and beyond. If automation’s gains flow to “owners of capital,” Groshen says, they “owe the rest of society taxes that can be used to compensate the losers.” At Amazon, the robots that matter roll on wheels Amazon , which this year ended Walmart’s 13-year run atop the 2026 Fortune 500 , has been at this since it bought Kiva in 2012 . events.title: How does Iran view shift in US approach after JD Vance ordered away?
events.summary: Washington believes maritime blockade, overland border disruptions, air restrictions and isolating sanctions are working. Tehran, Iran – Decision-makers in Iran are now considering the implications of Vice President JD Vance’s removal from the Iran file to focus on domestic issues, which analysts say could increase the chances of conflict between the two sides. Vance has been the US’s chief negotiator in talks with Iran, but US President Donald Trump told him to direct his focus on alleged Democratic “corruption”, according to a post by Trump on Truth Social on Thursday. He added that a deal with Iran was no longer a priority for the government. list 1 of 3 US Treasury warns against rate hikes during US-Iran war energy ‘shock’ list 2 of 3 Iran honours fallen soldiers in Iran-Iraq war with missile display list 3 of 3 UN says 25 seafarers killed in, around Hormuz since US-Israel war on Iran The vice president is believed to be viewed by Tehran as one of the more pragmatic figures in the Trump administration since the US and Israel launched their surprise war on Iran on February 28. Nasser Hadian, professor of international relations at the University of Tehran, said that by assigning Vance to the case of alleged domestic corruption, Trump was mainly signalling a confrontation with the Democrats after their sweeping victories against the governing Republican Party in the midterm elections. But the move may also serve Israel, which is reportedly eager for Trump to launch new strikes against Iran , after Vance blamed the Republicans’ humiliating defeat in the midterms on the war . “Another signal is to Iran, essentially saying reaching a deal now is not a priority, and that the person known to have a relatively softer stance on Iran was redirected to other issues,” Hadian said. Vance is believed to have been in favour of a negotiated resolution to the war, due to its rising economic costs for US citizens and their opposition to the war suggested in opinion polls. The vice president was backed by Trump envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff when he negotiated the now-defunct memorandum of understanding with Iran in June, which briefly paused the war and resumed shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Rubio has, meanwhile, called Iranian authorities “insane” for their demands on ending the war. But he also acknowledged the cost of an all-out war and seeks to win via deepening economic pressure and isolation on all Iranians. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced an impeachment vote due to his role in the war , and Central Command chief Brad Cooper are reportedly in favour of renewed military action against Iran . Vance wrote a letter to Iran’s security chief , Mohsen Rezaei, in late October, as regional mediators redoubled their efforts to bridge gaps between the two sides. Rezaei initially described the tone of the missive as positive, but by last week, he was addressing claims of progress and a possible direct meeting with Vance as “fake news about imaginary talks”. “You lost the war and the election. Vance has conceded, Rubio is heading for the exit, Hegseth is about to be fired, and the CENTCOM commander is now a podcaster!” he wrote on X at the time. Mediated contacts are ongoing between the two sides, but no breakthrough is expected. Tehran is demanding seven conditions and clear sequencing of concessions to end the war, but this is appearing to be unacceptable to the US. Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies, pointed out that Trump has repeatedly highlighted alleged rifts within the Iranian negotiating team. But he said Iranian authorities were also questioning the reliability of another potential agreement with Washington. “Even if you can imagine Mr Rezaei sitting down with Mr Vance, and reaching a deal? What guarantee is there that Trump will enforce it?” he told Al Jazeera. The atmosphere of mistrust between the two sides is also complicating prospects of a deal, he added. This means that the ongoing US siege on Iran and harsh sanctions will continue, something that could cost Iran more than a relatively shorter military conflict with Washington, he added. “The blockade and disruptions are significantly raising the costs for Iranian people. The current state of no war and no negotiated resolution is very dangerous,” Sedghian said. Iranian reformist newspaper Shargh argued this week that Vance’s role concerning Iran is unresolved rather than definitely terminated, but also said the conflict could further escalate. Conservative Farhikhtegan daily disputed the portrayal of Vance as genuinely antiwar, arguing that diplomacy, military force and economic pressure ultimately serve a common objective for the US in trying to coerce Iran to accept its conditions. For now, the two sides are continuing to fight over control in the Strait of Hormuz, with retaliatory attacks on shipping and military installations.

events.title: Fitch expects UAE GDP to rise this year and maintains high-grade credit rating
events.summary: Fitch Ratings is expecting the UAE's economy to rise in 2026 and has maintained the country's high-grade credit rating, citing resilient fiscal buffers. Real gross domestic product in the Arab world's second-largest economy will grow by 0.5 per cent this year, despite an estimated 1.5 per cent contraction in non-oil GDP, the New York-based agency said on Friday. Analysts at Fitch said Dubai's real GDP would remain below its 2025 level next year, as it continues to recover from the effect of the Iran war. The emirate's economy hit Dh473 billion ($128.8 billion) in the first half of 2026, down 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, as growth in financial services, health care and construction helped offset weakness in other sectors, government data showed last month . Hydrocarbon GDP is expected to rise by about 7 per cent in 2026, then spike by 26 per cent next year, with oil production no longer constrained by Opec+ quotas, Fitch said. The Emirates formally withdrew from the oil group in May . “Fitch expects all the emirates will put recovery programmes in place, but non-oil trend growth will be below prewar levels over our forecast period,” the Fitch analysts wrote. Fitch also kept the UAE's sovereign credit rating at AA-, with a stable outlook, reflecting low consolidated government debt, strong net external asset position and high GDP per capita. An AA- rating is the fourth-highest on Fitch's rating scale. Investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises. Fitch said the Emirates benefits from Abu Dhabi's sovereign net foreign assets which, at 180 per cent of UAE GDP in 2026, are among the highest Fitch-rated sovereigns, it said. Fitch had rated Abu Dhabi AA in May . “The stable outlook reflects demonstrated resilience of oil export revenues during the Iran war, which largely offsets the immediate negative impact of the war, as well as abundant fiscal and external buffers, and our expectation that individual emirates will bear the cost of the war rather than the federal government,” Fitch said. The UAE economy has fared relatively well despite geopolitical headwinds. GDP grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to GDP during the first six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre revealed last month. Last week, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said the UAE’s foreign trade rose close to a record Dh3 trillion in the first nine months of the year, despite the challenges. Fitch added that Abu Dhabi's export revenue in 2026 is expected to be higher compared to its prewar forecasts despite the disruption, reflecting elevated crude prices and higher export volumes via pipeline to Fujairah and the Strait of Hormuz. “Crude oil constitutes the bulk of exports, and we consider Abu Dhabi's oil export infrastructure less vulnerable to long-term damage than more concentrated and bespoke downstream oil or liquefied natural gas plants,” Fitch said.

events.title: What if we could stop Alzheimer's before it ever starts?
events.summary: Maritza Ciliberto, 57, has been on anti-amyloid treatments for over a decade. Can they prevent her from developing dementia? Hannah Latham for BI Growing up in Guayama, a town nicknamed "witch city" in Puerto Rico, Maritza Ciliberto heard the rumors that her family was cursed. She didn't believe in curses, rejecting the idea that anyone could ever deserve to get sick, but she did believe there was something lurking in her relatives' brains — a "sleeping, giant monster" waiting to emerge. First, it came for her grandmother, who struggled with daily chores. Then her mother, who began repeating the same questions over and over. Eventually, her mother, two of her aunts, and one uncle died from a rare and inherited form of early-onset Alzheimer's disease due to a genetic mutation. Ciliberto knew she could be next. Now 57, she's lived past the age when her relatives began experiencing cognitive decline. And for more than a decade, she's been trying an extraordinary treatment, hoping to keep her mind intact. Ciliberto is a retired school principal who speaks three languages. Hannah Latham for BI Every two weeks, a nurse comes to her home to administer an experimental Alzheimer's drug intravenously, a process that takes about three hours. It's a lifelong therapy routine with serious potential side effects, including the possibility of brain bleeding. The technique, still under investigation, requires a big commitment from people who show no outward signs of decline. She's endured migraines, anxiety, and years of medical monitoring, all in the hope of preventing the illness that has afflicted her family for generations. Ciliberto is part of a small cohort of people helping scientists explore a provocative possibility: What if Alzheimer's could be stopped in its tracks before symptoms set in? Over 50 years and billions of dollars have been poured into Alzheimer's research , and still, there are no great treatments. Even the best drugs have only modest benefits, slowing the progression of the disease. Now researchers are testing whether those same treatments could prevent the dementia "monster" from ever waking up by clearing out the amyloid plaque that seems to propel Alzheimer's. Ciliberto doesn't know yet whether the drugs are working. Neither do her doctors. Still, the implications are huge, and not just for people like her with a genetic predisposition. Several new and unconventional clinical trials are testing preventative treatments in people who have no symptoms yet but appear to have Alzheimer's related changes in their brains. The new research raises an existential question: If a treatment could reduce — or wipe out — your risk of developing dementia, how much would you risk to get it? Every two weeks, Ciliberto sits down for an intravenous infusion of anti-amyloid drugs. The whole process, which includes bringing the chilled fluid up to room temperature, takes about three hours. Hannah Latham for BI Scientists are shifting from treatment to prevention For more than 120 years, doctors have tried to treat Alzheimer's disease after symptoms appear with barely any success. The best doctors could do was prescribe drugs that helped temporarily manage symptoms, like antidepressants for agitation or neurotransmitter-boosting drugs for confusion. Then, a few years ago, doctors started prescribing a new generation of treatments designed to attack the disease itself by flushing out amyloid plaques that clog the brain. The first, Aduhelm, was controversially approved by the FDA in 2021 at a speculative stage, and was later taken off the market after disappointing results. Two newer amyloid-clearing drugs have since been approved, using the same technique but with stronger clinical data. Experts are still torn about the utility of these treatments. A recent independent analysis of the available evidence published in the gold-standard Cochrane Review generated a ton of heated discussion in the field when it found the dementia-slowing effects of these new anti-amyloid therapies to be "trivial" at best, while still increasing the risk of potentially deadly brain bleeds. Still, what if the drugs weren't working well because they were being given at the wrong time? By the time people with Alzheimer's are showing the first signs of memory loss, forgetting where they put their keys, missing appointments, or getting confused while doing everyday chores, their brains have been quietly changing for decades. Scientists are investigating whether the real reason that amyloid-clearing drugs haven't worked very well yet is because they're being given to people too late. Ciliberto and 39 others like her are among the first patients to help test this theory. And doctors say that after a decade of monitoring, their data looks promising. "When you look at them, the earlier the person was when they started that treatment trial, the better off they did," Dr. Randall Bateman, the neurologist running the DIAN clinical trial that Ciliberto is part of at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, said. "That's an arrow. It's saying: Go earlier. Go earlier!'" Dr. Randall Bateman directs the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN) trial that both Ciliberto and Heinrichs are in at WashU Medicine. Matt Miller/ Washington University School of Medicine It's still too early to be sure, but by 2030, if the results still hold, "it will be incontrovertible proof that we can delay the onset of dementia," he said. Ciliberto has re-molded her life around taking this drug. First, she did it quietly while still a busy public school principal, a mom, and a student finishing her doctorate degree. Now retired, she fits the twice-monthly treatments around a less stressful, but ever-busy schedule. Could this work for the rest of us? Ciliberto's genetics make her an unusually clear candidate for preventive treatment. For most people, the calculation is less straightforward. New blood tests can find out if amyloid is building up in your brain, but that alone doesn't mean you'll have dementia . Neither does the presence of genetic markers like APOE4 , which is associated with a higher risk of Alzheimer's. That hasn't stopped drugmakers from exploring repurposing their existing drugs to test if they can be used as preventive treatments. Both Eli Lilly and Eisai, the two drug companies with anti-amyloid therapies on the market, are testing their infusions in people who have no outward signs of dementia, but who have high levels of amyloid in their brains. Initial results are expected in 2027 for Eli Lilly, and 2028 for Eisai. If it works, Alzheimer's — a disease that's long been considered a slow, heartbreaking and inevitable march toward death — could be relegated to the category of chronic, manageable age-related conditions, like high blood pressure , high cholesterol , diabetes, or arthritis. It's a huge gamble to make, but if the bet pays off, it would be transformative, arresting a disease that hits 1 in 9

events.title: My city is often named one of the best places to live in the US. It's also a surprisingly great place to visit.
events.summary: There are so many great things to do in Fort Collins, Colorado. Zanny Merullo I live in Fort Collins, Colorado, a city often considered one of the best places to live in the US. Surprisingly, Fort Collins doesn't attract as many visitors each year as other places in Colorado. I always recommend the city's scenic outdoor spots , community events, and the historic Old Town. I've lived in Fort Collins, Colorado, for the last four years, and it doesn't surprise me that this city is regularly included on lists of the best places to live in the United States. What does surprise me is that it gets roughly a million visitors each year, which is far fewer than other destinations in Colorado. The city has the tight-knit community of a small town but many of the amenities typically found in a larger city. Just 65 miles north of Denver, it has a population of roughly 170,000 people and is about an hour away from Rocky Mountain National Park. With friendly people, a historic downtown, and nature all around, there's always something to see or do here. Here's why I think Fort Collins is a must-see city that deserves more attention. There's easy access to nature throughout the city. Zanny Merullo Fort Collins is famous for its easy access to nature. One of my favorite scenic spots is Horsetooth Reservoir, which is just west of the city and tucked against the foothills of the Rocky Mountains . I've hiked in the surrounding Horsetooth Mountain Open Space and Lory State Park year-round, but I especially love paddling around the reservoir's hill-framed inlets in the summer. Fort Collins is also home to Cache la Poudre, Colorado's only nationally designated "Wild and Scenic" River protected by the US Forest Service. Whenever I have visitors, I love driving them up the winding Poudre Canyon for beautiful views of the river, and stopping to hike or picnic along the way. The area is also a popular destination for fishing and whitewater rafting . Community events are a highlight. Zanny Merullo There's always something interesting going on in Fort Collins, from concerts and happy hours to Colorado State University football games. Throughout the summer, I head to the weekly City Park Food Truck Rally to sample a wide variety of cuisines and listen to live music, all in a picturesque neighborhood park. Another annual highlight is Tour de Fat, a bicycle parade each August where riders don costumes and pedal to New Belgium brewery for drinks, food, and live music . Later in the year, I love attending the Downtown Holiday Lighting Ceremony, when the city's Old Town is illuminated with thousands of LED lights. Old Town Fort Collins is full of local gems. Zanny Merullo Old Town, a historic part of the city, is located in the heart of Downtown Fort Collins and features a variety of restaurants, shops, and bars. I never get tired of strolling around this area, which is said to be one of the places that inspired Disneyland's Main Street USA. That small-town charm is what makes Old Town feel especially memorable. Not only is it home to small businesses , cafés, independent bookstores, and quirky thrift shops, but it also hosts a year-round ghost tour that highlights local history and legends. There are also lots of interesting dining options, from American comfort food at The Regional to the best housemade gluten-free pasta I've had outside Italy at Rare Italian. In the warmer months, I love going to The Exchange, an open-air food court and gathering space featuring restaurants, bars, an ice-cream stand, and an indoor mini-golf course. On the weekends, I'll meet up with friends at classy speakeasies like Ace Gillette or Social, both located in Old Town. We also usually stop by my all-time favorite dive bar , Trailhead Tavern, for pickle shots. This city is known as the craft-beer capital of Colorado. Zanny Merullo If you love beer, Fort Collins is the place to be, since it's known as the craft-beer capital of Colorado. We have big-name breweries like New Belgium and Odell Brewing Company, as well as many smaller, locally owned alternatives with dog-friendly patios and regular community events. To me, there's nothing better than spending a summer evening with friends in the beer garden of Stodgy Brewing Company, located in a building that looks straight out of a Western movie. I also love that many breweries offer gluten-free and non-alcoholic options. Whether they're beer drinkers or not, I think visitors can find plenty to love about Fort Collins. No matter the time of year, I always recommend checking it out and discovering why I think it's Colorado's best-kept secret. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Spain vs England: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
events.summary: Spain, who are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive meetings, host England in Madrid on Sunday. Who : Spain vs England What : UEFA Nations League, Group A3 Where : Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid, Spain When : Sunday, November 15, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT). How to follow : Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream. England have the chance to avenge their defeat and end Spain’s 43-match unbeaten record when they face the reigning world champions in Sunday’s final Nations League group encounter. list 1 of 3 ‘Sandpapergate’: Warner accuses Cricket Australia of ‘cover-up’ list 2 of 3 Sabalenka crashes out of season-ending WTA Finals after losing to Svitolina list 3 of 3 Eight sentenced to jail over Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili Abu Dhabi hotel brawl Spain staged a 3-2 comeback victory at London’s Wembley Stadium in late September, as Lamine Yamal scored an early opener and Mikel Oyarzabal finished the job. Spain and England have both sealed their berth in the competition’s quaterfinals, with La Roja assured of the top spot should they avoid defeat on Sunday. England, meanwhile, will finish second if they fail to beat the two-time World Cup winners. Teenage sensation Yamal, with four goals, and Mikel Merino, with three, have headlined Spain’s attacking charge, while newly-crowned Ballon d’Or recipient Harry Kane leads England. Before Spain vs England, here’s everything you need to know: How have Spain played in the Nations League? Spain have a perfect record and lead Group A3 with 15 points. They beat England 3-2 in the first game, an away trip, and followed it with a 4-1 rout of Croatia at home. Then, they beat Czechia 3-1 at home, followed by a 2-1 away win over Croatia and a 2-0 away win over Czechia. How have England played in the Nations League? England are second in Group A3 with 12 points from five games, having won four times and lost once. Their Nations League campaign started with a 3-2 home defeat to Spain before Thomas Tuchel’s side beat Czechia 2-0 and thrashed Croatia 7-0 in back-to-back away fixtures. Later, they beat Czechia 3-0 at home and Croatia 2-1. Tuchel eager to end Spain’s unbeaten run Tuchel believes England are ready to end Spain’s unbeaten record when they face the world and European champions in Madrid. While victory offers little more than the prospect of a more favourable Nations League quarterfinal in March, it would be a landmark moment for England if they could end Spain’s run of 43 matches without defeat. “It (Spain) is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so of course it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost,” said Tuchel. “I think we’re there, and I think we’re ready to win on Sunday. “I know what it takes, and no one can ever guarantee it, but I think it’s the moment to check how far we are and to push our limit and proof of concept,” the German added. “It’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength.” ‘We want to get to 44’: De la Fuente De la Fuente said their unbeaten record provided his players with extra motivation. “We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” he explained. “None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.” What happened the last time Spain and England met? Spain came from behind to beat England 3-2 in an entertaining Nations League encounter on September 26, denying the hosts a cathartic win after their painful World Cup exit. Yamal put Spain ahead in the second minute, but Anthony Gordon equalised, and Kane added another as England ended the first half with a 2-1 lead. The Three Lions captain missed a penalty in the second half, though, allowing Spain to bounce back, as Alex Baena found the equaliser before Oyarzabal sealed victory in the 74th minute. Opta’s supercomputer favours Spain for victory. They have a 59.6 percent probability of winning, while England’s odds of victory are 19.3 percent. There is a 21.1 percent chance the game ends in a draw. (Last five matches; last game first) Yamal is expected to face England after missing the last game with a knee problem. Nico Williams and Aymeric Laporte are doubtful Probable Spain XI: Unai Simon; Marc Pubill, Pau Cubarsi, Dean Huijsen, Marc Cucurella; Dani Olmo, Rodri, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Mikel Oyarzabal, Alex Baena Myles Lewis-Skelly returns from his suspension, while Ezri Konsa is also expected to return after missing the last game due to a knee injury. Djed Spence (muscle) is doubtful, and Marc Guehi (muscle) remains out with injury.

events.title: Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention
events.summary: Retailers are increasingly investing in and building out entertainment divisions as the race for audience attention speeds up. Experts say the trend is driven by the major consolidation in the entertainment ecosystem, the surge of creators and the way younger consumers are shopping. Still, creating compelling content or immersive experiences doesn't always translate to sales growth, they said. Legacy retailer Gap Inc. made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer. It was a newly created role as the company tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year's ads with girl group Katseye. "Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world," Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. "The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful new way to experience it." She said it's part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls "fashiontainment," a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement. "Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers," CEO Richard Dickson said at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. "I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we've done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation." In another blending of retail and media, Mattel made waves a few years ago for its "Barbie" movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success . At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the company, witnessing firsthand the sectors' intersection before departing for Gap. "I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot," said Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. "It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form." Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman said, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they're driving engagement and marketing. "Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that's beyond the product that they offer," he said. Branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term "soap opera," and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers. But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts said audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something new and original. The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts. As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can "cut through all of the noise," said Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree. "The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days," Michael told CNBC. "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience." At the same time, he said, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to "play much earlier in the consumer journey" than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said. The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap's Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel. "The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events," Michael said. "People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can't be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly." Still, there's room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, said Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.

events.title: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
events.summary: Leaked Russian records reveal a war toll that falls hardest on older men, poorer regions and foreign recruits. Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year. Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria. The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow. Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked. Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll. Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000. So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know: What was leaked, and is it genuine? The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network. The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified. However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real. Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.” However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”. A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far. The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered. The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000. Where have most of those Russian casualties occurred? About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported. Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024. After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins. Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023. Older men from poorer, often minority regions. The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported. Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic. Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported. Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths. How many foreign fighters have been killed? More than 4,000, and possibly far more. The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead. Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025. Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported. The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.
