events.title: Ukraine's naval drones made their name attacking Russian warships. Now they're taking the fight onto land.
events.summary: Ukraine uses the Magura drone to hit Russia's navy, and it's increasingly finding new targets in the air and helping operations on land. Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA Ukraine's naval drones have been hammering Russian warships. Now, the drones, including UFORCE's Magura, are threatening Russian ground targets. The naval drones "pose a threat to the Russian occupiers on land as well," a commander said. Ukrainian naval drones that have hammered Russia's navy are now coming for Russian targets on land. Magura drones made by Ukrainian-founded defense company UFORCE played an important role in Ukraine becoming a formidable force at sea even without a conventional fleet of warships. Naval drones have damaged and destroyed numerous Russian vessels, pushing Moscow to move much of its  Black Sea Fleet  away from occupied Crimea. Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate, the GUR, revealed in August that it had used Maguras as FPV drone carriers to strike Russian targets on land, leveraging a control vehicle equipped with the "Podlyot" radar complex, which detects aircraft, missiles, and drones, and a Parol-4 IFF interrogator, used to distinguish between friendly and hostile aircraft. The Maguras "pose a threat to the Russian occupiers on land as well," the commander of the GUR's "Group 13" said. "This marks a fundamental shift in the nature of the conflict," said the commander, who uses the call sign "Thirteen." Oleg Rogynskyy, the founder and CEO of UFORCE, told Business Insider that he couldn't comment on the operational specifics, but he said that "it's not hard to imagine" a Magura launching something like the company's heavy Nemesis drone, which could then fly inland to target Russian air defense systems. The Russian air defense systems, he said, were built to take out missiles, not incoming heavy bomber drones flying low at night. In other August wins, the GUR said that drones launched from Maguras destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, and then later that month, they hit two S-400 launchers and a ground-based antenna used to control Orion drones. A month earlier, a naval drone used by the 123rd Territorial Defense Brigade dropped a ground robot off on the Kinburn Spit for an unusual combat mission. And Ukraine is training for more operations like these. Rogynskyy said that Maguras were used in a September exercise to launch drones, drop off amphibious ground drones for a beach assault, and deliver supplies. He said he expects to see more creative uses as time goes on. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spotlighted the growing capabilities of Ukraine's naval drones in an address to the UK Parliament. "We started with simple kamikaze sea drones. Then we built drones with turrets that can shoot down helicopters," he said. "Now we have drones that can shoot down Russian fighter jets from the sea. We have developed boats that carry other drones. We also have boats that strike targets on land from the sea." The GUR said in October that after destroying ships in Russia's Black Sea Fleet , "the Magura drone was significantly improved." It explained that now "it is a multifunctional platform capable not only of sinking surface objects, but also of carrying missile weapons, as well as aerial drones for striking ground targets." Before they became drone carriers, Magura drones were armed with alternative weaponry for engaging non-naval targets. In 2024, for instance, one shot down a helicopter with a missile. Last year, the GUR said that Maguras had been used to shoot down Russian fighter jets. Rogynskyy said some of these uses were a surprise to the company. "I didn't expect it. It's the ingenuity of Ukrainian engineers and Ukrainian soldiers that really drives this," he said. UFORCE, which also makes ground drones, AI software, and command-and-control systems, is one of Ukraine's biggest defense companies. Founded in Ukraine and headquartered in London, with major hubs in Kyiv and Washington, DC, it has also attracted significant international interest. The company's Magura drones have been involved in multiple multinational military exercises. UFORCE has also developed a new MV7 model for UK waters and is partnering with RECONCRAFT , an American special-operations boat maker, though no new production runs, customers, or contracts have yet been announced. UFORCE announced on Thursday that it raised $700 million in a Series A funding round from investors, including the UK government and Silicon Valley-based venture capital firms, bringing the company's total valuation to $6 billion. The company wants to scale its manufacturing both in Ukraine and in partner countries to strengthen their defense. Talking about this round of investment, Rogynskyy told Business Insider that "it's time to scale." He said that the future of naval warfare "is all about fully unmanned navies and autonomous patrol presence, et cetera, as well as autonomous standoff." In the near term, he said, many navies want a hybrid approach, coordinating operations between classic crewed assets and drones. He predicted that "pretty much every navy on the planet is going to be scaling itself using cheap, attainable, unmanned assets that are AI-controlled." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How SAF successes in Sudan’s Kordofan could turn tide against the RSF
events.summary: The SAF successes in Kordofan are seeing the battle against the RSF turn in favour of the Sudanese government. Khartoum, Sudan – The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in west Kordofan this week, shifting the war against the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in its favour. On Friday, the Sudanese army took control of al-Khuwai, according to local media. This is one of the main towns in West Kordofan and a strategically important site in the army’s ongoing campaign against the RSF in the resource-rich state, which began several weeks ago. list 1 of 3 Sudan factories struggle to restart after devastating wartime losses list 2 of 3 Sudan war and climate change see parents struggle to feed their children list 3 of 3 Sudan teachers go on strike over meagre salaries and dilapidated schools So far, the offensive by the SAF and allied Darfur forces has succeeded in breaking the RSF siege on al-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and surrounding areas. It has also opened up new routes for the army in central and southwest Sudan, paving the way for significant SAF advances in South Kordofan, all the way to Babnusa and the approaches to North Darfur, including an important road linking al-Nuhud, the site of gold mines, and al-Khuwai. The RSF, alongside its alleged allies in the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdelaziz Al-Hilu, still holds al-Nuhud and parts of South Kordofan. But its recent defeats in southern and western Sudan could weaken the paramilitary’s ability to coopt tribal groups in the region. “The RSF’s shift from attack to defence will alter its military composition, which was built on demanding rapid tribal support,” Mohamed Ali, an independent Sudanese analyst, told Al Jazeera. “The Kordofan region is not a social stronghold for the RSF; therefore, it is expected to withdraw from the region and reposition its forces in Darfur. This would give the army a strategic advantage in Kordofan and could make Darfur the new epicentre of the conflict sooner than expected.” The RSF’s main social and tribal support base is among the Arab communities of south and east Darfur, including areas around Nyala and el-Daein, along with border areas with neighbouring countries. The RSF has relied heavily on mobilising tribes and civilians in areas under its control, said Mohiedeen Mohamed, an expert on Sudanese military affairs. This is particularly true when the paramilitary comes under attack from several fronts and reinforcements are desperately needed to hold the line. But this informal coalition is also vulnerable to the changing circumstances in the war, with a number of tribal and other groups defecting from the RSF in recent weeks, as the SAF gains ground. “When the RSF expanded into parts of the Kordofan region, it established alliances with certain tribal groups and local communities,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera. “However, these alliances can be understood, at least in part, as arrangements driven by military and political necessity, rather than necessarily reflecting the longstanding social and historical integration.” After the downfall of former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir in 2019, a power struggle between General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan , the head of the SAF, and his former ally in the RSF, Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo , emerged, developing into a nationwide conflict between the two sides in April 2023. Fighting between the SAF and RSF has resulted in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with about 150,000 people killed and more than 14 million of Sudan’s 53 million population displaced in the ongoing war. Following SAF’s military successes in Khartoum and other areas, fighting has focused on the remote, impoverished but oil-rich and strategically important Sudanese provinces of Darfur and Kordofan. The recent battles in Kordofan form part of a broader struggle over geography, economic resources, and supply routes connecting Sudan’s central regions with Darfur and beyond. The RSF still consolidates control across all five states in Darfur, including el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, which fell to the RSF in October 2025 after a brutal siege and bloody reprisals that saw thousands of civilians killed, tortured, detained or raped . The United Nations has identified Kordofan as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict and said fighting in the area is complicating an already dire humanitarian situation. Continued fighting has seen about 4.5 million civilians flee to Chad, Egypt, South Sudan, and other neighbouring countries. Civilians are paying the highest price in the war, with drones targeting them and civilian infrastructure, including homes, schools, health facilities, power and water plants. About 160 people were killed in drone attacks over several days in October in western regions of Sudan.

events.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says an unexpected career move got her discovered by Steven Spielberg
events.summary: Catherine Zeta-Jones. JC Olivera/Getty Catherine Zeta-Jones recalls how she was discovered by Steven Spielberg in the late 1990s. Spielberg saw her in the CBS miniseries, "Titanic." He had her screen test for "The Mask of Zorro," which he was producing. Catherine Zeta-Jones was in her 20s when she made a decision that would change her career forever. At the time, the Welsh actor was famous to UK audiences for starring in the popular early-'90s British series, "The Darling Buds of May." But she yearned for more, so she decided to move to California and see if she could make it in Hollywood. With six months on a visa, Zeta-Jones had to get work quickly, and auditions were a bit of an ego check. "I'd been in this business since I was 9 years old, professionally in theater and in television, and a few films in Britain at that point," Zeta-Jones told Business Insider . "But I'd go into casting agents, and they'd be asking me what I had done." She ended up taking a role on the 1996 CBS miniseries "Titanic." Though it wasn't a "huge leap" for her, it led to something even better: attention from Steven Spielberg. The director happened to be watching the show one night and liked what he saw. He suggested she screen test for "The Mask of Zorro," which he was producing. A week later, she was "shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas." The rest is history. events.title: AI's four colliding crises
events.summary: AI's titans were handed an extraordinary mandate: Police yourselves. But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers. Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on. Why it matters: The collision of safety scares, political blows, financial turmoil and leadership scandals threatens to derail AI's once seemingly unstoppable ascent. The big picture: Just six weeks ago, President Trump announced that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord . But cracks were already showing and, since then, four crises have converged. 🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out. Now Democrats are planning a flood of AI bills once they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reports . They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify. 🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach , revealed in July , was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall. AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity. Axios' Madison Mills reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents and that unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts. 💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns. Tech stocks tumbled , with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic's IPO may not be what some hoped, with its projected valuation coming in roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. 🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation, following revelations about affairs, is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies. Nvidia's stock slide exemplifies the risk of putting so much power in the hands of so few AI executives. Pop culture has turned on the AI titans , with three year-end films — " The Social Reckoning " and " Musk ," out last month, and " Artificial ," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Reality check: The AI industry's hurdles are partly growing pains — investors start demanding returns, lawmakers seek accountability, the public grows skeptical. The trust collapse echoes the moment social media companies went from Silicon Valley darlings to public enemies. But AI's reckoning — just like its rise — has come much faster.

events.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
events.summary: ‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% last month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said. Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”. Pill told the Financial Times: “My view would be, we will see evidence that motivates further rises,” adding that the central bank would “do ‌what is necessary to get inflation back to 2% through time”. The chief economist is one of a number of the Bank’s policymakers who believe the UK economy has gained in strength over the last year, handing workers the power to bid up wages. Recent figures showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, to give an annual rate of growth that was only surpassed by the US among the G7 group of wealthy countries. With inflation expected to rise to 5% in spring next year, driven by high oil and gas prices as a result of the Iran war, Pill expects public and private sector workers to demand substantial pay rises, which would keep inflation high for a longer period. Pill said he considered an end to the US-Israeli ‌conflict with Iran and a fall in energy prices to be a “very low probability”, indicating that he was poised to vote for another ​quarter-point increase next month. “My bias, for what it’s worth, is that I worry about the inflationary impact being magnified by second-round effects,” he said, adding that he believed the central bank should have acted sooner to combat inflation. “In my ⁠view, we waited too long.” While the Bank has not seen evidence of wage increases or companies being able to pass on higher costs to consumers, Pill said the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence. “As we go into next year, we will begin to see some evidence, and it could play out in one direction or another – we’ll see.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Financial markets expect UK interest rates to rise to almost 5% in 2027. Pill said these expectations were “not outrageous”, hinting that he could vote for more substantial increases in the cost of borrowing at the next meetings of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) because the “ability to be ​modest [in the scale ​of rate rises] has diminished”. City analysts have interpreted the increasingly hawkish comments of Pill and other MPC members as making an interest rate rise in December almost inevitable. But there is disagreement about the strength of the economy, with many concerned that further increases in the cost of borrowing will hit the manufacturing sector and the construction industry, which has contracted for much of the year. Households are also likely to cut back on spending in the new year, when the energy price cap is expected to rise to almost £2,000 for a typical home and council tax bills increase by an average of almost 5%.

events.title: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Lutnick has become the face of the Trump administration's troubled response to Chinese espionage and potential national security threats. The most intense scrutiny is coming from Republicans on the Hill, fellow Cabinet members and the MAGA base. Why it matters: Regulators and policymakers on both sides of the aisle want someone's head for an affair that may have exposed sensitive technology to the nation's top foreign adversary. Two names are currently at the top of that list: former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and now Lutnick. The big picture: Over the past year, Lutnick slow-walked broader administration efforts to address suspicions that Singapore-based company Megaspeed was illegally diverting chips to China, Axios first reported . Administration officials had pushed to place Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which would have restricted exports of U.S. tech to the company. Driving the news: On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed as much. "Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC . Trump himself supported taking action on three occasions, but those efforts were delayed by Lutnick, Axios reported . There's a widespread belief in Trump's broad circle of advisers that the Nvidia scandal might be too much for Lutnick to survive — but Trump is standing beside him for now. Behind the scenes, the White House has not expressed concern regarding efforts to have Lutnick testify before Congress. MAGA commentators are also tearing Lutnick apart on shows like "War Room with Steve Bannon," while Republican senators openly take him to task. For the record: " Secretary Lutnick plays a fundamental role in advising the President across many different industries. The reports you have issued are inaccurate and false and literally misstate the topic, creating a false impression," the Commerce Department said in response to Axios' inquiries. Friction point: The brewing scandal hangs in part on a CIA warning that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who ran Megaspeed and was also alleged to be a Chinese spy. That warning appears to have been ignored by Commerce Department officials, sources told Axios. Context: Last fall, CIA intelligence indicated Huang was the target of the espionage, which was reported in a "book" assembled by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence for a small circle of administration officials with top secret clearance, according to sources familiar with the matter. In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's also White House national security adviser, compiled a memo about the issue to ensure that Cabinet officials with "equities" in Nvidia and AI were informed, one of those sources said. "The memo was made so that Lutnick and Bessent and others knew what was up," said one source. "Howard was given the memo. He ignored the memo," a second source said. In May, as Trump traveled to China aboard Air Force One, Rubio verbally briefed the president as a "reminder," one of the sources said. Reality check: Through it all, Trump has repeatedly been in Lutnick's corner. The president has defended Lutnick time and again, whether over tariffs, immigration or the latest China tussle. There are no indications Trump has changed his stance since publicly defending Lutnick on Thursday. The bottom line: While Trump continues to defend Lutnick, administration officials and congressional Republicans have clearly picked a target.

events.title: Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic
events.summary: Dario and Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah each stand to make $250 million in cash proceeds and to hold stock worth upwards of $18 billion after Anthropic's IPO. The co-founders were previously at OpenAI, ultimately leaving at the end of 2020 to start a frontier lab focused on safety. Four researchers, a former journalist, a public policymaker, and an engineer founded Anthropic in 2021. Six years later, the artificial intelligence company is about to go public, with trading expected to begin on Nov. 19, in what will be one of the biggest IPOs on record. Those seven co-founders are poised to each be worth many billions of dollars. At the end of 2020, siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei were vice presidents at OpenAI , the company that kicked off the generative AI frenzy with the launch of ChatGPT. But the two had grown frustrated with their employer over its approach to AI safety. Fearing a world where AI models' capabilities would progress faster than our understanding of them, the duo launched Anthropic early the next year. They took a handful of OpenAI colleagues with them: Tom Brown, the company's research engineering lead on GPT-3; Jack Clark, a policy director; Jared Kaplan, a contract research consultant; and Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah, both members of OpenAI's technical staff. They were all deeply concerned about OpenAI's ambitions to focus on commercialization, and they now stand to be some of the first to cash in on the AI boom. "They really started Anthropic not because they were hoping to get rich, but they started Anthropic because they like wanted to shape this really important thing in the world, and they thought that other people might do it worse than them," said Jeffrey Ladish, who joined Anthropic as a contract safety engineer in September 2021, and now serves as the executive director of AI safety institute Palisade Research. Collectively the co-founders own about 10% of Anthropic. Each has about 240,000,000 class A shares, or about a 1.4% stake. During Anthropic's most recent funding round, those shares — valued at $58.90 each — amounted to about $14 billion in value for each co-founder. If Anthropic's IPO reaches its target of $70 to $78 per share , or a market valuation of nearly $1.4 trillion, it would push those stakes to $17 billion to $18 billion. "It's extremely hard not to be influenced by your incentives," Ladish said. "You have investors, and money is not just like an end; it's also a means." Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. The face of Anthropic is CEO Dario Amodei. He holds the most shares of the bunch: 245,259,100 including shares subject to voting proxies. Amodei, 43, didn't get his start in business. He comes from the world of research, obtaining a doctorate in computational neuroscience from Princeton University in 2011. He then went to work at Stanford University as a postdoctoral scholar from 2011 to 2014. Even in the private sector, Amodei's experience was focused on research. He worked at China's Baidu , leading research on speech recognition from 2014 to 2015, followed by a stint at Google Brain working on deep learning and neural networks, foundational scientific frameworks for today's large language models. He joined OpenAI in July 2016. On the Big Technology podcast in July 2025, Amodei said he got into AI to solve the "almost intractable" and "slow moving" problems of biology. "I think my reason to start a company was that I had worked at other companies and I just didn't feel like the way those companies were run was really oriented towards trying to have that impact," he said, adding that the desire for impact was often used by companies as an insincere ploy to recruit talent. At OpenAI, Amodei is credited with co-inventing reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), alongside Anthropic co-founder, Tom Brown. RLHF is a fine-tuning method used to align model outputs with human needs. That could mean training a model to speak politely or to not offer violent or harmful solutions to problems. Four years her brother's junior, Daniela Amodei, 39, serves as the president and board chair of Anthropic. The Amodeis are both San Francisco natives, growing up in the Mission District, just a few miles away from Anthropic's current headquarters. The pair were teenagers during the height of the dot-com bubble and its subsequent fallout, both attending Lowell High School, a magnet school and one of the most prestigious public schools in the country. After graduating, Daniela went on to study English literature and politics at the University of California, Santa Cruz, earning her degree in 2009. Daniela started her career in politics, working for Matt Cartwright, a Democrat representing what was then Pennsylvania's 17th congressional district, and then moved into tech, taking on various roles in risk management at Stripe for five years.

events.title: Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expect
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? A nuclear treaty and the US’s war on Iran are priority topics for China, Russia, US leaders. But Ukraine is unlikely to be raised. US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed . On Friday, Washington also confirmed Trump’s attendance at the summit, which will take place from November 18-19. list 1 of 4 Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China list 2 of 4 Southeast Asian leaders to meet as Trump visit highlights trade disruption list 3 of 4 Ukraine is running out of options, and Russia knows it list 4 of 4 Ukraine, Russia race to build military satellite networks as war rages on Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, the White House said. But they come amid significant global turbulence: Russia’s war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war on Iran and ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing. “I think what we’ll see is some pretty impressive photo-ops with a lot of really bombastic rhetoric from Trump,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at the UK’s Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. However, he added, the three “collectively or unilaterally, are not able to bring about an end to the conflict in Iran or Ukraine”. So what does each side want and what will be the likely outcome? Each leader has his own priorities, but there are some issues all will want to discuss. A top issue for Russia and the US is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February. The treaty was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals. Russia currently possesses the largest number of warheads, followed by the US and then China, which is rapidly building up its own arsenal. Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. China is understood, however, to be reluctant to join an agreement it was not involved in forming. A senior Trump administration official told Reuters this topic will start the conversation but that “we do not expect to get any kind of agreement”. Officials also say the world leaders will discuss the Iran war , which the US and Israel launched on February 28. While full-scale strikes have, for now, ceased, the conflict remains in a deadlock . After more than 100 days, the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and oil and gas prices are still volatile as ships in the strait continue to face Iranian strikes and seamines. One-third of China’s crude oil supply transited the strait before the war. The conflict is also hampering demand for Chinese exports. Russia, meanwhile, has profited from rising energy prices and recent sanctions relief from Washington amid supply crunches – particularly of diesel. Trade wars and the race to control microchips used to power artificial intelligence are straining relations between Beijing and Washington. Trump hit China with a 145 percent tax hike last year, while Beijing retaliated by imposing 125 percent levies on US imports. Tensions mounted further over China’s restrictions on exports of rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced chips and other technology. The two countries have since reduced tariffs and struck several deals following Trump and Xi’s meetings in South Korea and Washington However, the recent scandal at chip firm Nvidia has prompted the US to allege that China was spying on CEO Jensen Huang. Beijing denies this. It is very unlikely. A Trump administration official told reporters the US president will not bring up Russia’s war on Ukraine, although Kremlin officials previously suggested the conflict could be discussed. China, an ally of Moscow’s, has said the Ukraine war is a European issue. US officials also note that Washington is pursuing peace talks, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting both Ukraine and Russia this week. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” an official told reporters. President Trump has accused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of “not wanting” to end the war, while Kyiv has reiterated allegations that the US has restricted its Starlink satellite connection that allows it to operate attack drones. Trump has also blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices because of its strikes on Russian oil facilities. At the same time, Trump has feted Putin, agreed to allow Russian diesel into global and US markets, and lifted oil sanctions on Moscow. What does each side want from this meeting? For President Putin, the meeting could provide a positive photo opportunity and a platform to project power while sidelining the Ukraine conflict, analysts say.

events.title: Wealthy parents pay $75,000 for Alpha’s two-hour AI school day. Half of its K-8 students missed the math target
events.summary: Alpha School, the network of AI-driven private schools charging parents up to $75,000 a year, has won backers from Silicon Valley to the Trump administration. Its own data show most of its students aren’t reaching the model’s central promise. Only 42% of Alpha students met the network’s goal of learning twice as fast in both math and reading, according to internal data first reported by The New York Times . The findings land as Alpha pushes into public schools, where districts are adopting its software in hopes of fitting more learning into less time. What Alpha promises parents Alpha has no traditional teachers. It employs what it calls “guides,” whose job, according to the company’s marketing materials, is to “make every student feel valued and motivated.” Guides don’t plan lessons or grade homework, Fortune reported in September . The core of the pitch is that students will “learn twice as much as their peers in two hours of academics a day” using TimeBack, an app Alpha markets as an AI tutor. Cofounder MacKenzie Price says the app personalizes and accelerates learning for each student, freeing the rest of the school day for workshops on skills such as public speaking and relationship building. The network has grown fast. A spokesperson told Fortune in September that Alpha had more than 1,200 students. The Times put the figure at about 1,500 across roughly 50 campuses, in line with the expansion plans Alpha announced in August . That pitch has drawn AI optimists. “I definitely think using AI well is a skill in the future, if not the skill, so it’s kind of a disservice not to have that in school,” Sarah Cone, a venture capitalist whose 8-year-old daughter attends Alpha’s New York campus, told Fortune in September. In September 2025, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon toured Alpha’s Austin campus and called its model “the most exciting thing I’ve seen in education in a long time.” LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman have both publicly backed Price and Alpha on X. Even the X account of Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder serving more than 11 years in prison for fraud, praised Price . Where students are falling short Math is the bigger gap. About half of K-8 students at Alpha’s private campuses missed the goal of learning math twice as fast, and roughly one in five missed their reading targets, according to the Times ‘ review of the network’s data. Students who started behind fared worse. About a fifth of Alpha’s private school students scored at or below the 50th percentile nationally in math last fall, and only 37% of that group met the network’s 2x growth goal by winter, the Times found. The two-hour premise is also in question. Guides and parents told Wired that students worked late into the night to meet the school’s goals. One parent of a 13-year-old reading at an 11th-grade level said reaching those goals came with “stress and anxiety.” Former employees told 404 Media that Alpha’s AI generated faulty lesson plans, which internal documents said sometimes did “more harm than good,” and that the company scraped other online courses without permission. Alpha’s model is reaching public schools More than 2,600 public school students in Texas and South Carolina now use Alpha’s platform, according to company documents reviewed by the Times . That is a tougher test: public schools can’t remove struggling students, the Times noted, and they lack the prize incentives Alpha uses at its private campuses. The Houston Independent School District, the largest in Texas, is piloting the software at two schools. Superintendent Mike Miles told the Times that students spent more time on Alpha’s apps than planned, cutting into other activities. He still wants AI in the district’s toolkit, calling it an important tool for students to be “successful in a different world and workplace.” Research points to a learning penalty Alpha’s expansion comes as schools grapple with falling math and reading scores and growing evidence that how students use AI matters as much as whether they use it. A study of 26,811 secondary students in central China found that homework scores rose 18% after students adopted generative AI tools, while closed-book exam scores fell 20%. The OECD’s latest PISA results found that daily AI users scored lower in science than nonusers, while moderate users performed about the same . Professors have told Fortune that students who lean on AI summaries struggle with sustained reading. “Today, if you assign that amount of reading, they often don’t know what to do,” Timothy O’Malley, a theology professor at the University of Notre Dame, told Fortune ‘s Preston Fore in June . “It’s not even an inability to critically think,” Jessica Hooten Wilson, a professor of great books and humanities at Pepperdine University, told Fortune . “It’s an inability to read sentences.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
events.summary: Robot startup Foundation has failed to pay employees since missing its Oct. 30 payroll, angering some workers after its CEO borrowed $4.6 million from the firm last year to buy a luxury home, according to people familiar with the matter. CEO and co-founder Sankaet Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, raising governance concerns among prospective investors. Foundation's widely reported $24 million in Pentagon contracts actually stems from its 2024 acquisition of Boardwalk Robotics, which held some existing government research contracts, the people said. Pathak's previous company, Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of customers without access to deposits. Pathak reportedly took loans from Synapse as it neared bankruptcy. Foundation Future Industries , a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company. The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak , borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said. Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025. A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts . Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation. The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts. "What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview. That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is. Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business. "We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands." Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism. "Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight." Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts." While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets. Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said. Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

events.title: The case of Nvidia and the growing risk of AI and corruption
events.summary: In 2025, the UN Office of Drugs and Crime and the Organization of American States co-convened a panel ( slideshow & video ) which examined whether AI is the biggest corruption risk in history. In November 2026, the panelists’ deepest fears about the AI-corruption relationship came true, but not in the way they expected. The panelists feared that AI would enable corruption by making it easier to launder money, give bribes, or produce disinformation. Instead, they learned that the corruption of AI did not start inside the technology itself but with its leaders, heads of state, government officials, and tech CEOs, steering the direction of AI governance. As we see today, America’s approach to AI governance, using export controls to regulate the supply of AI and its components, is fueling corruption. We utilize Transparency International’s definition herein– the abuse of entrusted authority for private gain. I believe that one company, Nvidia , has become the poster child for corruption in the U.S. Last year, the Trump Administration restricted sales of chips to China under U.S. law out of fears that would provide the Chinese military with an advantage or could undermine U.S. leadership in AI. The now former CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, used flattery and donations to influence the Trump Administration’s AI export policies. And in December, Mr. Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell the H200, an older but still powerful A.I. chip, to China, as long as the U.S. government was given a cut of the sales. (Another company AMD also received an exemption). In so doing, the U.S. gained a financial incentive for loosening controls of AI infrastructure to China However, the Congressional Research Service reported that .”Article I, Section 9, Clause 5 of the U.S. Constitution,prohibits the federal imposition of export taxes and duties (not user fees), and 50 U.S.C. §4815(c), which prohibits BIS from collecting fees for considering or issuing export licenses.” Additionally, last year, Nvidia’s General Counsel, Tim Teter, seemed to interfere in an investigation of Nvidia’s sales to Chinese and Malaysian entities. And now we’ve learned that although senior administration officials such as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were warned about the dangers surrounding Nvidia and its now former CEO, they took no action. This corruption and inaction puts U.S. national security and the American people at risk. While export controls may be useful and necessary, they are particularly vulnerable to corruption because they sit at the intersection of high-value restricted goods, bureaucratic gatekeeping, in customs, business, and trade policymaking agencies, and complex cross-border supply chains. When governments restrict access to lucrative technologies, including dual use items such as chips or AI, they can create massive financial in centives for bad actors to bribe officials or exploit regulatory blind spots to bypass the rules. Export control systems rely on government officials to issue licenses, classify goods, and clear shipments through customs. This concentration of discretionary power allows corrupt officials to solicit bribes in exchange for faster approvals or looking the other way. At the same time, U.S. agencies struggle to coordinate trade, customs, and anti-corruption efforts, which are controlled by different agencies. Export controls also create situations of artificial scarcity and high profits, particularly for dual use items such as AI systems. Some buyers may be willing to pay extremely high prices to receive a limited supply of AI services. Not surprisingly, both competitors of Nvidia that produce high speed chips such as Google, and, as well as Open AI, Amazon , Anthropic , and Microsoft—three of Nvidia’s biggest clients— support legislation that would further limit Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. Finally, export controls often involve opaque national security exemptions. Because export decisions often involve classified intelligence or sensitive defense deals, licensing and procurement processes frequently lack transparency and accountability. Such situations make it difficult for independent watchdogs to spot irregularities However, the Trump Administration fired many inspector generals in 2025, including at the Department of Commerce, along with antiorruption prosecutors. . Given these problems, export controls are not the best tool to prevent our adversaries from acquiring advanced AI systems or chips because they present many opportunities for corruption. Yet Politico h as reported that it is almost impossible for members of Congress to support loosening export controls. Studies have shown such controls are rarely effective. Hence, Congress should weigh a different approach Morreover, current expor t control implementation can harm U.S. economic and technological competitiveness. . While there are no easy answers, , the U.S. should work with its Western allies to to manage technology transfers that might threaten our shared security interests The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage hits governments
events.summary: Tech company says operations restored to all customers and regions affected by one of worst IT failures in years Microsoft has said its service has been fully restored after a massive outage that saw widespread disruption to governments, businesses and public services around the world. The technology company said on Saturday morning it had restored service to the remaining customers affected by one of the worst IT failures in years. On its Microsoft 365 status page, the US-based firm said: “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. “Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.” The outage, which began on Thursday, affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hours-long episode had affected some of their operations. In the UK, where NHS England has a five-year deal to use Microsoft 365, vital public services were hit, with hospital staff resorting to paper records and one union reporting that ambulance services had suffered a “serious impact”. The already backlogged court system was also hit, with juries in some cases being sent home early or prisoners not being sent to court, while at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester staff scrambled to locate a fax machine. In the US, school districts told parents they must reach out by phone or online apps to contact their child’s school, while staffers at the House of Representatives told Politico they had lost a day of work. One detention facility in Colorado said they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees and told anyone needing to post bond for immediate release to do so in person at the jail. In Australia, many people who rely on Microsoft 365 reported being unable to access their inboxes, including at councils, courts and schools. The federal police and Asio, Australia’s national domestic security and intelligence agency, were also affected by the outage. Asio’s director general, Mike Burgess, said the agency’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”. Across Europe, government agencies in the Netherlands, Belgium and France reported problems, with a French municipality instructing citizens to use the phone instead of emailing. In Japan, government email services became unavailable and staff resorted to text messaging. The shipping firm Sagawa Express was unable to accept some online reservations while Taisho, a major pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone. The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies told Reuters that fund management services had been disrupted. Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories. Approximately 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems began at about midday on Thursday in the US and at 6pm in the UK. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives The Washington-based company apologised on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents. It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” after a recent network change. The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when multiple communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. The outage has fuelled concerns in the UK about an overreliance on a small number of tech companies. Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, told the Guardian an outage of this size was usually “the result of some surprising interaction between systems. Each of the systems is normally quite well understood but interactions between them are complex and frequently the cause of large outages like this. “It’s very hard to build a complex system without there being some risk of some failure.” Tim Clement-Jones, a former chair of the House of Lords artificial intelligence select committee, said the widespread outages of vital government services were an “I-told-you-so moment” highlighting Britain’s dependence on US tech. Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science, said: “This problem serves to emphasise the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.

events.title: Three killed in Russia as Ukraine claims US floated NATO membership option
events.summary: Zelenskyy says the US asked for the first time whether Kyiv would cede land to Moscow in exchange for Ukraine’s NATO bid. A Ukrainian drone attack has killed a mother, father and their 24-month-old daughter at their home in Belgorod, a Russian region bordering Ukraine, according to Russian authorities. The deadly attack came on Saturday in Proletarsky, about 20km (12 miles) from Ukraine’s border as Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed the army intercepted 29 Ukrainian drones overnight, including several over the Moscow region. In turn, Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 96 drones from Friday evening, of which 81 were shot down or electronically suppressed as of early Saturday. It reported hits at eight locations and falling debris at two others, while a local power supplier reported outages in parts of northeastern Sumy. Meanwhile, in Friday’s comments to reporters that were under embargo until Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said United States negotiators had asked during this week’s Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, the transatlantic military alliance. Zelenskyy said the question had been raised for the first time but that no concrete offer existed. Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine would not withdraw its troops but could put the issue to a referendum if Kyiv received firm security guarantees, funding for its armed forces and money for reconstruction. “NATO is back on the agenda,” he said. Donbas comprises Donetsk and Luhansk, two eastern Ukrainian regions partly occupied by Russia. Moscow demands a Ukrainian withdrawal from areas Kyiv still controls, while also opposing Ukraine joining NATO, whose members pledge to defend one another. Zelenskyy said on Friday that he would not amend Ukraine’s constitution to make it neutral, arguing the move would not guarantee lasting security. Ukraine has been defending itself, with Western assistance, against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. This past week brought a resumption of US-mediated direct talks between the Russians and Ukrainians, which raised hopes of an early end to the war. However, apart from renewed prisoner exchanges, there appears to have been little progress. European representatives are set to take part in the next round of talks. Zelenskyy said the European Union and NATO are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because … it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations”.

events.title: 'Strangers' author Belle Burden says her divorce left her feeling financially powerless. Here are the habits she's changed after being a 'cautionary tale.'
events.summary: Belle Burden (left) now manages her own finances. The Washington Post This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Belle Burden 2.0 The original cheating scandal of 2026 didn't involve a leather jacket and possible espionage. It was Belle Burden, in her now-viral book, "Strangers," who revealed that her husband of 20 years left her for another woman without any explanation. In the book, Burden — who calls herself a "cautionary tale" — also said that in her marriage, she trusted her husband with the family's financial decision-making, even signing their joint tax returns without reading them. Slowly and gradually, the former corporate lawyer writes that she didn't realize that her husband was putting his investments and bonuses in his name alone, while using her once sizable trust to buy homes for their family — an important point if you know how their pre-nup was set up. Entrepreneur Emma Grede, who encourages women to not be afraid to talk about money in her book "Start With Yourself," sat down with Burden at the Washington Post's Global Women's Summit, held in New York City, earlier this week. Burden explained that she took her hands off of managing her finances because there was a voice in her head telling her that even though she was smart enough to pass the bar, she "couldn't understand the complexities of my financial life, investments and assets, and I think that is cultural conditioning." Grede asked the New York Times bestseller what she's doing differently now that she's begun the next phase of her life , which includes her book being adapted by Netflix. Burden said she's now "fully in control and understanding all of my investments and assets. And I read my tax returns." "I'm fully capable of understanding it … and that the knowledge is so much better than the not knowing, even though that was very comfortable," Burden continued, "it's actually quite joyful to understand and claim your financial life." Even though she knows people cringe when they read about the financial mistakes she made in her marriage, Burden said hearing and reading how women have smartened up after reading her book makes it worth it. "I did not expect that it would be prescriptive in this way or inspire women to change their behavior on money," Burden said at the Summit. "But … if that's my purpose on the planet, I'm really good with that." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Travel chaos continues after the FAA's nationwide ground stop halted nearly 9,500 flights
events.summary: Passengers at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport saw flight-information boards full of cancellations and delays during the FAA's ground stop on Friday. Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images Almost 9,500 flights were canceled after a 4-and-a-half-hour-ground stop for all US flights Friday. The public was "never in danger" during the halt, which was blamed on a communications issue. While flights resumed late on Friday evening, widespread travel disruption is expected for days. Widespread travel disruption is expected across the US this weekend as aviation recovers after all flights in the country were grounded on Friday afternoon. The FAA halted flights nationwide for about four-and-a-half hours after an issue with air traffic control systems,  stranding travelers in airports  and canceling about 9,500 flights. Even with airspace reopened, Friday's closure promises to snarl air travel for days as airlines scramble to get airplanes and crew back in place — and thousands of delayed or canceled passengers back on their way. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said late Friday that the "public was never in danger" during the airspace closure. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference that the FAA system experienced "inconsistency" in its data systems that communicate with airplanes. Because of that, a ground stop was called at 3:54 p.m. ET. He said there had been 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the stop, all of which landed safely using alternative systems. By late Friday night, more than 9,500 flights had been canceled across Friday and Saturday, with more than 8,200 halted on Friday alone, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. Over 1,200 flights on Saturday were already canceled as of Friday evening, though that number is likely to increase substantially as the day goes on. Read more Business Insider coverage of the nationwide ground stop : Nearly 5,000 flights were canceled across the US after an FAA ground stop. Here's what to do if your trip was affected . Trump's transportation chief demands $50 billion to prevent another huge FAA fiasco FAA SMART AI system vendor, Microsoft, says ground stop wasn't their fault Photos show trouble at airports nationwide as FAA grounds all flights 'I called my mom and cried': Passengers describe chaos at JFK during nationwide ground stop Two Canadian airports are bracing for travel chaos to ripple north College football games could be derailed by the FAA ground stop Duffy and Mullin said the nation's air-traffic control system was outdated and blamed Friday's issue on its age. They called for Congress to cough up $50 billion for its modernization — up from the $30 billion previously pitched in September. "I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump, and our new IP switches did not go down," Duffy said. "It's the old hardware that went down." The IP switches are new voice communication systems designed to replace the decades-old analog voice switches that much of the national airspace system still relies on. Duffy and Mullin also said the fault wasn't related to AI or cybersecurity. Mullin said he'd seen "zero evidence" that the issue was a cyberattack or a problem with artificial intelligence, which he dubbed "SI," for the Trump Administration's preferred term, "superintelligence ." Duffy said they were still "working on the details" of exactly what happened — what caused it and how it could be prevented in the future. He said he couldn't guarantee it wouldn't happen again when asked if the traveling public should feel safe when flying in US airspace. That flying public was stranded in airports around the country — checking airport monitors only to see their flights delayed or canceled. Because the events of the day weren't the airlines' fault, passengers would have little recourse for meals or hotels . How the FAA's nationwide ground stop went down Timeline of Friday's key events (all times ET) 3:36 p.m. — US air traffic control begins experiencing issues. 3:54 p.m. — FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all planes. Roughly 7:30 p.m. — Over 4,000 flights have been canceled. 8:15 p.m. — Nationwide ground stop lifted. 10:30 p.m. — Almost 9,500 flights across Friday and Saturday have been canceled. About 20 minutes after the ground stop was ordered, Duffy said it came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." People were quick to question whether SMART, a new FAA AI tool to help air traffic control that started deploying this week, was involved. ASI, the company that makes the SMART system for the FAA, said that Friday's issues weren't "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Duffy also said SMART was not at fault. Mullin said earlier Friday, when asked if the AI system might be related to the outage : "That's what we're looking at." He also said that it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to Microsoft, which had faced massive issues across its services this week. Meanwhile, the FAA had said the ground stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." Three hours after traffic was halted, more than 4,000 flights had been canceled or did not take off, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. By 10:30 p.m., that figure grew to nearly 9,500. As of early Saturday morning, that number remained the most up-to-date. That number includes flights scheduled to depart the US on Friday or Saturday. Chicago O'Hare topped Cirium's list with 205 cancellations, followed by Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson — the world's busiest airport — with 195. More than 100 flights were canceled at major airports in New York, Boston, San Francisco, Dallas, and Denver. Homeland Security said FAA ground stop wasn't a safety issue Mullin said the ground stop wasn't a safety issue. He called it a communications-related issue. He said he didn't want people to assume this is a safety threat to the American people or "another 9/11." Still, many planes had to divert or turn around. Among the flights affected was Delta Air Lines Flight 958, which was traveling from Los Angeles to New York's JFK. Almost four hours into its journey, at 4:11 p.m., the Boeing 767 turned around and diverted to Cincinnati. Another Delta flight, from Atlanta to JFK, changed course over the Eastern Seaboard and diverted to Baltimore. Pilots in the air have a system for these issues Mark Stephens, a retired Delta Air Lines pilot, told Business Insider that pilots have a system for these situations to maintain safe distances from other aircraft and land within their limits. Planes en route during a ground stop can still land, Stephens said, noting that they "continue via the flight plan, and then start using backup methods." He said there are digital tools that can connect them with air-traffic control and their airline's dispatch to obtain routing

events.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
events.summary: Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves. Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up. Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month. These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers. Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines. Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California. The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food. A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices. Truck freight costs are up almost 25% over the past year, the largest annual increase since 2022 and on par with the surge seen during the pandemic-era inflation shock. The big picture: It's unclear how much of the surge in producer prices will be passed along to consumers. But steeper price increases were already showing up at supermarket checkout counters last month. Grocery prices rose 0.4%, the biggest monthly increase in 6 months, driven by higher prices for meat, dairy products and snack foods. Fresh vegetable prices climbed 2%, including a nearly 8% jump in lettuce prices.

events.title: Nearly 9,500 flights were halted across the US after an FAA ground stop. What to do if your trip was affected.
events.summary: People stranded at Miami airport amid the ATC outage on Friday. Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images Nearly 9,500 flights were canceled or halted after a nationwide air traffic control outage on Friday. This is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies. Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled. US airlines are canceling thousands of flights after a rare air traffic control outage affected the US . As of 10:30 p.m. ET, nearly 9,500 flights scheduled to depart the US on Friday and Saturday had been canceled or did not take off, according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. More than 8,200 of those flights were scheduled for Friday; another 1,200 were Saturday flights. Collectively, nearly 20% of scheduled flights out of the US on Friday and Saturday were canceled, per Cirium. The cancellations came after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop around 3:45 p.m. The stop was lifted around 8:30 p.m., but after so many cancellations, flight chaos is nearly guaranteed to stretch into the weekend. If you're wondering what your options are as the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due to the outage would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted. 1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the US Airline passengers have some customer rights in the US. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events, such as weather. That also includes air traffic control delays. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: No phone number. The best way to contact Frontier is via online chat or email. JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers .  Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a winter storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as  Chase's Sapphire Reserve  and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs.  Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim — but it also doesn't hurt to make the claim anyway, even if the answer is no. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). events.title: McKinsey boss Bob Sternfels laid out how companies can prepare for an Nvidia-like crisis
events.summary: Bob Sternfels, global managing partner at McKinsey. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Nvidia scandal holds key reminders for business leaders about how to prepare for a crisis. Boards should imagine and discuss as many scenarios as possible, said McKinsey chief Bob Sternfels. When crisis does strike, thinking about long-term outcomes during the chaos is key, he said. As they watched Nvidia's chaotic week unfold, many board members and executives may have found themselves wondering: "What if our CEO has an affair that gets us embroiled in a reputation-shaking scandal?" Bob Sternfels, global managing partner at McKinsey, has some advice for them. The Nvidia crisis has highlighted the importance of corporate governance, Sternfels said in an interview with Bloomberg on Thursday. It's a reminder to have these discussions and prepare for all imaginable situations so that they're not on the back foot when they arrive, he said. "Having a playbook, even if it's close, is much better than figuring it out in the heat of that moment," Sternfels said. McKinsey, which Sternfels has led since 2021, is one of the world's leading consultancies and advises clients on improving operations, offering guidance on everything from choosing the best technology to implement to handling the unexpected. Sternfels said the best responses to any crisis are long-term rather than knee-jerk reactions to the immediate situation. It's about finding a way to stay steady during the chaos, he said. "There's an immediacy to respond, and you have to cauterize and make a decision, but it also has to be: what are our longer-term objectives? Where are we trying to go?" said Sternfels. On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO. His departure followed days of reports about his personal life, including accusations of a close relationship with someone US officials suspect to be a Chinese intelligence asset and an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Huang's downfall will have ripple effects across the AI industry and raises questions about the impact a single leader can have on a company's success. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday. Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, Huang has spent more than three decades nurturing the chipmaker into a $4 trillion giant. He is known for embracing a flat leadership model, an approach he has credited as key to the company's success. Also crucial has been his geopolitical reach: Huang's Taiwanese roots and deep personal ties to Taiwan's technology sector have been instrumental in building Nvidia's AI supply chain, and he has the US president on speed dial. Many are now asking how Nvidia will fare without its leather-clad, celebrity leader. Sternfels told Bloomberg that navigating the influence of a well-known, public-facing CEO comes down to leadership development , meaning systematically developing generation after generation of leaders so a company is more robust. McKinsey has found a gap in that kind of planning among clients, he said: "Not many companies are really focused on leadership development. They're focused more narrowly on succession planning." Leadership development doesn't just happen at the CEO level, but at multiple levels in an organization, Sternfels added. Whether the board CEO or the CEO of a top team, it's good practice to have people in leadership who can serve as an independent, objective voice in governance decisions and present a counter viewpoint, he said.
