events.title: Eight sentenced to jail over Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili Abu Dhabi hotel brawl
events.summary: A brawl broke out between the two MMA fighters and their team members inside a hotel before a wrestling event. The Abu Dhabi Criminal Court has convicted 10 people over a mass brawl ⁠involving mixed ⁠martial artists Usman Nurmagomedov, Merab Dvalishvili and their teammates at a hotel. The brawl broke out ahead of a wrestling event organised ⁠by Real American Freestyle (RAF), where Usman Nurmagomedov’s brother Umar and Dvalishvili were scheduled for matches against different opponents. list 1 of 3 Salah breaks Egypt scoring record, Tunisia lose to Libya in AFCON qualifier list 2 of 3 Goalkeeper Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel death list 3 of 3 Sabalenka crashes out of season-ending WTA Finals after losing to Svitolina “An Abu Dhabi court has convicted 10 defendants in connection with a brawl ‌inside a hotel and has sentenced them to six months’ imprisonment … along with deportation from the country,” read the announcement from the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department on Friday. ESPN reported that six members of Team Nurmagomedov were sentenced to six months in prison, fined 300,000 dirhams (approximately $81,600) and ordered to be deported after serving their sentences. According to Abu Dhabi-based The National newspaper, former UFC bantamweight ⁠champion Dvalishvili and a friend were fined 50,000 dirhams ($13,600) for “disturbing public security and assaulting others”. Two additional people were handed six-month prison sentences for privacy violations after they filmed the ⁠brawl and published the footage online, the reports added. The court also ordered the confiscation of their phones and deletion of the footage. The brawl broke out on Wednesday when Georgian Dvalishvili, who was scheduled to appear at RAF Abu Dhabi on Saturday, was being interviewed in the lobby of the Yas Hilton. PFL lightweight champion Usman – the cousin of retired MMA legend Khabib Nurmagomedov – and his associates approached Dvalishvili. Videos shared online showed ‌Usman coming in from behind and slapping Dvalishvili, which started the melee. Usman was not scheduled to feature at the RAF Abu Dhabi card but travelled to the UAE capital to accompany his older brother, Umar, who was scheduled to face Urijah Faber. Later on Friday, the event organisers removed Umar from the card, replacing him ‌with ‌Saba Lazishvili, Dvalishvili’s friend who was also involved in the brawl. RAF cofounder Chad Bronstein said Dvalishvili has been released from custody. He remains available for his scheduled match with Marlon Moraes. “I’m pleased to share that Merab Dvalishvili is back with us in Abu Dhabi,” Bronstein said in a statement. “We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the relevant authorities in Abu Dhabi for their professionalism and support.” Dvalishvili posted several videos on social media after the incident and released his personal statement on X, saying: “Just want to let everyone know I have been released, and I am good, healthy and ready to go. “I want to thank everyone in Abu Dhabi for your help in resolving this matter … I do hope that they release everyone; I would not press charges. I want peace and the best for all,” he added. Wednesday’s incident wasn’t the first time Dvalishvili and Team Nurmagomedov clashed. Tensions also escalated in January last year after Dvalishvili defeated Usman’s older brother Umar in a UFC bantamweight title fight. They also had a smaller altercation at an RAF event in Georgia in July.

events.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status
events.summary: An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports. Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year. Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts. The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years. The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break. The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity. Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C. What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control. "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision. The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection. By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally. The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases. Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths. Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness. While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC. How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts. Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year. The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina. Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

events.title: SpaceX not being honest about ‘political’ reasons for slowing Starshield, says Zelenskyy
events.summary: Throttling of Elon Musk’s military-grade satellite system affecting whole frontline, says Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system , saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”. Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones had been in place for five days. They could no longer fly at speeds of more than 161km/h (100mph), he said, with connections at higher speeds lost. As a result, incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones could no longer be intercepted . Ukraine’s own mid-range strikes against military targets in Russian-occupied territory were also severely affected, he said. Speaking to the Guardian and other journalists at the presidential palace in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said he had asked his military leadership to raise the issue with Elon Musk’s company SpaceX, as well as with the Pentagon and the US state department. There was “no clear explanation” as to why Ukraine’s operations were being throttled. He said SpaceX had told Kyiv that there were “no restrictions”. The claim, Zelenskyy suggested, was untrue with problems detected across the “entire frontline”. “There have been discussions with the company at the institutional level. The ministry of defence spoke with SpaceX . They replied: ‘We are not imposing any restrictions.’ They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case,” Zelenskyy said. He added: “The question is not whether we believe them or not. There may be some further checks. But every day, we test this in different directions. Every day, we get the same confirmation. So these are not isolated cases; they are widespread.” Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. It follows a similar issue last month, and coincided with US-brokered talks last week in Abu Dhabi featuring Ukrainian and Russian representatives. The Kremlin insists Ukraine give up the entire eastern Donbas region. But Zelenskyy categorically ruled out giving away further land to Russian “terrorists”. He also revealed that US negotiators, Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and real estate developer Steve Witkoff, had asked if Ukraine was willing to give up the Donbas in exchange for membership of Nato, or Nato-like security guarantees. Details of the proposal were vague, Zelenskyy said. They did not appear to involve US peacekeeping troops on the ground, he added. He said the war could only end with a ceasefire agreement, alongside meaningful security guarantees, underwritten by western partners. Zelenskyy also dismissed an offer by Putin for a “ humanitarian mission” in the eastern city of Kostiantynivka as a ploy. Russia has called for a five-day ceasefire, modelled on a truce last month in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, from where civilians were evacuated. “It’s an absolutely primitive move. Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” Zelenskyy said. He said civilians had already fled the area as fierce street-by-street fighting continued, with huge Russian losses. Zelenskyy said he had proposed repeating the Oleshky truce in nearby Russian-occupied villages and towns in south Ukraine, along the Dnipro River. Putin rejected this. His true goal was to swallow up Kostiantynivka and the Ukrainian garrison cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Zelenskyy said. He also called Russian attempts to discuss Europe’s security architecture – a topic raised last week by the Trump administration – as “concerning”. The Kremlin has called for Nato to return to its pre-1997 configuration, before eastern European countries including the Baltic states joined the alliance. Putin first made this demand in 2021, in the runup to his big Ukraine invasion. Its revival after nearly five years of full-scale war, Zelenskyy said, was an alarming signal, indicative of imperial thinking. “Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact,” Zelenskyy said, stressing: “We cannot turn everything upside down.” Ukraine’s president said his recent conversations with European leaders who met in Dublin had brought tangible results. They included pledges from Denmark to supply ammunition for F-16 jets – used to shoot down Russian drones – as well as energy support packages for Kyiv and other cities. Russia was “betting everything” on its winter campaign, he added. In recent months Moscow has escalated its attacks on Ukrainian cities, in an attempt to make civilians capitulate. The US Congress could pressure Putin to de-escalate by passing laws on sanctions and giving Ukraine weapons, Zelenskyy said.

events.title: Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea
events.summary: Activists dumped rocks off Norfolk coast on site of Burnham-backed project in protest against seabed trawling The giant offshore windfarms backed by Andy Burnham this week may face unexpected stumbling blocks after Greenpeace activists unwittingly dumped about 15 tonnes of boulders on to the site as part of a campaign against seabed trawling in the North Sea. Greenpeace created the “boulder barrier” to safeguard harbour porpoises off the Norfolk coast by dropping giant stone blocks, each weighing up to 2 tonnes, on to the sea floor to prevent a method of fishing known as bottom trawling. The barrier will pose an additional challenge for the green energy developers because most of the boulders were dropped on to the site earmarked for one of the UK’s biggest planned windfarms, known as the Norfolk Vanguard project. Greenpeace began dumping boulders on to the site, without consent from the marine authority, days before the prime minister told the Cop31 summit that the UK would invest £1bn of public money in the Vanguard West and Vanguard East windfarms in what is believed to be the biggest investment of its kind in UK history . The Guardian understands that Greenpeace checked the seabed for any existing cables, pipelines or shipwrecks, but it was not aware of the plans to build the Vanguard East windfarm. The creation of the underwater barrier in one of “the most heavily trawled” areas of the southern North Sea was timed to coincide with the premiere of the BBC’s Blue Planet III documentary , narrated by Sir David Attenborough. Some boulders bear the signatures of celebrities including Simon Pegg and Benedict Cumberbatch, who have voiced marine conservation documentaries, and agreed to support the Greenpeace campaign. However, they are likely to be removed within months after renewable energy developers agreed a £12bn deal alongside the UK government to begin building the offshore windfarm next year. Industrial fishing activities, including bottom trawling, are also likely to move elsewhere to avoid the construction area. The Guardian understands that the offshore wind developer, the German utility company RWE, is in talks with Greenpeace to verify the exact placement of the boulders so that they can update the seabed surveys they began last summer. The company is also investigating any potential impact to the construction of the project or its undersea cables. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning A spokesperson for RWE described its communication with Greenpeace as “constructive” and said the company would “continue to investigate the precise implications” for the Norfolk Vanguard East project. Will McCallum, the co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said any suggestion that the boulders would cause a genuine obstacle was “absurd”. “Anyone familiar with offshore wind in the North Sea knows that energy companies routinely move naturally occurring boulders from the seabed before building windfarms,” he said. “Some of these boulders can be 10 times heavier than those we placed. “Greenpeace has long championed offshore wind and will continue to do so. While we wait for this windfarm to be built, our boulders will provide an essential barrier to destructive bottom trawlers that are decimating the seabed in this protected area.”

events.title: Ukraine, Russia race to build military satellite networks as war rages on
events.summary: Ukraine seeks to break its reliance on Starlink while Russia develops its own satellite constellation for military communications. Kyiv, Ukraine – Looking like a tiny desktop tower with wing-like solar panels, the Obria Nano satellite is a small step that could herald a giant leap for Ukraine’s military. Launched by Himera, a Ukrainian company known for ergonomic military radios, and GomSpace, a Danish small-satellite manufacturer, the first Obria Nano could eventually grow into Kyiv’s own constellation of military satellites, its creators hope. list 1 of 4 Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks? list 2 of 4 Kyiv says Starlink restored as attacks in Ukraine and Russia continue list 3 of 4 Palantir harvests battlefield data that Ukraine pays for ‘with blood’ list 4 of 4 Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on The nanosatellite marks Ukraine’s “first historical step toward establishing resilient and sovereign satellite communications capabilities,” the company said on October 27, almost four weeks after the Obria Nano had reached orbit. In mid-October, Kyiv also signed up two Finnish companies, the Nokia telecoms giant and the ICEYE space startup that owns a “self-illuminating” radar technology for obtaining high-resolution satellite imagery in any weather, to look into developing a network of military satellites. Kyiv’s efforts are rooted in one concern – the nearly total dependence of Ukraine’s military communications on SpaceX, Elon Musk’s satellite communications giant that operates Starlink, a constellation of more than 10,000 low-orbit satellites. On Thursday, the speeds of Starlink and Starshield, its military component operated by the Pentagon, were limited for Ukraine, leading to “significant disruptions” of their operation along the front line, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Before this, Starlink was also disrupted last month. Kyiv realises that “it’s possible to create an absolutely new system, but it will take several years,” Anatoly Zak, a US-based space expert, told Al Jazeera. “In the nearest year or two, Starlink and [its military-grade component] Starshield are absolutely necessary.” Since 2022, Ukraine developed a love-and-hate relationship with Musk, his volatility, shifting loyalties and political demands. “Musk’s mood swings play a significant role,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “There were times when Musk helped Ukraine, and times of very negative reactions.” Ukrainians hailed Musk’s decision to provide Starlink services and modems to Ukraine free of charge. The military, hospitals and government agencies operating critical infrastructure quickly made a backbone of their communications. But in late 2022, Musk refused to activate Starlink coverage in Russia-occupied areas, slowing down or stopping Ukraine’s successful counteroffensive. The world’s wealthiest man also said that Kyiv should remain “politically neutral” in the future, officially cede Crimea to Moscow and conduct United Nations-supervised referendums on Russia-occupied territories. “If you want to understand what Russia has done here, come to Ukraine and you will see it all for yourself,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in response. “And then you will tell me how to end this war, who started it and when it can be ended.” Meanwhile, Russia has reportedly smuggled thousands of Starlink terminals and used them for comms and drone attacks. This February, Musk put an end to the practice by allowing only certified modems to operate in Ukraine. Kyiv’s attempts to find an alternative to Starlink followed the October 14-24 speed limits for Ukrainian drones imposed without prior warning by Starlink and Starshield. Drones and drone interceptors moving faster than 60km/h (37mph) lost signal and could no longer reach their targets. Musk accused the Pentagon of limiting the speed and admitted that the decision was his only after The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had personally authorised the slowdown. Both Musk and Kyiv realise that Starlink and Starshield are the Ukrainian military’s survival tool. When it comes to his highly publicised position towards Ukraine, Musk has to balance his own emotional outbursts and the interests of SpaceX, the crown jewel of his business empire that comprises two-fifths of his net worth, analyst Fesenko said. “If he tries to throw Ukraine under the bus, it may work as very negative advertising for his business, including the Starlink system,” Fesenko said. Russia’s bid to create military satellites Another factor is Russian President Vladimir Putin’s calculated flattery towards Musk – on October 28, he called him a “real genius”. “Putin apparently wants to use the methods he’s used towards [US President Donald] Trump – flattery, unlimited flattery,” Fesenko said. Putin mentioned Musk while talking about Russia’s attempts to create its own version of Starlink.

events.title: Forget the 529. These parents are saving for a future without college.
events.summary: Parents are rethinking their 529 savings plans as AI challenges higher education. Nataliya Konovalova; Matthew Crowson Parents are rethinking how to save for their kids' futures, as AI complicates the value of degrees. Some parents are shifting away from tax-advantaged 529 education savings plans. Others keep funding 529 plans, betting the rules will change in an AI future. When Nataliya Konovalova's sons were babies, she set up tax-advantaged 529 savings plans for them. On their birthdays, she'd tell relatives: no gifts, just contributions. As the boys got older — they are now eight and 10 — she began to change her mind about the value of a college education. Konovalova read stories about degree-holders working at McDonald's , and prestigious fellowships that take students straight out of high school . AI was the final straw. Konovalova had long discussions with her husband, who works in tech, about how AI is tightening the entry-level job market. Ultimately, the couple halved their contributions to the boys' 529 plans. "I honestly don't think they will go to a traditional four-year college," she said. For decades, these tax-advantaged plans have been the bread and butter of education savings. Parents can spend investment gains tax-free, provided the money goes toward qualified education expenses like tuition, textbooks, laptops, room and board, and more. The number of 529 plans across the US has grown 80% since 2010, with the average balance more than doubling since then. But AI is putting higher education to the test . Students use it to cheat and currently face an entry-level hiring crisis after graduation, which many blame on AI. Tech execs say chatbots are better than human teachers, and Silicon Valley-types are pitching AI-ified college alternatives . As AI makes the value of a college degree harder to predict, some parents are changing how they save for their children's futures. Business Insider spoke with six families who are reducing their 529 contributions, moving money into more flexible accounts, or continuing to save while questioning whether traditional college will provide the best return on their investment. Of the 921 K-11 parents polled by Intuit Credit Karma/Harris, more than a quarter said they're rethinking how much they need to save for education, and 15% have already reduced their savings. Even AI's biggest names seem unsure. A mom of two asked Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman whether she should save for college in 2025 . "Probably not," he laughed off, before correcting the record. "I don't know. It's really hard to judge." The parents waving goodbye to 529s David Graham thinks college might still be worthwhile by the time his 12-year-old son finishes high school — but not by the time his 8-year-old twin girls graduate. The 52-year-old retired physician from Billings, Montana, set up multiple savings accounts for his kids. Two years ago, he chose to stop funding their 529s entirely. It wasn't an easy decision. Graham thinks that colleges will struggle financially thanks to declining birth rates. He's watched "learn to code" turn from salient advice to an ironic jab. He likes the hybrid Alpha School model, which leans heavily on AI instruction, and believes that AI tutors will drive down the cost of education. At this point, Graham estimates that his son has $50,000 in his 529, and his twin girls have $15,000 each. While he bets that his kids aren't college-bound, he has the money to fund their degrees if they choose otherwise — and is willing to sacrifice the tax benefits. "If he wants to go to school, I'll just write a check," he said. Michael Reynolds, a certified financial planner from Indianapolis, said that about 30% of the parents he worked with were redirecting some funds away from 529s as they doubt the future value of college. "More and more conversations are happening around: Do we put all our eggs in this basket?" he said. Omar Khan is one doubter. Instead of a 529, the millennial father of two is investing for his children via taxable brokerage accounts , knowing he'll pay tax on the gains. He believes the value proposition for brand-name colleges may fade. Khan wants the flexibility to use that money for whatever his kids' futures look like. Should they go into a technical field, buy a house, or bootstrap a company, they'll be set, he said. To save or not to save Matthew Crowson isn't abandoning his 529 — but he's hoping it'll loosen up. The 39-year-old physician is saving for his two sons, aged 3 and 5. He also has a front-row seat to higher education's AI transformation: Crowson is on the faculty at Harvard Medical School. Crowson said some of his best students don't need to show up for class at all; they can learn on their own using AI tools and then come to him with questions. He expected students to start questioning the high cost of tuition, especially compared to the low cost of a chatbot. Should the college-pocalypse come , the government will need to change the 529 rules. Crowson is anticipating this: He hopes the government will expand the definition of "school" by the time his kids grow up (apprenticeships and continuing education are already qualified 529 expenses). Better yet, he's hoping for a "get-out-of-jail-free card" that lets parents draw down all their funds tax-free, no matter where they spend it. "That's a very cautiously optimistic take," he said. The rules have bent before. In 2018, the government allowed parents to use some 529 funds for private high schools . Six years later, the government allowed parents to roll over some money from a 529 into a Roth IRA tax-free. Parents can now use the funds tax-free on post-graduate courses and certificates, too. "Even if you're not saving exactly for college, there are still other ways to be using that money," said Eric Reale, a New York-based financial advisor. Some AI-enmeshed parents still see the value of a 529 plan. Matthew Seeger, who oversees AI strategy for a software company in Chicago, has been saving thoroughly for his three- and five-year-old kids. He wants to spare them the financial burden that college can be. Even so, he's getting worried about AI's longer-term impacts, especially on jobs. But a whole other group of parents are certain AI abundance is coming — and that college is getting the chop. Yet many of their kids loathe the tech. While 9 in 10 kids have used AI, according to a Common Sense Media report , only 26% think the technology will have a mostly positive effect on their lives. While Business Insider spoke with Graham, the Montana dad who had stopped 529 contributions entirely, his 12-year-old son arrived home. Graham asked: Do you use AI? "No," his son responded quickly, before amending his answer to "every once in a while" and running upstairs. "They actually hate AI," Graham said of his kids. "And I don't let them use the H-word." events.title: A warning for the new Congress: Don’t stop at ‘affordability’
events.summary: It was a night of historic wins for the candidates who understood that “affordability” was at the heart of this election. But the lesson of this election is bigger than the price of eggs and gas, and every candidate – Democrat and Republican – who won should be careful not to miss the point of what voters really want. As Black business leaders who are experts in navigating and building economic opportunity when the system doesn’t deliver, we had a hunch “affordability” wasn’t telling the whole story. So we spent months before Election Day asking voters and confirmed we were right. Through internal polling conducted by Workbench Strategies during July 2026 of 1,400 voters, including an oversample of 400 Black voters, and our two-way texting conversations with voters, we found that they gravitated toward a combination of solutions that provide immediate relief from rising costs and build pathways to help them get ahead. For example, nearly half of all voters chose both caps on medical and prescription costs (45 percent) and increasing wages to keep up with the cost of living (43 percent) as a top-three priority. Black voters were even more focused on higher wages, with 56 percent choosing it as a top-three priority. And over and over again, voters in focus groups conducted by HIT Strategies said that they wanted to take control of their own economic futures and for leaders to remove barriers to opportunity. It was easy to see leading up to the election that candidates who recognized these concerns and built agendas around addressing both affordability and economic opportunity would be rewarded at the ballot box. Now that we can sit with the results of the election, it’s clear that what voters were calling an affordability crisis is also an economic mobility crisis. And now, the newly elected Congress has only 18 months to demonstrate it understands the difference and begin to deliver on both. Yes, lowering prices matters – but that only helps Americans get to the end of the month. Helping Americans really get ahead will take solutions that make it possible to own a home, finance a business, compete for a contract, and turn a lifetime of work into lasting financial security for their children and grandchildren – in other words, it will take building pathways to work, wages, and wealth. This conversation matters for more than economic reasons: our democracy is still on the line. A growing body of research finds links between economic inequality, institutional distrust, and democratic backsliding . If elected officials fail to create meaningful pathways for far more Americans to get ahead – making sure work pays, wages rise, and wealth can be built – they should not be surprised when voters look elsewhere for answers in 2028 and beyond. Nor should they expect trust in our economy, our institutions, or our democracy to rebound on its own. Fixing this requires a bold, affirmative economic plan – and for our leaders to realize they’re on the clock with voters to deliver. The good news is that there are solutions that address both sides of the challenge: actions that can help families manage rising costs today while expanding the pathways that help people get ahead over the long term. Lawmakers should lower costs where families feel the greatest pressure. That means promoting competition in prescription drugs, lowering grocery costs, and expanding proven tax credits that help working families keep more of what they earn. But lowering costs alone is not enough. Leaders must also expand pathways to work, wages, and wealth by increasing access to homeownership, supporting entrepreneurship and small business growth, expanding opportunities for workers to own a piece of corporate profits, raising wages, and ensuring that economic growth reaches communities too often left behind. Finally, leaders must restore trust that the economic rules are fair. That means increasing transparency in concentrated markets, enforcing fair competition, and ensuring tax regulations do not disproportionately reward those who accumulate wealth. If leaders do not take immediate steps to address rising costs and make the country’s founding promise of opportunity a reality for more Black Americans, and consequently all Americans, we’ll continue in a downward spiral: lack of faith in economic opportunity causes lack of faith in democracy, which harms the whole economy. Every leader who won in 2026 should take this warning seriously and signal to voters that they understand the mandate underpinning those wins. The clock starts now. events.title: When Walmart pulls out of town, the stores next door don’t pick up its shoppers — their sales are down 20% a year later
events.summary: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay , while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect : Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop . But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest . What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic. Vivek Astvansh , Associate Professor of Quantitative Marketing and Computational Data Science, Binghamton University, State University of New York ; Preetinder Kaur , Assistant Professor of Marketing, University of Guelph , and Pushpinder Gill , Assistant Professor of Marketing, Toronto Metropolitan University This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. events.title: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
events.summary: On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.” New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms. None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls. According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe? Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.” Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other. In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed. Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, New York, in April. With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia . The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia . Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come. Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year. A commercial launch seemed just around the corner . But deadlines kept getting pushed back .

events.title: My 107-year-old grandmother inspired me to choose an unconventional wedding venue: her senior-living community
events.summary: The author said hosting her wedding at an unconventional location — her grandmother's retirement community — will give her the best chance of having her there in attendance. Courtesy of Catherine Work. My fiancé and I chose our wedding venue specifically so an important guest can be there. We'll be getting married at the retirement community where my 107-year-old grandma lives. I don't see this as a compromise. The venue is beautiful, practical, and meaningful. When my 107-year-old grandmother casually mentioned that she doesn't like getting in and out of cars, I realized I knew the perfect place for my wedding: her retirement community. I didn't grow up in, and don't currently live in, the same place as most of my family, including my grandma. So when I started thinking about wedding venues , I was drawing a blank. Then I realized that the location that would be easiest for everyone was the retirement community I've visited more than 100 times since I was little. The venue has a pond, beautifully landscaped grounds, and plenty of space. All things many people would look for in a wedding venue. But for me, the best part is knowing that the most important guest will be most likely to show up: my grandma. The author says the venue she picked has lots of green space and has a special connection to her family. Courtesy of Catherine Work. It's not a traditional wedding venue, but it has everything I want Maybe you're picturing a gray, sterile environment. This place is far from that. While the community my grandmother lives in may not look like a traditional wedding venue , and there is always a puzzle being put together somewhere, it does have a lot to offer. There's a pond surrounded by flowers, multiple rooms to reserve, and ample parking. There's also the benefit of my grandma being able to get from her apartment to the ceremony in just five minutes. The author said she is hosting her wedding on her grandmother's 108th birthday to make the occasion extra special. Courtesy of Catherine Work. My whole family already knows the location, because they visit regularly. I also have fond memories of the place: the juniper trees out front, taking long walks around the pond, spotting swans and bunnies nearby, and, of course, sitting in my grandma's apartment. It's a place that's already special to me. I know choosing an untraditional location that has probably never hosted a wedding could be risky, but it helps that the wedding will be small and I have so many relatives who live nearby to help. When I proposed the idea to my partner, he immediately said yes. He had visited the location many times and thought it was a great idea. He also liked that we didn't have to search very much to find our venue. Other aspects will be unconventional, too The decision to host my wedding at this unique location has made me rethink what we're actually trying to accomplish with a wedding. Rather than choosing a venue based on what looks impressive in photos or what couples are "supposed" to do, my fiancé and I are choosing a place based on the people we most want there. The rest of our wedding will be equally untraditional: pies instead of cake, I won't be wearing white, and many of the most common wedding rituals won't be part of the day. The author said many of the details of her summer 2027 wedding will be unconventional, including the dress she plans to wear. Courtesy of Catherine Work. Thankfully, my family is on board. Nobody objects to me saying my vows at a senior living community. They all know how much my grandma means to me, and it's a family value to be practical and think about others. The decision is also partially selfish. Not having to look at other venues helps combat decision fatigue, and this location ticks all the boxes I wanted. I wanted a space with lots of nature nearby and something close to the catering company I am working with. I don't see this as a compromise or settling in any way. The wedding is coming up next summer; it's planned for my grandma's birthday, which just happens to fall on a Saturday that works with our schedule. We won't be allowed to have loud music, alcohol, or fireworks because of the location, but I wouldn't have wanted those things at another venue either. I want the day I get married to be low-stress, with my partner and me surrounded by nature and the people we love most. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Apps like DoorDash or Uber Eats rely on a small group of superusers, new federal data shows
events.summary: Food delivery services like DoorDash and Uber Eats rely largely on a small group of frequent users, according to federal data. Bloomberg/Getty Images Delivery services like DoorDash and Uber Eats rely on a small group of superusers, new data show. Many people don't use the services at all, according to the federal survey data. Food delivery companies have reported steady growth with no sign of customers pulling back. Delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats are growing fast, thanks in large part to a group of superusers. Consumers in their mid-40s or younger who order hundreds or thousands of dollars worth of food a year for delivery appear to be a key customer base for the apps, according to data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances. "Those are where probably most of their revenue is coming from," said Jeremy Horpedahl, an associate professor of economics at the University of Central Arkansas. "It's super important for them to retain those customers." The data also suggest that many people don't use delivery services at all, Horpedahl said. The survey is conducted every three years and asks 5,000 households a range of questions about how they earn, spend, save, and invest their money. The latest data was collected in 2025 and released in October. The data suggest that food delivery services don't have as wide a consumer base as other companies in the retail world. Stores like Walmart and Dollar General have warned in recent quarters that shoppers are pulling back on spending or looking for better value on what they do buy. That trend extends to households with six-figure incomes , the retailers have said. At the same time, orders and spending on DoorDash and Uber has kept growing with no similar pullback. "Surveys like this are a helpful snapshot, but they capture only one slice of how people use DoorDash today," a DoorDash spokesperson said. The company has recently added more grocers and other retailers to its platform, the spokesperson added. It is also growing its paid DashPass membership to retain some of its most frequent users. Horpedahl said he reviewed the data by dividing the numbers into spending percentiles, or groups of 10% each. The bottom percentile represents respondents who said they spend the least on food delivery, while the top percentile includes those who spend the most. For the eight bottom percentiles, the median consumer spent $0 on food delivery. That suggests that many people who responded to the survey have never used food delivery apps at all, Horpedahl said. Those in the top 10% of spenders, meanwhile, appeared to be frequent users. The median consumer under 35 in that group spent $1,800 a year on food delivery. For those between 35 and 44, the figure was $2,400 a year. A relatively small group of users willing to spend hundreds or thousands of dollars per year on food delivery could explain why delivery services continue to post strong earnings results while many retailers and brands warn about consumers reigning in their spending, Horpedahl said. "It could be true that 95% of people are pulling back," he said. "But if this group is still spending, that's why Uber Eats could be saying 'Yes, we're still seeing strong revenue.'" The Survey's food delivery question doesn't ask specifically about DoorDash or Uber and includes other services, such as pizza delivery. It also likely misses some customers who have ordered delivery once or twice in the past but forgot about those purchases while answering the survey, Horpedahl said. The results suggest that companies have an opportunity to lure in first-time users, he said. Grabbing some of the superusers from rivals, though, could prove particularly lucrative, Horpedahl said. "If you get just one percent of those going to the other company, that would be huge," he said. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash, Uber, or a similar service? events.title: From Gen X to Gen Z, ‘unicorn game’ GTA VI’s multigenerational pull is a threat to Hollywood’s holiday blockbusters
events.summary: Thirteen years after its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives on Nov. 19. The sixth installment in Rockstar Games’ open-world crime series launches on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and its pull is likely to be felt well beyond gaming, wherever other entertainment competes for the same audience’s time. When Grand Theft Auto V came out in 2013, it generated $800 million in sales in its first 24 hours. It has since sold nearly 235 million units, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive’s latest earnings release . The new game is on pace to crush those numbers. Sensor Tower estimates GTA VI had logged about 12.1 million digital preorders worth roughly $1.18 billion as of the morning of Nov. 13. If it were a movie, GTA VI would already be one of the year’s top-grossing films. Its preorders alone top the roughly $1.01 billion that The Super Mario Galaxy Movie has grossed worldwide, according to The Numbers’ 2026 worldwide box office chart . The stakes for Take-Two are enormous. Analysts estimate the publisher has spent $1 billion to $1.5 billion on the game, as Fortune has reported on CEO Strauss Zelnick’s bet . Earlier this month, Take-Two held its forecast of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for the fiscal year ending in March, saying preorders were running well ahead of its expectations. Fans are clearing their calendars. In a survey of nearly 1,500 users by digital marketplace G2A.com, 29% said they had already requested time off from work or school to play the game. G2A also says its preorders surged 152% week over week in the most recent seven days. That kind of planned absence has fueled viral estimates of what GTA VI will cost the U.S. economy , though economists told Fortune those fears are overblown. G2A founder Bartosz Skwarczek tells Fortune , “GTA VI is much more than a game launch. It’s a global cultural moment that shows just how deeply gaming has become part of people’s lives.” Rival game publishers are steering clear of GTA VI Zelnick has called GTA VI the “ most anticipated entertainment property of all time ,” and the rest of the industry seems to agree. Publishers have largely moved their releases out of its way, leaving this quarter unusually quiet. “This Fall has been the most depressed Fall we’ve ever seen in terms of game volume,” Colan Neese, senior vice president of gaming at research firm Screen Engine/ASI, tells Fortune . “Basically every game that was going to come out this Fall tried to release in September and then it just fell off a cliff in October.” The only other major releases this month look like counterprogramming. Blizzard launched World of Warcraft: Forever on Nov. 4, and Nintendo released its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 on Nov. 5. The former is a PC and Mac game, platforms GTA VI won’t reach at launch. The latter is family-friendly and sells to a different crowd than GTA does. GTA VI’s shadow could stretch into the new year. “It’s going to be really hard for a game to break through in December,” says Neese. “And then the question goes, how long does that shadow last? Does it go into January? Does it go into February?” Neese points to Sony, which pushed God of War Laufey from Feb. 16 to May 20, 2027 , a move he reads as steering clear of GTA VI. Sony’s Santa Monica Studio said the extra time would go toward “putting in the finishing touches.” Why GTA VI pulls in Gen X, millennials, and Gen Z at once Hollywood may feel the squeeze, too. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens Nov. 20, the day after GTA VI, in what Fortune has called a thin November box office that GTA VI is set to test . In December, Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three both open on the 18th, each vying to be the entertainment event of the year. Little do they know that their greatest competitor might be a video game with a vast, multigenerational audience. “Grand Theft Auto VI is a unicorn game because it’s reaching elder millennials and young Gen Xers who grew up on Grand Theft Auto III through Grand Theft Auto V. It was a decade where they released multiple Grand Theft Autos and we all grew up with the game, played it constantly, and then it culminated with GTA V, and then it just went away when we went into our thirties. “Now, we’re in our forties and all of a sudden, we have a new Grand Theft Auto and we’re all excited to ride the nostalgia,” explains Neese. “Then you have an entire generation who only had one Grand Theft Auto game, which is Gen Z,” Neese continues. “They grew up with Grand Theft Auto V streamer culture on Twitch and YouTube. They had Grand Theft Auto V and then Grand Theft Auto Online, which has also brought in early Gen Alpha. “So, you have this really interesting moment where multiple generations are just going to be sucked into this thing.” How Rockstar earned the hype Rockstar has a track record that justifies the anticipation. Between GTA V and VI, the studio released Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018, which has shipped more than 89 million units and remains one of the best-selling games of all time. GTA VI itself was delayed twice, first from fall 2025 to May 2026 and then to Nov. 19, giving Rockstar more time to polish what Neese sees as a landmark. “They purposely built a new engine. They’ve made it incredibly realistic,” says Neese. “They did a lot of research into the Southern Florida setting and culture and tried to bring this world to life. “They put a lot of research, time, and technology into making this and it’s the pinnacle of game creation for humans. It’s like the Sistine Chapel or the Notre-Dame of what a game can be made by humans, and candidly, I don’t know if we’ll ever see the likes of this again.” Former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder made a similar case in Fortune this week, arguing that GTA VI will be the last pre-AI blockbuster video game of its kind . Gaming’s growth leaves Hollywood playing catch-up If 2013 doesn’t seem like that long ago, consider that the gap between then and now is longer than the stretch between the first and last Harry Potter movies, or between Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith and The Force Awakens. It’s also longer than the full runs of era-defining shows like Game of Thrones, Breaking Bad, The Office, Friends, and Seinfeld. Meanwhile, the gaming industry has boomed. Americans spent $60.7 billion on video games in 2025, according to the Entertainment Software Association’s 2026 Essential Facts report , nearly triple the roughly $21 billion they spent in 2013. The same report counts 212.3 million Americans who play video games, about two-thirds of the population. By comparison, 53% of U.S. adults told the Pew Research Center in

events.title: At first, multigenerational vacations helped reduce stress. Now, it's become so much more.
events.summary: The author loves going on family trips with her parents. Courtesy of Nicole Findlay My son is 9, and we've been going on multigenerational trips with my parents since he was little. In the beginning, having extra hands mostly just helped reduce stress while traveling. Being together in new places has meant so much more, though, over the years. Our first multigenerational trip was in Carmel-by-the-Sea. My little guy was only 3 months old. In the beginning, vacationing with my parents made trips feel less stressful. If I ran out of diapers, my dad would run out and get them. If my son got bored, my mom would draw pictures with him. Multigenerational travel meant I had time to put my feet up and drink a cup of coffee before it got cold. Over the years, traveling with three generations has become so much more meaningful than simply an extra set of hands. Now that my son is 9, I feel like we're in a sweet spot: my son still thinks I'm fun to be around, my parents are a huge help, and we all enjoy vacationing together. Over the last decade, we've traveled throughout California and Hawaii, internationally to the UK, and most recently, to Oregon. So far, this is what I've learned about multigenerational travel: Some of the best family time happens when we're doing nothing at all Easily, the best part about multigenerational travel is that my son gets to know his grandparents better. There's something special about waking up in a new place, still in PJs, planning days over pastries, attempting puzzles, playing a board game, and trying to find something decent to watch on TV with a remote that only has a guide button and no streaming apps. We're forced into time together without the typical daily distractions. There's no homework , work calls, or chores to be done. When our family opts for multiple bedrooms and a shared living space, our downtime can be just as fun as our outdoor adventures. We don't have to do everything together My dad and I like to run. My mom loves art, my son is obsessed with toy stores, and my husband likes fresh air and a good book. It's OK to split up. On our most recent trip to Oregon, my son and I rode horses through Ponderosa Pines in the Deschutes National Forest while my parents lingered over coffee nearby. The next day, my dad, son, and I hiked across ancient lava at the Newberry National Volcanic Monument — my mom opted for a stroll along the river and a little shopping. In Hawaii, my parents are happy to babysit so my husband and I can sneak out for Mai Tais. And in the UK, we opt for family-friendly activities, but everyone has the freedom to do their own thing. Nobody feels like they're missing out. We want to spend time together — that's the whole point of multigenerational travel — but we don't have to do everything together. New activities can surprise you My dad loves astronomy, and so does my son, so I bought a stargazing experience in Sunriver that I knew they'd love. The area has been internationally recognized for protecting its night skies, so I anticipated some cool sights, especially after my son climbed a ladder to look through a tall telescope and whispered, "Wow." I followed, and I was completely blown away when I saw Saturn — rings and all. I never would have booked this myself, and I'll never forget it. Earlier that day, my son also got my parents to go down a pretty scary waterslide at a nearby rec center. I only wish I had recorded them flying through the air into the pool. For me, multigenerational travel is about sharing interests , experiencing new things, and seeing new places with the people you love. Whether we're looking at Saturn through a telescope or sitting around a breakfast table in our pajamas, we're making the most of every trip we get to take — although I'm not sure if my parents will go on another waterslide. events.title: South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February
events.summary: The vote, first expected in 2022, will now be held on February 11, according to the country’s election commission. South Sudan has delayed its first-ever presidential and parliamentary elections until February, the latest in a series of delays to the long-sought vote, as ethnic and political tensions deepen. The country’s election commission announced on Saturday that the polls would be held on February 11 next year, instead of December 22 this year. It did not give any reason for the decision. list 1 of 3 South Sudan’s Kiir dissolves government ahead of first national elections list 2 of 3 In maps and charts: South Sudan’s 15 years of independence list 3 of 3 At least 26 killed in clashes along Sudan-South Sudan border region The world’s youngest country, which continues to grapple with violence despite a 2018 peace deal that ended five years of civil war, has delayed the vote at least three times since setting 2022 as its election year. In September, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration. That step allowed the country to move towards elections without first completing a permanent constitution or census – two processes that were previously tied to the transition. But analysts and watchdogs warned that move dismantled a key power-sharing arrangement, consolidating power in Kiir’s hands and raising the risk of renewed widespread conflict. “This amounts to a constitutional coup through legislative reforms,” Yasmin Sooka, chair of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, said in October. “Whether elections take place or not, South Sudan will still need an inclusive political settlement, protection for civilians and institutions capable of preventing further violence,” she added. Kiir’s government forces and followers of detained former Vice President Riek Machar have been involved in escalating, deadly confrontations in recent months. Other ethnic tensions and cattle-rustling battles have also complicated the picture in one of the world’s poorest countries. South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, but Kiir’s and Machar’s forces fought a civil war from 2013 to 2018 that killed at least 400,000 people. Machar has been under house arrest since last March, accused of crimes against humanity. Thousands mobilised for registration drive Under the new election timetable, voter registration is due to begin on Saturday, November 14 and continue until November 28. A 45-day election campaign period will run from December 27 to February 9, followed by a one-day silence period before the February 11 poll. Gabriel Bol Deng, chairman of the National Elections Commission, said a total of 3,161 registration centres have been set up across the country, with more than 22,000 staff recruited for the operation. According to the World Bank, about 90 percent of South Sudan’s 15 million inhabitants have no state-recognised identification, complicating their registration. Such people, particularly in rural areas, will be identified by community leaders and issued an “identification form” enabling them to vote, Deng said.

events.title: 3,000 flights cancelled as FAA ground stop chaos stretches into 2nd day
events.summary: The chaos from the FAA's nationwide ground stop lingered into early Saturday morning, with thousands of flights cancelled as airlines played catch-up. Why it matters: Millions of travelers will find themselves inconvenienced over what the government says was simply old technology that couldn't keep up with modern upgrades. Driving the news: As of 5:15 a.m. ET Saturday, nearly 3,300 flights into, out of, or within the United States were already cancelled for the day, per FlightAware . Nearly 1,000 flights already had delays. Between the lines: The most heavily impacted airports were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, New York's JFK and Boston Logan. Among the major airlines, FlightAware's data showed Delta more affected than United or American. Zoom in : The ground stop wreaked havoc on college football in particular, with many schools unable to travel to their game locations. ESPN reported a number of high-profile match-ups were postponed to either late Saturday or Sunday as a result. What to watch: Whether Congress responds to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's request for $50 billion in emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system. This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum 5 hours ago FAA lifts ground stop after hours-long delays snag travelers 14 hours ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 16 hours ago This year’s bug count just passed 100K 16 hours ago Meatbags suck at spotting lying LLMs, so let AI narc on itself 16 hours ago The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service.

events.title: A market sell-off and a career-changing call: Inside Jake Woodson's first day as a Goldman partner
events.summary: Jake Woodson, 34, is one of Goldman's youngest new partners. Goldman Sachs Jake Woodson, a former Rising Star of Wall Street , is one of Goldman's youngest new partners. After a chaotic day, Woodson celebrated with colleagues at a pub and had a quiet dinner with his mom. The trader brought Business Insider inside the big day and shared what he plans to do with the title. Thursday, November 5, was among Jake Woodson's more chaotic days as a trader at Goldman Sachs. AI stocks were plummeting after the midterms, all three benchmark indexes were falling, and, in the middle of it all, Woodson's phone was ringing with one of the most important calls of his career. Everyone on the trading floor went quiet as Woodson, 34, said hello to firm president John Waldron, who congratulated him on being promoted to partner, Goldman's highest-ranking title outside the C-Suite. Woodson, who oversees trading in leveraged corporate debt and loans and was previously one of Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street, is the second-youngest among the 109 executives who earned the promotion this year. "It was high-fives and hugs, and then right back to trading for the rest of the day," Woodson said early the next week, adding that, though his memory of the moment is foggy, he thinks colleagues on the leveraged finance credit desk applauded. His mom was at the center of the day Woodson said he took a few minutes during the work day to call his mom, dad, and brother. He rang his teary-eyed mom first, partly since he'd flown her to New York from his hometown outside of Vancouver, Canada. "I flew my mom out because I figured either I'm not going to make it and I could use a shoulder to cry on, or I really want her there to be a part of it," Woodson said. "I've lived a six-hour flight from my family for 12 years, so it's nice to be able to show them it was worth it." His mom joined Woodson and Goldman's larger credit business that evening in the private room of Monk McGinn's, a pub near the office. She mingled with around 50 internal colleagues and 20 clients who came, meeting some of the people who have defined her son's life for more than a decade. None of Woodson's family works in finance, and he said his mom doesn't know much about his job beyond the fact that it happens at Goldman, so it was special to bring her into his world. The two of them ducked out of the pub earlier than most to have a quiet dinner at Woodson's apartment, FaceTiming his dad and brother in Canada. Woodson celebrated again at a dinner with friends on Friday night, before his mom flew back to Vancouver and he drove to the Catskills alone. He spent Saturday by a lake, breathing air more similar to that of the mountains in British Columbia than of Tribeca. How he got there Woodson didn't always expect to end up at Goldman, even though he studied finance in college. He grew up in a suburb 45 minutes outside of Vancouver and went to the University of British Columbia rather than the Ivy League schools that tend to dot Wall Street resumes. "If you were a betting person, you probably wouldn't bet that there would be a Goldman partner coming from that suburb," Woodson said. He was accepted into UBC's Portfolio Management Foundation, a program that provides hands-on training in investing and finance to a small group of students. That program, with its strong alumni network and ties to Goldman, changed his life more than anything else. Woodson joined Goldman in 2014, starting in investment-grade private credit. He was a distressed credit trader during the pandemic, and, as the head of US distressed credit trading, steered his team through the 2023 banking crisis, before becoming the head of leveraged finance trading this fall. The trader feels some responsibility for representing those who don't start as interns , or come from a target school, or tick most of the other stereotypical finance-kid boxes. He said he's one of many at Goldman who want to ensure that the firm continues to invest in a range of young talent. Continuing to execute When he was one of those younger people, Woodson probably would have expected making partner to feel like a final, grand accomplishment. "It's almost the opposite. It's just the beginning of growing into this role and continuing to operate at a high level," he said, adding that most focused on strengthening his team. Balancing the daily demands of trading and managing people "how they deserve to be managed" will likely become a bigger challenge, Woodson said, and may just demand working more hours . Woodson is one of the rare leaders who is simultaneously respected and liked, a former boss told Business Insider last year. Part of that, Woodson said, comes from treating people, whether internal colleagues or clients, kindly and well, even when it seems disadvantageous in the short term. "It was instilled in me by my mom and maybe Canadian culture that treating people the right way over time is the right thing to do for a number of reasons. It's the right thing to do morally, but it also tends to lead to better outcomes," he said. Beyond setting a good example, his mom also gave him one of the best gifts he received: appropriately cheesy, multicolored, six-foot-tall balloons. Read the original article on Business Insider
