events.title: Rivian's spinoff thinks America's $51,000 average car price creates an opening for e-bikes
events.summary: Also, a Rivian spinoff, is selling the launch edition of its consumer bike. Amber De Vos/Getty Images for ALSO America's car prices are at a record high. Also, a Rivian spinoff thinks its e-bikes could be an antidote to the US's SUV obsession. Bringing a full-size vehicle to the grocery store is "like we're using a 747," the president said. Cars are expensive . So, why not drive more two-wheeled options? That's what Also, a spinoff from EV-maker Rivian, is trying to convince customers. After months of delays, the company has begun delivering its $3,500 to $4,500 TM-B e-bikes to customers. "The bike is almost like a Trojan horse for what's coming," Chris Yu, the cofounder and president, told Business Insider during a sit-down interview. As cheap new cars keep disappearing from the US market and the average vehicle transaction price hovers above $51,000, several companies see an opportunity with small vehicles. Toyota, for example, is bringing a tiny kei truck to the US market with a max speed of 25 mph. Fiat's golf cart-like Topolino launched this summer. Business Insider has also spoken to several Slate Auto early adopters who plan to use their $24,900 trucks as around-town cars. Also thinks you can accomplish the same trips on a bike. Yu's main argument: Around-town transportation should take a page out of the aviation sector's book. There's a wide array of plane types that perform very different tasks — but on American roads, DoorDash deliveries, school drop-offs, and hourslong trips are all accomplished with the same vehicles. That's "like we're using a 747" to go shopping, he said. Yu's vision isn't a replacement for the ever-popular SUV. Instead, 10 years in the future, the perfect garage will have a family SUV for long-haul trips, an e-bike for school drop-off, and a yet-to-be-announced Also product that could accomplish a family's grocery run autonomously. Also began as a skunkworks project inside Rivian before rolling out as a stand-alone company. It's promising software-heavy products, including the TM-B, which gets a touchscreen, removable battery, and pedal-by-wire drivetrain. The company partnered with DoorDash this year to develop and deploy autonomous delivery vehicles, and said its recent $150 million funding round would help it develop multiple autonomous vehicle types for moving people and goods. Getting that first proof point on the road has not been easy. Also missed its original spring delivery target for the TM-B, and customers only began receiving the bike this fall. Yu said the company was squeezed by surging demand for memory, chips, and high-performance circuit boards — all components used in AI servers and robotics. He said the delays taught ALSO to communicate more regularly with its reservation holders. "Our customers called us out, and rightfully," he told Business Insider. "People care. I remind employees all the time, it's an incredible privilege for us to have a bunch of people care; there are so many companies that don't have a Reddit audience." events.title: Nvidia’s AI boom created a $9 billion foundation led by Lori Huang. Here’s where the money has gone.
events.summary: The Huangs run a $9 billion family foundation. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Lori Huang is the president of the $9 billion Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. She and Jensen Huang created the foundation in 2007, and have since focused donations on education. The foundation's fate remains unclear after Jensen's affair, but history offers some clues. Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia, but there's still a big question over what comes next for the $9 billion foundation that's led by his wife, Lori. The couple established the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation in 2007, when it listed $13,000 in net assets and made zero donations, according to a tax filing. It named Lori Huang as president and Jensen Huang as CFO and secretary, neither of whom earned a cent from their roles. Nearly a decade later, the foundation's assets have ballooned to a multibillion-dollar fund, growing alongside Nvidia's power and profits. Now, the foundation's fate is unclear after Jensen Huang's extramarital affair and possible foreign influence scandal. History may offer a clue. After Bill and Melinda Gates divorced, they initially remained co-chairs of the now-$92 billion Gates Foundation. Melinda Gates resigned in 2024 and received $12.5 billion from Bill Gates for her own philanthropic work. Like its president, the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation keeps a low profile, boasting no website or list of employees. Here's what we know about the foundation, and where it's been putting its money. Oregon, a university with special meaning The charity reported its first donation in a 2008 IRS filing: $40,000 to Stanford University for a building fund. Since then, donations have grown exponentially in scale and scope. Between 2023 and 2024, the most recent available tax returns, its net assets nearly tripled from around $3.34 billion to $9.13 billion. From the start, the foundation has focused in part on Oregon State University, where the Huangs met as lab partners in an electrical engineering class. In 2024, it committed around $30.5 million to the university across three donations, according to a filing. A 2022 press release from the school said the foundation supports "higher education, public health, and STEM initiatives across the US, alongside local community organizations in the San Francisco Bay Area." The foundation uses a fund favored by the wealthy In 2024, the foundation donated some $126.3 million, with around 65% going to a donor-advised fund , a type of account that lets donors immediately get a tax deduction and advise on where to direct the money. Donors, like the Huangs' foundation, don't report their gifts to individual organizations on tax returns, but to the donor-advised fund itself — in this case, some $82.5 million to Schwab Charitable Fund, since rebranded as DAFgiving360. DAFs have become increasingly popular with the wealthy in recent years and, unlike private foundations, don't have payout requirements. The Huangs have supported mental health causes The foundation has also donated nearly $11 million to Crisis Text Line, which provides free mental-health support, and around $1.68 million to Mental Health Innovations, a charity that uses digital innovation to support mental health. The Huangs have also supported other causes: more than $516,000 to the hunger-focused group Second Harvest of Silicon Valley; $100,000 each to Doctors Without Borders and a college for adults with developmental disabilities; and a combined $95,000 to other organizations. Tax filings for 2025 aren't yet available, and won't shed light on how the foundation manages the current scandal. Lori Huang hasn't commented publicly on the future of her role as president, or anything else related to her husband's reported infidelity and resignation. events.summary: World number two Sabalenka’s campaign at the WTA Finals came to a disappointing end after she failed to the reach the semifinals of the season-ending championships. Elina Svitolina overwhelmed Aryna Sabalenka in the deciding set to seal a ⁠6-3, 3-6, 6-1 upset on Friday and reach the semifinals of the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells, where she will face Linda Noskova. Svitolina absorbed and redirected Sabalenka’s power effectively, breaking the ⁠Belarusian six times before sealing her first victory over her opponent in more than six years with a forehand winner on her fourth match point. list 1 of 3 Goalkeeper Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel death list 2 of 3 ‘Sandpapergate’: Warner accuses Cricket Australia of ‘cover-up’ list 3 of 3 Salah breaks Egypt scoring record, Tunisia lose to Libya in AFCON qualifier With the win, Svitolina improved to 2-6 against Sabalenka in their career meetings. “It was a bit of a roller-coaster match,” Svitolina told reporters. “I played well in ‌the first set but lost a little bit of rhythm. She played well in the second and served much better. I was really happy with the way I could come back in the third after losing the first game.” The Ukrainian again did not shake hands with Sabalenka after the match, maintaining her policy of not doing so with Russian and Belarusian players following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine . Svitolina, the 2018 WTA Finals champion, will face Noskova on ⁠Saturday for a place in the final. The defeat ended Sabalenka’s season ⁠on a disappointing note. The second seed won Brisbane International in January and then Indian Wells and the Miami Open in March to complete the “Sunshine Double” but did not claim another title after that. Sabalenka also surrendered the world number one ⁠ranking to Elena Rybakina at the US Open. She had entered the season finale among the favourites after Rybakina withdrew on the eve of ⁠the tournament because of illness. Sabalenka declined to speak to the ⁠media following Friday’s loss. Shnaider, Andreeva’s friend and doubles partner, replaced Karolina Muchova, who ‌withdrew before the final day of round-robin matches with a gastrointestinal illness. Andreeva had already secured her place in the semifinals before facing Shnaider and will meet American Jessica Pegula on Saturday. The eight-day, $10m ‌tournament was moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells Tennis Garden due to the United States-Israeli war on Iran . The event will be played in Charlotte starting next year.

events.title: I'm Microsoft's ex-VP of HR. Not all workplace romance is a mistake — but it can get messy quickly.
events.summary: Chris Williams Chris Williams is a former VP of HR at Microsoft and an executive-level advisor and consultant. He writes that mixing work and romantic relationships is complicated; he met his wife at work. While Nvidia's recent turmoil is an extreme case, mixing business and romance gets messy quickly. The recent turmoil with the former CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang , is an extreme example of the danger of romantic relationships at work, especially extramarital ones. Add in allegations of international espionage and cutting-edge technology angles, and you have a world-class scandal — at the root of which is a tale as old as time: Mixing business and romance is complicated. I'm the former VP of HR at Microsoft , and I've also been happily married for 43 years to someone I met at work. I understand why one's job is a place to meet people, and I reject the assumption that all workplace romance is a mistake. I've seen it work well, but those are the exceptions — it also gets messy quickly, even with the best of intentions. Consider the outsiders Relationships are hard enough without the challenges of work. Add in performance evaluation, promotions, and payroll, and it quickly makes for a complex soup that gets bitter because of the subtlety and judgment involved. I know this complexity firsthand. As a software development manager earlier in my career, I managed someone and worked for their husband, the CEO. The arrangement was set up to avoid having her work directly for her spouse, but it left me squarely in the middle. I gave her a glowing performance review ; she criticized my embellishment. On her next review, I was honest and direct; her husband rebuked me and asked me to change it. There were other, less direct examples of how the business-related relationship affected everyone around it: Did her colleagues refrain from criticizing her work because of who her husband was? Did her arguments in product discussions always win? People outside the relationship may have modified their behavior in ways large and small, and that impact is almost always unknown or uncertain. Reporting line isn't the key Relationships between a person and their direct or indirect manager are a problem; that's why most companies explicitly prohibit that. But influence spreads well outside the reporting chain of command. Of course, at the CEO level, there is no role that is outside the line of reporting, making any internal affair problematic. In my career, I've seen this happen with even the best of intentions — even with everyone, including HR, being aware of a relationship, with it all in the open. Despite the most earnest statements from senior leaders reinforcing the need for fair treatment, honest appraisal, and open communication about their partner, the relationship has an impact. Someone in a relationship with a senior manager wields power, even unintentionally. The relationship can also have a chilling effect on others, or draw unwarranted scrutiny and criticism because of jealousy or concern over lax standards. HR can't always expect honest answers about the impact. They may try to investigate or uncover bias or other impacts and run into roadblocks. Often people won't admit it, or worry that HR is not an objective observer in the situation. After all, they work for the company. It's a clear no-win situation. Good intentions are not enough I've seen very mature and respectful relationships at work handled well; I'm living proof of that. My now-wife and I worked for a company that had a policy against all in-company dating. We were peers; her team used the computer systems I managed. We never left work at the same time or told anyone we were dating. Yet I can still hear the joking my wife got when her colleagues wondered aloud if her printouts came out faster because I was in charge of the printer. These days, the very best and most mature senior leader can bend over backward to ensure that their partner gets no special treatment. They can recuse themselves from, and request outside review of, all decisions regarding their partner. They can be the most responsible leader possible. But they can't control the impact on others. They can never know for certain how others will see it or what others will say, or not say. The relationship will always have the potential to taint any decision that involves judgment, which all the most important decisions do. Compensation , promotion, and performance are all judgment calls — the relationship has the potential to color them all. Even worse, if the affair is extramarital , it comes with a host of other concerns. There are wide-ranging impacts on company perceptions, internal morale, and even blackmail and other risks. It changes from being ill-advised to being potentially catastrophic. Departure is the cleanest break The only clean break is for one of the people in the relationship to move on — to go work for some other firm, but that isn't always straightforward. If your spouse is a senior executive, there's impact. Suppliers, competitors, or unrelated companies can see and want to leverage that influence. But at least the direct possibility is removed. The junior person doesn't have to be the one who leaves. Often the senior person has better job prospects. So it shouldn't be taken for granted that the junior person is the one to go. But the cleanest solution is that one of them should go. Romance is not the problem Romance in business is hard to avoid completely. People are side-by-side for hours at a time. Relationships can and will happen. And I can say from personal experience that they can end well. But they often get complicated, especially when authority is in the equation. My recommendation is strong: Separate work and personal lives as quickly and cleanly as possible. Don't ask everyone else to make way for your relationship. They often can't. events.title: I spend 2 months in Italy every year with my kids. I love how differently children are raised there.
events.summary: Marcela D'alterio started spending two months in Italy because it was cheaper than summer camp. Courtesy of Marcela D'alterio Marcela D'alterio is a 43-year-old mother of two children aged 7 and 5. She said Italy offers a better quality of life for children during the summer. Financially, she said it is cheaper for her to live in Italy for the summer than in New Jersey. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Marcela D'alterio . It has been edited for length and clarity. Five years ago, my husband, our two young children, and I decided to spend two months in Italy over the summer . My husband is from Italy, and his family was still living in a small town in the south of the country, in the Naples region . That summer, I quickly discovered that the quality of life in Italy was much better than in the US — and significantly cheaper. Ever since that initial visit, we've been living in Italy for two months every summer. We feel part of the community Everything in Italy is geared toward community. People live in each other's pockets, and being around other people is simply part of everyday life. Here, children are active members of the community . We're often out with friends late into the evenings. Rather than putting them to bed and finding a babysitter, they come along with us to everything we do. They aren't expected to be kept hidden away. Marcela D'alterio's husband is Italian. Courtesy of Marcela D'alterio They've learned to interact with people who are different from them, such as older people and children they meet on the street who don't speak English . Life is simpler in Italy In Italy, my kids spend two months of the year outside, in the sun and in the water, with friends and family. I know that so many children and teenagers in the US are struggling with their mental health , and I often wonder if part of the solution might be as simple as getting outside in the sun and talking to people. My kids don't have phones or game consoles . Their fun happens in nature and starts with their imaginations. When we do have special days out in Italy as a family, the cost is much cheaper than in the US. One of our favorite things to do is visit beach clubs, which cost us about $16 for the whole day. All the beaches near us are free to enter and park at. I want my kids to be global citizens Growing up in South America , I have always believed it is important for my children to understand that the United States is not the center of the world. I don't want my children visiting other countries one day and being difficult because their food or drink order isn't prepared the way they would have had it in the US. I want them to appreciate other cultures and understand how people in other parts of the world live. By living in Italy for a significant amount of time each year, they are learning that the world is much bigger than the US. Once based in Europe, we can easily access other countries, as flights are relatively affordable. So far, we've been to Spain and England and have explored other regions of Italy . It's cheaper than staying in the US A couple of years ago, we started thinking about putting my kids in summer camp instead of going to Italy for the summer. But then I started doing the math. Camp for both of my boys would cost us $4,400 for the summer. That figure doesn't take into account the cost of any of the trips or additional activities offered. Although the camps keep them busy, most activities take place inside buildings rather than outside in the sun. When they're not in camp, we would also pay a fortune during the summer to entertain our kids. Just going to the closest beach — which you'd assume would be a cheap day out — costs $15 per person to get onto the beach and $30 to park. Here in Italy, we don't have to pay for our kids to have a memorable summer. The beach, the outdoors, and the community give them the best two months of their lives every year. I can work remotely, as can my husband, so we can continue earning money while we're here. We use credit card points to pay for our flights. For the first three years we came, we rented an apartment, and it cost us about $3,000 for the two months — less than the cost of summer camps. But two years ago, we decided to buy a property instead, based on the fact that we knew we'd continue to come every summer. For us, coming to Italy every summer isn't just about giving my kids a better quality of life — it's a smart financial decision too. We'd be spending a similar amount during the summer if we stayed in America. We'd like to retire in Italy My husband and I are both working toward early retirement in Italy — we love it that much. Once we have a passive income stream we can depend on — about $5,000 each month — we hope to live in Italy permanently. For now, spending two months there every summer gives us a little taste of the life we hope to have one day. It's become more than just a summer holiday for our family — it's a way of life that gives us more time together, a stronger sense of community, and a quality of life we simply don't want to give up. events.title: Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for work
events.summary: How long will it take? What challenges will they face? Series to shine light on one of biggest crises facing UK ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers Britain is at risk of creating a lost generation. Across the country, almost a million young people – one in eight – are struggling to make the leap from school to the world of work on a lasting basis. Before the landmark Alan Milburn review , which is expected on Tuesday, the Guardian is launching a new series to chronicle the lives of eight young people battling to get a start on the career ladder. The eight, drawn from across the country, will share their stories of jobseeking in uncertain economic times, after the chaos of the Covid pandemic during their final years of education and with AI now upending the jobs market. The series comes as Andy Burnham promises to restore hope for the next generation by helping more young people into work, with his government pushing to tackle the rise in the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to the highest level in a decade. Each participant in the series will offer reflections on their dealings with employers and the welfare state. The youngest is 20 and the oldest 26 – just outside the age range used to compile the official statistics, but critical to include as the revolving door on insecure work can have a lasting impact well beyond early adulthood. The long-term scarring effects from being Neet can be profound. For those who reach the age of 24 without ever having worked, even if they re-enter the jobs market successfully they stand to lose up to £300,000 in earnings over their lifetime as a result. For many the experience is one of endless job applications, rejection letters and outright ghostings by employers. Exacting a heavy financial and emotional toll, it is a situation made worse in a status-driven social media age. The toll on mental health is a recurring theme for those feeling as if their adult working lives are yet to start. Many also feel guilt and shame around the fact they are still living at home and relying on parents. Frances, 25, from London, said: “I feel unbelievable guilt given my academic and general life chances, but I can’t even seem to get seasonal work as a retail assistant or bar worker.” Alice, 24, from Bristol, said: “There have been a couple of occasions where I’ve not been able to sleep. I’ve cried in the middle of the night and just thought: ‘I don’t want to do any of this.’ Every setback is tricky to pick yourself back up from.” On Tuesday Milburn will publish his final official report into young people and work. Handing recommendations to the government, the former Labour cabinet minister will warn of a structural failure by the market and the state that has sent the number of young Neets soaring to a million. Setting out his report as a fork in the road moment for Britain, Milburn will call on ministers to shake up the benefits system while ramping up employment, alongside education and health policy changes to help more young people into work. In the Guardian project, many of the young people involved are on universal credit. Some have a small amount of insecure work – none have found meaningful work on a sustainable basis. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning They have a wide range of educational backgrounds – from one with degrees from both Oxford and Cambridge Universities, to another who did not achieve maths or English at GCSE. Far from the caricature of a workshy, snowflake generation, for most their ambitions are similar to that of their parents and grandparents – wanting to get on in life – but they face a time when living costs are spiralling, getting on the property ladder is tough, and where working hard is no-longer a guaranteed route to prosperity. Aamir, 25, from London, said: “The universal credit people told me I’d done everything right. You can do everything right and still lose. I feel like the social contract is broken in Britain.” For Burnham’s government the focus will, however, go beyond reinjecting a sense of hope. By getting more young people into work, the ambition is to boost Britain’s economy and to ease the pressure put on the public finances by a rising benefits bill. With so many Neet young people, employers miss out on new recruits, and businesses lose out on an army of potential consumers for their goods and services. For the state, there are big costs attached to a weak economy and the cost of supporting those out of work. Milburn estimates the cost of Britain’s youth jobs crisis amounts to £125bn a year. But for employers there will also be a need to be change their approach to supporting young jobseekers, particularly for those with health conditions, disabilities or additional needs.

events.title: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores that will price essentials 30% below retail — and bodegas are fighting back
events.summary: New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses . What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see. That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide. How the plan will work New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all. While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices. In this respect, the stores offer a “ public option ” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives , like public schools and city hospitals. Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable. At his May announcement , Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” A fresh form of intervention Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program , known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets. This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “ the submerged state .” Bringing the state into the open Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate. Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business. events.title: Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush
events.summary: In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of GPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d launched his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial users at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites. The big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning new deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.”  At the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. In early 2024, the board was searching for its third leader in five years. The sitting chief agreed to depart when Bitfarms named a successor, but in May—believe it or not while still CEO—instead filed a $27 million suit for “wrongful termination and breach of contract,” plunging this Canadian exemplar of all-green, hydro-driven Bitcoin mining into legal warfare. Pounded by a sharp drop in the token’s prices, Bitfarms’ stock was languishing, and a rival pounced. Two days after the board fired the CEO, Riot Platforms unveiled a hostile $930 million takeover bid for Bitfarms at a lowly $2.30 a share, 75% below its peak in late 2021. After Bitfarms installed a “poison pill” defense, Riot launched a website dubbed “A Better Bitfarms” trashing allegedly poor corporate governance, and demanding the departure of the co-founder named as interim chief. The board tapped Gagnon to both quell the war versus Riot, and pursue the strategy of total transformation he’d been advocating. In July of 2024, Gagnon took the helm, and over the next few months, helped broker an agreement where Riot named a director of its choice, and the co-founder left the board. Riot halted its attack and has since sold its shares. While battling for Bitfarms’ independence, Gagnon kept his sights locked on engineering the Big Pivot. He describes the mission as “pursuing a strategy of steering the business away from Bitcoin mining, and taking it over to a pure energy infrastructure play in support of AI and high-performance computing. We’d shift our focus entirely to addressing the defining constraint of the most important technology of our lifetime.”  The venture needed a rebrand, so Gagnon picked “Keel” to evoke the structural backbone of a vessel that, as he says, “provides stability and converts energy into forward motion,” a reference to the stable long-term leases that he expects to provide a smooth and lucrative course versus the storms he encountered in Bitcoin. He’s now attempting to pull a hat trick seldom seen in the corporate world, the total reinvention of a large enterprise, including in product and nationality, on a crazy-rhythm beat. On April 1, 2026, the franchise was reborn as Keel Infrastructure and changed its domicile from Canada to the U.S. The photo on Gagnon’s X profile reprises the nautical theme, adding a whimsical accent. Gagnon grins from a porthole-sized frame, sporting his usual oversized rimless glasses, and a gold-braided yachtsman’s cap displaying his user name, “Captain Keel.”  Buying beer instead of Bitcoin Now 37, Gagnon is making by far his biggest wager yet in a career that careened from mining Bitcoin in remote oil patches by rescuing flared natural gas to rehabilitating some of the world’s dirtiest energy sites under the banner of AI.  Gagnon is the son of two American parents who settled in Hong Kong, where he attended international grammar and high schools that offered lots of, as he puts it, “Mandarin as a second language courses.” He gained a bachelor’s degree in business and economics (and a minor in Mandarin) at the Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business in 2011, on the Bloomington campus. “I got fascinated by Bitcoin, and could have bought it for 73 cents,” he recalls. “Instead, I did what every college kid does. I bought beer.” Over the next three-and-a-half years, he reflected on that choice while watching Bitcoin climb 1,400-fold to over $1,000. Returning home, he attained a master’s in computer security and networking at the University of Hong Kong, where he took cryptography courses that renewed his interest in the science of generating cryptocurrencies. After graduating, Gagnon worked as a network technician at a company that offered mobile applications for investor conferences and other events. After less than two years, he quit his job and moved again, this time to Taiwan. His new venture: Building and running a jerry-rigged Ethereum mine at the home of his girlfriend’s (now his wife’s) parents in Taipei. “Everyone thought it was Bitcoin 2.0, so I figured, I’m not going to miss this opportunity like I missed Bitcoin as a sophomore,” says Gagnon. The business drew unwanted attention by using ten times the electricity of a typical home in Taipei—specifically, the phenomenon alerted the police. “They couldn’t figure out what we were doing,” he recalls. “They thought we were growing marijuana upstairs and kept raiding the house, like on a weekly basis. So we had to explain to the police every week that we weren’t doing anything illegal.” It took only a couple of intolerable months before Gagnon saw the necessity of uprooting his facility from his future in-laws’ home.  Gagnon then ran his operation in Guangzhou on China’s mainland, but shut down after two years due to a tough regulatory climate. “Let’s just say that the laws were somewhat selective for a young foreigner navigating a new industry,” he avows. In 2019, he joined Bitfarms, one of several Bitcoin miners, including HIVE, that sprouted in Quebec during the 2017 to 2018 boom, drawn by the province’s plentiful and relatively inexpensive hydroelectric power. As chief of development, his charge was expanding the business to the U.S. and other energy-rich areas of Canada.  Gagnon focused on the huge but remote Alberta oil patch. “I was always looking for the cheapest energy sources for mining, and that was Alberta,” he says. The producers were “flaring” the natural gas created from drilling, since no pipelines existed for sending it to population centers. Gagnon created the first containerized Bitcoin data center that incorporated a generator and offered 100% financing. events.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
events.summary: ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson tests DraftKings’ guardrails at a Manhattan bar this spring. After a ProPublica investigation published this fall, the company closed Pearson’s account. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news. “Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”  I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said? In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler , recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists. As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses. What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”   So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.  In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X .) So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly? DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks. Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment Lisa Seville and Nadia Sussman/ProPublica The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story. Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action . In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.   On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact .  That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers. I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry. In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here . If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org . The post I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account. appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Netanyahu may fall, but his far-right legacy in Israel is going nowhere
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Israel’s far right is accused of embedding a hardline agenda so deeply that reversing it may prove almost impossible. As Israel’s opposition looks to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speculation has centred on the possible fate of the current government’s more hardline, right-wing elements, including the parties led by the unapologetically pro-settler Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir , convicted of inciting terrorism. While all members of Netanyahu’s cabinet, with the unflinching backing of the opposition politicians hoping to supplant them, have supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and attacks on regional states, it is Smotrich and Ben-Gvir who have been the focus of international attention and lightning rods for criticism by Western governments. list 1 of 4 Israeli soldiers are also settlers in West Bank: Al Jazeera investigation list 2 of 4 Netanyahu fights to stay relevant as Israel’s opposition closes in list 3 of 4 Netanyahu’s legacy: Personality politics reshapes Israeli democracy list 4 of 4 Prominent Israeli settler denied entry into France With talk of Netanyahu looking to form a unity government with Eisenkot, both ministers have publicly opposed a government led by the former chief of staff. In the run-up to the vote, Ben-Gvir took the unusual step of claiming that Netanyahu now has a choice of selecting himself to “save Israel”, or Eisenkot. Smotrich, meanwhile, has warned his ultra-Orthodox political allies against entering negotiations with Eisenkot, saying he will “dump them” once he uses their votes to oust Netanyahu. Netanyahu formed a coalition government with Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) and Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party in 2022, giving both several of Israel’s most important cabinet positions. Smotrich became finance minister, granting him control over the Israeli budget and a number of institutions in the occupied West Bank, while Ben-Gvir was named national security minister. Drawing on a wellspring of hardline Zionism, Jewish supremacy and what critics describe as unapologetic racism, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have exploited their political leverage to advance Israel’s most hardline policies over the past three years. They have also transformed their ministries to reflect their hardline ideological projects. Both have been enthusiastic proponents of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, repeatedly threatening to withdraw their support from the government when it appeared Netanyahu might falter in the face of international pressure about the huge number of civilians killed, famine, and withholding of aid. In September 2025 , Ben-Gvir threatened to bring down the government if Hamas remained in existence following the release of the captives under United States President Donald Trump’s proposed Gaza plan. Both ministers have repeatedly called for the annexation, settlement and ethnic cleansing of Gaza. Smotrich has encouraged the expansion of illegal settlements within the West Bank and, in the eyes of his opponents, bears culpability for the explosion of settler violence and pogroms across the occupied territory. In June 2025, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were sanctioned by a wave of Western countries . Ireland and the Netherlands imposed travel bans on the two ministers, while other countries froze their assets. Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin said these measures were taken due to their shared “desire to see the elimination of Palestinians from Palestine”. However, analysts said the ministers and their movements should not be treated as a homogeneous entity or be isolated from Israeli policy in general. “I would argue that we should not treat Ben-Gvir and Smotrich as a single bloc, since exclusion from government would affect them in opposite ways,” Arie Perliger, of the University of Massachusetts Lowell, who has led studies into the far right in Israel, Europe and the US, told Al Jazeera. “Ben-Gvir’s power is populist and performative, and opposition suits him.” Ben-Gvir’s roots in the outlawed Kahanist movement had, in tandem with many right-wing movements, relied upon their historical exclusion from power as evidence of a betrayal by the establishment, he added. Smotrich, meanwhile, had used his position as finance minister to co-opt part of the settlement programme and force through his explicitly Zionist agenda. This means he would have more to lose if he were “cut off from budgets, portfolios and control over settlement policy”. “Smotrich’s case is the reverse. His achievements were bureaucratic rather than rhetorical,” Perliger said. Both figures have been accused of transforming their ministries in ways that will linger long after they leave government. As part of the 2022 deal with Netanyahu that secured his finance portfolio, Smotrich was given the additional role as a minister in the Ministry of Defence.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get
events.summary: Jensen Huang has lost his job, his board seat, and roughly $10 billion in paper wealth since admitting to an affair. If his 41-year marriage ends, California law could put a far larger share of his fortune in play. Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and director this week, days after confessing in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress Nvidia’s interim CEO and made longtime director Harvey Jones its first board chair while it searches for a permanent successor. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” The admission followed a New York Times report that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing, and that she had a close relationship with Huang. China has denied involvement. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said this week that she left Singapore in February and was barred from returning after a police investigation, which it said “did not concern espionage.” Two more relationships have since been reported. The New York Times reported on November 11 that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five people who had worked at the company. A day later, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee , whom it did not name. Powell did not respond to the Times, and Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters . Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort and said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” An FBI inquiry into his relationship with Alice Huang is also underway. Huang has not announced plans to divorce. But a split would test how California divides a fortune built almost entirely on a single stock, and the answer would turn less on his headline net worth than on how the couple’s Nvidia shares were acquired and held. Most of Huang’s Nvidia stake sits in trusts he shares with his wife Huang reported beneficial ownership of about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or 3.58% of the company’s outstanding stock, as of March 23, 2026, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement . Nvidia ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list worth more than $4 trillion . Jensen and Lori Huang are co-trustees of their living trust, which holds about 528.5 million shares, and of two other family trusts. Together, the three trusts hold nearly 669 million shares. Another 73.3 million shares are held by limited liability companies whose sole member is the living trust. Lori Huang also runs the family’s philanthropy. She is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, Fortune reported . The foundation holds about 58.7 million Nvidia shares, but the proxy states that neither spouse has a pecuniary interest in them. The distinction matters. Beneficial ownership and control of shares do not by themselves establish personal ownership, or determine how assets would be divided in a divorce. California’s community-property rule gives each spouse half of what was built during the marriage The couple met as lab partners at Oregon State University and married in 1985, eight years before Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. They live in California, a community-property state, where assets acquired during a marriage are generally owned jointly and divided equally in a divorce. “In California, all property acquired by a spouse during marriage is community property,” Christopher Melcher, a Los Angeles attorney who specializes in high-net-worth divorces, told the New York Post . “She would be entitled to 50%.” Under California Courts guidance , community property generally includes earnings and assets acquired between the date of marriage and the date of separation. Property owned before the marriage or acquired after separation, along with gifts and inheritances, is generally separate property, and some assets can be a mix of both. That means Lori Huang could be entitled to half of the community-property portion of the couple’s Nvidia holdings, not necessarily half of every share tied to her husband. The outcome would depend on how the shares were acquired, how the trusts are structured, whether separate and community assets were mixed, and whether the couple signed a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement. A court would need to examine those details before deciding what either spouse receives. California is also a no-fault divorce state , meaning either spouse can seek a divorce without proving infidelity or other wrongdoing. Infidelity, even across several reported relationships, generally does not entitle one spouse to a larger share of community property. Huang’s net worth is a moving target Huang is worth about $145 billion and ranks as the world’s 13th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as Fortune reported . That figure is a market estimate, not a tally of marital property, and it rises and falls with Nvidia’s stock, which shed $450 billion in market value in the days after his admission. Huang has described his wife’s role in the company in plain terms. “Every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview with CNA. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Tesla invites select customers to order their own driverless Cybercab
events.summary: Elon Musk's Tesla Motors is inviting select customers in the US to order its fully autonomous Cybercab, the company's new focus after scrapping the Cybertruck earlier this month . The Cybercab, also dubbed the Robotaxi , is being sold for personal use for $29,990 before taxes and is expected to be delivered in December, the Texas-based company said in a post on X. That makes it Tesla's cheapest vehicle, $7,000 lower than the entry-level variant of the Model 3. Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use pic.twitter.com/LDIkKuseAZ — Robotaxi (@robotaxi) November 13, 2026 However, the Cybercab requires a $3,600 annual autonomy subscription, which is the fee to use its driverless capabilities – a non-optional feature as the vehicle does not have a steering wheel or pedals. Maintenance and insurance costs are excluded from Tesla's pricing. Also, Cybercab deliveries are limited to Texas, one of only two states – the other being Florida – where Tesla's Robotaxi services are authorised to operate in a handful of cities. The driverless cab will be arriving in Arizona and Nevada soon, according to the company's website. Tesla described the launch as “early access” and “limited release”. It is unclear how many customers have been invited, whether the period will be extended and whether deliveries will be made available in Florida. “Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use,” Tesla said. The Cybercab was released to much hype in October 2024, nearly a decade after Mr Musk first told Tesla shareholders that the company's cars would achieve full autonomy within three years. In 2016, he said that by the end of 2017, a Tesla car would be able to drive across the US without human intervention. In 2019, he said Tesla would have one million robotaxis on roads in 2020. None of those came to fruition. There were several reasons for the delay and failed promises, most notably the challenge of developing the technology, as well as regulatory scrutiny – especially after accidents involving driverless cars, and what has been perceived as grandiose ambitions in such a short period. The company, however, was able to stick to its roll-out plan for the Cybercab after its pledge in 2024. The Cybercab is also one of Tesla's focal points moving forward after it announced on November 6 that it would cease production of the polarising Cybertruck pickup. Mr Musk defended the Cybertruck this week, saying that its order rate “far exceeds” the production rate and that “the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production”. Tesla also unveiled its next-generation Roadster in another hyped launch last month, with its top-end Rocket variant model having the ability to “fly” using thrusters made by Mr Musk's other venture, SpaceX.

TOKYO – Tesla said on Nov 13 it was inviting select customers to buy the Cybercab robotaxi for personal use, marking a push towards delivering fully designed autonomous vehicles to customers. Tesla posted the announcement on social media platform X with an image of the golden butterfly - door two-seater, priced at US$29,990 (S$38,660) with an “Autonomy Subscription” of US$299 a month. Chief executive Elon Musk said in a post on X that the offering would be available across the US as Tesla receives regulatory approval. “The monthly fee is too high,” Musk said, adding that it should match the cost of Tesla ’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) driver-assistance system and connectivity for other models, which is about US$115 a month. The electric vehicle maker aims to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of 2026, Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice-president of vehicle engineering, said in October. The Cybercab will work unsupervised in all the same geo locations as Tesla’s robotaxi services , Tesla’s head of artificial intelligence, Ashok Elluswamy, said in a separate X post. Tesla launched its unsupervised robotaxi service in Austin, Texas, in June 2025, expanded the offering to Dallas and Houston in April 2026 and rolled it out in Miami in July 2026. REUTERS

events.title: Qatar and Turkiye sign a mutual defence pact: What do we know?
events.summary: Analysts say the pact, agreed amid the US-Iran war, aims to deter attacks rather than build an offensive alliance. Qatar and Turkiye have welcomed a new mutual defence agreement that commits them to a common position against any external armed attack on either country. The pact followed Friday’s high-level meeting of the Turkiye-Qatar Supreme Strategic Committee in Istanbul, chaired by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. It comes as the region deals with the fallout of the United States-Israeli war on Iran and disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz . So what is in the agreement, and why does it matter now? Here’s what you need to know: According to a joint communique, the deal aims to strengthen collective defence, promote regional security and establish a common position against external armed attacks targeting either or both countries. It reflects “not only the commitment of its signatories to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, but also their shared vision of contributing to a more secure and stable regional order”, the statement said. The two countries agreed to consult one another on security threats and defence policy. They also agreed to expand joint military exercises, defence industry collaboration and personnel training exchanges. The communique, as reported, did not set out what could trigger the agreement or what form a joint response would take. Other agreements reached at the meeting covered education, consumer protection, and peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution, Qatar’s Al Raya newspaper said in an editorial on Saturday. Not an offensive one, analysts say. Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that the goal is not to form an alliance against any particular country. Instead, he said, it is meant to raise the cost of any potential aggression so that others are deterred from attempting it. He said cooperation already rests on an extended military partnership, including a Turkish military presence, joint training and defence manufacturing. The partnership is moving to a more advanced level, based on converging security doctrines and a shared view of where threats come from and how to deal with them, said Al-Etaibi. The region is braced for more conflict. There are fears of a renewed military escalation, pushing states to build up their defences and deterrence, Al-Etaibi said. The deal comes amid Israel’s aggressive military posture and growing questions over the future reliability of the US security umbrella. Regional states are looking to new alliances built on deterrence, joint arms manufacturing and less dependence on outside powers. In the communique, Ankara and Doha said the war on Iran and its regional repercussions must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy. They called for “the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz”. Why does defence manufacturing matter? Because supply chains have become a weak point. Al-Etaibi said disruption to navigation in Hormuz has made it harder to rely on foreign military supply chains. Producing weapons locally and securing spare parts is now a strategic necessity, not just an economic choice, he said. Mahjoob Zweiri, an academic and Middle East policy expert, told Al Jazeera that the move to joint manufacturing marks an advanced strategic stage. Military industries require billions of dollars of investment and long-term commitments, he said, as well as mutual trust over technology transfer. He said the war had shown why countries need their own manufacturing capacity, pointing to Iran, which kept fighting by producing much of its weaponry at home. The communique also welcomed the Badr memorandum, signed by Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia. It described the memorandum as a step towards collective defence through “the development of indigenous capabilities”, including joint production, technology development, information sharing and stronger supply chains. The Supreme Strategic Committee was set up under an agreement signed on December 19, 2014, according to Anadolu. Friday’s meeting was the 12th such forum. Al Raya described it as a key framework for monitoring agreements and expanding cooperation. Zweiri said the new pact reflects a high level of trust between Doha and Ankara after a series of political and security tests the relationship has faced since 2014. The relationship goes well beyond defence. Turkish contracting companies have carried out 206 projects in Qatar worth $20.8bn, according to the communique. events.title: Binance targets full reopening of withdrawals by next week
events.summary: Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November, after covering 95% of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform. Binance said it will reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week after a US$6.3 billion hack in October. The FBI and Binance blamed North Korea, while Pyongyang denied it; investigators linked the attack to the North Korean group “TraderTraitor”. The theft exposed digital asset risks and raised questions for Binance, which has promised to repay customers in full and has changed its finance leadership. Binance said on Nov 14 that it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week, as operations normalise for the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange after a security breach linked to North Korea saw US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) stolen from the platform in October . “This week, we reopened withdrawals for 87 networks. We will aim to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week,” the company said in an X post. Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November , after covering 95% of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in what experts describe as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever. The FBI and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as “TraderTraitor”. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off the heist, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. The company’s finance chief Kaiser Ng left the company just over a week after the heist , to pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance. He was replaced by longtime finance executive Justin Yek, who was most recently vice-president of finance at Airwallex. REUTERS

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, a new agency set up to investigate suspected misuse of public money, said in a statement late on Friday that searches took place on November 12 and 13 in Budapest and three other parts of Hungary. list 1 of 2 Moscow announces sudden death of Russia’s envoy to US list 2 of 2 Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacks Its investigators found Hungarian forints, euros and US dollars in farm buildings, warehouses, a home and “a high-value safe in a secluded location”, as well as beneath the ground in forests. The agency released footage showing officers digging outdoors after dark and examining piles of cash, which was later deposited with the state treasury. Finance Minister Andras Karman said on Facebook on Friday that 12 treasury employees spent eight hours counting it. The discovery comes amid an investigation into Miklos Sesztak, Hungary’s development minister from 2014 to 2018, who is suspected of receiving more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks tied to overpriced secondhand bus purchases by a state transport company and government construction projects. Orban has previously accused the new government of using the investigations to force him out of politics. Other former ministers have been arrested in separate cases, as has Gyorgy Matolcsy, the former governor of Hungary’s central bank, which sets monetary policy. His case concerns alleged misuse of public assets held by a central bank foundation. Matolcsy has denied wrongdoing. A survey published this week by Hungarian news website HVG by pollster Median suggested that 70 percent of respondents considered investigating suspected corruption under Orban and holding those responsible accountable very important.

events.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
events.summary: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report , it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

events.title: Football kit giveaway aims to boost participation
events.summary: Millie Bright said she wanted girls to feel "comfortable and confident" in their kit Former England captain Millie Bright has helped hand out new kit to grassroots football teams in Leeds as part of an initiative aimed at keeping girls in sport for longer. Thirty teams based in communities facing social or economic challenges were chosen by anti-discrimination charity Kick it Out for the donation. Bright, who began her career at Doncaster Belles, said it was "vital" to keep girls playing sport. "Every young girl deserves a kit, no matter what level they play at, and, whilst the top of the game is doing really well, real life still exists. People can't afford to give their children kits, but that doesn't mean they should go without." Craig Gilmore set up Champions CIC, in Beeston, six years ago, to provide free Saturday morning training for children in the local area, as well as breakfast and lunch. "With the cost of living, football's expensive [and] bills come first," he said. "We work with a lot of families that can't afford the direct debits and the ongoing costs of grassroots sport nowadays. "The new kit is amazing. It gives them that sense of belonging, that team pride, it's a massive boost for them." Bright spoke with young footballers during the event in Leeds The new kit was provided by Kick it Out, in partnership with the Morrisons Foundation. They hope it will inspire these girls to continue sport as young women and adults. "Girls' participation struggles with drop-out rates," said Gemma Clark, from Kick it Out. "One of the barriers is kit. We want to remove that barrier so that more local girls can keep playing." Bright told the BBC she was fully behind the campaign. "As a girl or a woman, it's about feeling wanted and equal," she said. "We deserve to have kits. I don't want to see any girl dropping out of the game because they don't feel valued or comfortable. "These are the days that really make a difference. Hopefully this shows the girls that the people at the top care. The power of having a kit is a small gesture, but has a massive impact."
