events.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services
events.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. The company apologized for the lengthy delay and said it did not suspect malicious activity. Microsoft said Saturday service had been restored across products. Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. O n Saturday , Microsoft said it had addressed the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. The connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade," Microsoft said in a Friday statement. The software giant added that the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers. Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning. Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec Amazon’s Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET on Friday, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online. In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday. Governments and businesses review impact Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress. "Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

events.title: Warner accuses Cricket Australia of ‘cover-up’ in ball-tampering scandal
events.summary: Former opener Warner was banned for a year for his involvement in the 2018 ‘Sandpapergate’ incident in South Africa. David Warner blasted Cricket Australia’s handling of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal as “a cover-up” on Saturday, escalating a row that has torn apart the sport. Former opener Warner, who was banned for a year over his part in the “ Sandpapergate ” incident in Cape Town, lashed out at what he claimed was “a shoddy investigation”. list 1 of 3 Goalkeeper Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel death list 2 of 3 Reijnders’ hat-trick fires Dutch to 7-0 rout of Greece, Germany beat Serbia list 3 of 3 Salah breaks Egypt scoring record, Tunisia lose to Libya in AFCON qualifier “As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” he said on Instagram. “If that’s correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn’t know? “It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose, and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. Festering wounds over what happened in the third Test at Cape Town were reopened this week when Usman Khawaja released his autobiography. In the book, he alleged that the whole team knew about the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing. A Cricket Australia probe concluded that only then-skipper Steve Smith, his deputy Warner and Cameron Bancroft were in the know, with all three sent home from South Africa in disgrace . Starc, Hazlewood, Lyon and Pat Cummins all denied publicly in a 2021 statement that they were aware of the plan. On Friday, Cummins, now the Test captain, held a lengthy news conference to rubbish Khawaja’s latest claims, calling them “ 100 percent wrong “. In response, Warner accused him of throwing close friend Khawaja “under the bus”. Starc also stated during the week that “we weren’t aware of things being taken on the field”. Hazlewood and Lyon have yet to comment. Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening their investigation and, in a statement on Saturday, said all players had been given the chance to come forward. “As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since,” a spokesperson said. “Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players’ right to provide their own version of events.”

events.title: Tout offers £1m of U2 tickets on StubHub, raising questions about ‘bot’ clampdown
events.summary: Artists and industry figures call for culture secretary to ‘shut down the touts’ by outlawing resale for profit One tout is advertising £1m of tickets for U2’s long-awaited 2027 tour through StubHub, raising questions about the website’s condemnation of professional ticket traders who use “bot” software to scoop up tickets and exploit genuine fans. Seats for the four-night London leg of the Irish band’s The Greatest Show on Earth tour sold out last week, shortly after going on sale. Fans chasing tickets appear to have been beaten to the punch by prolific touts using sites such as StubHub to charge eye-watering mark-ups. StubHub listings for U2’s gigs at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London show more than 2,000 tickets listed by a single tout despite strict limits on how many can be purchased by each buyer. Vladyslav Skrypka, who claims to be based in Harlow, Essex, advertised more than 1,800 tickets for one of the nights alone, with some on sale for more than four times face value. If all of his tickets were to sell for the sums listed, Skrypka would stand to make more than £1m. The findings come amid clamour from artists and music industry figures for the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, to move forward with plans that she outlined a year ago to “shut down the touts’ racket” by outlawing resale for profit. A ticket tout ban bill is due to be published during the current parliamentary session, which might not end until well into 2027. In the meantime, thousands of tickets are still falling into the hands of touts, with some listings bearing the apparent hallmarks of “bot” use, which has been illegal since 2018 . In an interview with the BBC last week, StubHub International’s chief executive, Bob Kupbens, said: “We don’t support bots and we’d love for both the government and primary to do a better job of policing that to make sure those kinds of things don’t happen.” Adam Webb of the music industry-backed campaign group FanFair Alliance said that the sheer volume of U2 tickets on StubHub indicated either bot use or a practice known as “speculative selling”, where touts agree a sale first, then hope to procure tickets later. Like the use of bots, “spec” selling is illegal. Webb said: “StubHub claims all their orders come 100% guaranteed but have they seen evidence of Vladyslav’s receipts? “Are they not concerned that these tickets may have been acquired by the kind of technology that Mr Kupbens so publicly deplores?” StubHub International, owned by the US investment group Digital Fuel Capital, did not address specific questions from the Guardian about the listings or possible bot use involved in obtaining the tickets. The company said it “does not allow speculative selling, and sellers must confirm they own, or have a right to, the tickets they list”. A spokesperson said: “We are firmly against the use of bots. They are used at the point of primary sale, before tickets reach any resale marketplace, which is why we have called for stronger enforcement at source.” Ticketmaster disputed the suggestion that it and other primary agents were responsible for bots, saying it blocked 20bn bots a month and spent millions on doing so. It said resale sites, such as Viagogo and StubHub, created the incentive for bot use. A snapshot of StubHub’s listings, taken this week, showed 7,819 U2 tickets advertised for resale. More than 2,000 were held by Skrypka, with thousands more in the hands of other professional ticket “traders”, an industry term for touts, defined by selling more than 100 tickets a year. Only 562 were from private sellers, such as fans who can no longer attend or use all of the tickets they bought. A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We are fully committed to stamping out ticket touting for good. For too long, fans have been ripped off and we’re determined to right that wrong. “We are bringing forward legislation in this parliament and will ensure that our measures are truly effective, enforceable and future-proof.” The Guardian has approached U2 for comment. Messages to social media pages believed to belong to Skrypka went unanswered.

events.title: Singapore-based billionaire Leo KoGuan vows to halt Nvidia buys after Jensen Huang exit
events.summary: Leo KoGuan, who has a US$13.2 billion fortune, began investing in Nvidia in March. Leo KoGuan said he will not buy more Nvidia shares after Jensen Huang’s exit, calling Huang “the supreme creator” and saying, “No further investment without Jensen.” KoGuan said he has invested about US$1.3 billion in Nvidia, but his stake could not be independently verified. He began buying in March and has also backed Tesla, SpaceX and Alphabet. Huang was abruptly removed after reports of three affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. KoGuan said investors should buy and hold super-intelligence companies for the long term. Billionaire investor and Nvidia shareholder Leo KoGuan expressed support for Jensen Huang on Nov 13 and said he will not increase his stake in the tech company with someone else at the helm. “No further investment without Jensen,” KoGuan said in a text message, saying he has invested around US$1.3 billion (S$1.7 billion) in Nvidia. In a series of posts on X, KoGuan called Huang “the supreme creator” and acknowledged that while the executive had made errors, “we must prioritise rewards” rather “than punishments”. The posts followed Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia after reports of three affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. That ended his decades-long reign over a company at the centre of the artificial intelligence buildout and, by extension, the global economy. Singapore-based KoGuan, who has a US$13.2 billion fortune, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, began investing in Nvidia in March. It was a notable move for an investor whose net worth for years had been tied up largely in one stock: Tesla. The size of KoGuan’s Nvidia stake could not be independently verified. Earlier this week, KoGuan said on X that he is also an investor in Space Exploration Technologies and Google, whose parent is Alphabet. He told Bloomberg that he plans on increasing his positions in those companies. Investors must buy and hold super-intelligence companies for the long term, he wrote on X. “I hope and plan to invest in Jensen Huang if he creates or buys” another super-intelligence company, he wrote on Nov 13. “I hope he will offer me the opportunity to invest in his future company.” Bloomberg

events.title: What do Christmas market traders say about rising prices?
events.summary: Nils Borstel said his business was making less money despite more than doubling the price of a sausage Mention Christmas markets these days and the conversation often turns to rising prices – from £8 bratwursts, £11 Yorkshire pudding wraps and even £5 for a few marshmallow sticks. But what do the people behind the stalls think? Are they benefiting from the hikes or are their own profits being squeezed? Traders at Manchester's Christmas markets told the BBC they were feeling the pressure of increasing bills for staff, ingredients and energy, with some saying they were making less money despite charging more. One trader said it costs at least £4,000 a day to run each her four stalls, while another has cut prices to keep customers coming back. Nils Borstel, 25, helps run Bratwurst King, a family business which has operated at the markets since 1999. He said a sausage that previously cost £3.50 now sold for £8, with much of the increase taking place over the past five or six years. "But we don't earn more money," he said. Manchester Christmas market traders explain prices Borstel, whose family operates four stalls across the city centre, said rising costs for meat, electricity, staffing and accommodation had forced the business to increase prices. About 15 workers travel from Germany to help run the stalls, alongside staff recruited in the UK. He said that despite busy crowds and dry weather during the opening weekend, people appeared more cautious about spending than in previous years. For example, some customers were now buying one portion of food to share, rather than purchasing one each, he said. Borstel said he had seen a change in spending habits since 2019, when customers were more willing to buy food and drinks without worrying about the cost. He acknowledged that prices were high and did not want to increase them, but said the they were necessary to cover expenses. Poppy (left) and Neve questioned whether the portions they bought justified the prices Among those questioning the costs were Neve and Poppy, both 18. Neve, a student, said she had spent about £15 on one dish, while Poppy, who is taking a gap year, paid £11 for a Yorkshire pudding wrap. "I think it was pricey for what it was," Neve said. Poppy also felt she had not received much food for the money, although said it was tasty. Both said they enjoyed going into the city and looking around the markets, while Neve sympathised with traders, saying she thought the cost of renting space could force businesses to raise prices. Charlotte Whittle, director of CT Catering, has been trading at the markets for 10 years and now operates four stalls. She said each stall cost at least £1,000 a day to run, bringing her total daily operating costs to at least £4,000. Whittle, who employs a range of staff, said customers often underestimated the work and expense involved. Before the markets opened, her business spent two weeks preparing its stalls, with another two weeks needed to dismantle them after Christmas. CT Catering director Charlotte Whittle says her business employs 57 people across four Manchester market sites She said the costs included staff wages, accommodation, deliveries, storage, packaging and card payment fees. Parking three vans in Manchester city centre could cost £100 a day alone, she said, with the vehicles needed to replenish stock throughout busy trading periods. "They think that you're just selling cookies," she said. Whittle, who began her business selling homemade cakes at street food markets, said the cost of stock and packaging had increased significantly over the years. Although she had increased some prices, she said she had chosen to absorb part of those costs rather than risk putting customers off. "We've had to take a massive cut on profits," she said. She also argued that the standard of street food had improved and customers were receiving food comparable in quality to that served in restaurants. But not every trader has responded to rising costs by putting up prices. Clark Murphy, whose family has traded at the markets for 22 years, runs Mr Crimble Crumble, which sells fruit crumbles from two stalls. He said the business had kept most prices unchanged for three years and had reduced the cost of its largest portion by £2. Clark Murphy (left), pictured with his nephew Davis, said his business had reduced the price of its largest crumble Murphy said cooking oil and biodegradable packaging had become more expensive, but the business wanted to retain customers who returned each Christmas. "We haven't increased our prices for three years now," he said. A notice at one food stall offered customers £1 off each drink or dish if they paid in cash He said the business remained profitable, although margins were under pressure and card payments added to operating costs. At another food stall, a notice offered customers £1 off each drink or dish when paying cash. "Card fees are crazy – help us keep it simple," it said.

events.title: Analysis: Companies love a ‘rockstar’ CEO. Until they depend on one
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s resignation has put Nvidia’s succession planning and its dependence on its founder under scrutiny. Analysts and industry experts say Huang’s value extended beyond technology to supplier relationships, customers and his influence across the AI industry. Nvidia’s transition raises a broader governance question for boards: Can a company remain resilient when one leader becomes central to its strategy and identity? When Jensen Huang quit, it struck me how quickly the conversation shifted from his departure to whether Nvidia could manage without him. It wasn't about whether the company had the technology, customers or talent to keep growing, but whether anyone else could do what Huang had been doing for the business. That made me wonder: did investors believe in Nvidia, or just Huang? The company is hardly short of capable people. Interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013. Nvidia has experienced engineers, established customer relationships and a leading position in the artificial intelligence chip market. But, listening to guests on CNBC this week, I noticed how much of their concern was about the influence Huang had built outside Nvidia. On Friday, just a day after Huang quit, Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" how Huang would persuade executives at smaller companies that make critical components to commit capacity to Nvidia. This helped it secure "the majority of supply chain capacity," he said. Without Huang, competitors could try to persuade those suppliers to allocate more capacity to them, Patel argued. And so the big question is, how much of Nvidia's advantage comes from its technology and how much comes from the relationships Huang built? There are obvious benefits to elevating CEOs to be rockstars . They can attract investors, open doors and give a company a new identity. A charismatic leader attracts attention, reassures investors and makes a company's strategy easier to sell. Huang was particularly good at this. He helped shape the conversation about where AI was heading and made Nvidia central to it. Donning his trademark leather jacket, Huang took to stages around the world , courting world leaders to lay out his vision and explain why Nvidia would be at its center. Before Huang resigned, Eric Ross told "Squawk Box Asia" that Huang "is the company." That may sound like an endorsement, but it also helps explain why his departure has raised so many questions. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon made an interesting distinction on the same program, also before Huang's departure. Nvidia had capable executives who could keep the business running, he said. What was harder to replace was Huang's vision. "They need a visionary like that," he said. But for a company whose valuation reflects not just what it sells but expectations of what AI could become, replacing that vision may prove harder than replacing the CEO. Duncan Clark pointed to another part of Huang's job. He had become a bridge between Silicon Valley, Asia and Washington, and one of the most prominent voices for the wider AI industry. "I don't think you can replace him with one individual," Clark said on "Access Middle East" on Friday. Replacing him with multiple people is "going to take time, and it won't be the same," he added. That distinction may be important. Nvidia's board has begun a search for a permanent CEO and said it will consider both internal and external candidates. But whoever takes the job may not personally assume every role Huang had come to play around the company. Some of his responsibilities and relationships could end up being spread across Nvidia's broader leadership team. For now, the board is emphasizing continuity. New chair Harvey Jones said Kress is backed by an experienced leadership team and that Nvidia expected its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Kress, meanwhile, pointed to Nvidia's people and leadership team as strengths as the company moves forward. Other boards will be watching, particularly those that have allowed their CEOs to become the face of everything their companies do. When a charismatic leader is the only person outsiders hear from, it becomes harder to convince them that anyone else can take over. There is also the question of accountability. Clark described Nvidia's situation as a governance failure. And my colleague, "Squawk Box Europe" anchor Steve Sedgwick , raised a similar point on Friday about how corporate America has approached ESG. Much of the political debate has focused on its environmental component, Steve said. President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked environmental and climate policies using phrases such as "green scam." But Steve questioned whether the governance element has been overlooked, particularly at some of America's biggest technology companies.

events.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
events.summary: Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais . In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France. Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further. Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais. Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate. In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore. The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years. EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France , have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues. It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal. Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting. But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting. Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time. “This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?” He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said. The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent. Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche. He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars. The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint. Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question we are asking all the time.” This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

events.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
events.summary: Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption. The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Published 19 hours ago Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world Published 20 hours ago In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said. "We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible." Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

events.title: Food bank sees donations drop by 10% each year
events.summary: The year ending in 2024 saw a 9% drop, then another 13% in 2025, and finally a 6% drop in 2026 A food bank that has seen a drop in donations of about 10% each year since 2023 is hoping government stockpiling advice will not affect the public's generosity. Someone eats a meal provided by Cambridge City Foodbank "every two minutes" and it claims to have provided more than 260,000 in the past year. In October, the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign and encouraged households to stock up with enough non-perishable food and water to survive for three days in case of an emergency. Chief executive Steve Clay says he does not know if this will affect the Christmas appeal - their busiest period - but confesses: "It is a concern." A government spokesperson said it had "no serious evidence of stockpiling or indeed a supply shortage" with the campaign and it had worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns. Steve Clay, chief executive of Cambridge City Foodbank, said they had discussed the possibility that stockpiling would affect donations The food bank team estimates it will provide more than 45,000 meals to people in the city between 13 November and 15 January. Clay says that with cold weather and pressure on spending, Christmas is "more difficult" than the rest of the year. "Budgets are tighter, more has to be spent on fuel and energy," he said. "So people are contacting us all the time for emergency support and we need to make sure that the support is always there and is continuing to be there." Donations are used to purchase emergency hampers, treats or provide advice and assistance. While the food bank's doors close on Christmas Day, meals they have provided mean more people can enjoy the festivities. Every pound donated, up to the first £15,000, would be doubled as part of a match-funding commitment. Dr Liam Loftus, development director of the food bank, said: "As we head into winter and the cold draws in, thousands of individuals and families will be forced to make the heart-breaking choice between heating or eating. "This winter, can you take two minutes of your time to support our Winter Appeal? "You'll be helping restore hope and dignity to people facing hardship and providing one of your neighbours with their next meal at what should be one of the happiest times of year." The government spokesperson said of the Be Ready campaign: "We've worked hand-in-hand with voluntary organisations and charities, including food banks, to address any concerns and ensure the guidance is as accessible as possible. "Where households can act, that frees up emergency services to prioritise those most in-need during any emergency." Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. events.title: ‘An environmental and welfare disaster’: British salmon loses its organic status
events.summary: This week the Soil Association withdrew certification from organic salmon after 20 years. What went wrong? The first haul of farmed salmon in Britain was a relatively modest 14 tonnes, produced off the west coast of Scotland near Fort William in 1971. For Unilever, the vast multinational that pioneered salmon farming, it was a triumph after years of experimenting with how to cage fish, battle against diseases and cope with the wild weather. Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. By 1976, it had expanded into three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes of fish each year. Today the British farmed salmon industry – worth £1bn a year – produces about 205,000 tonnes of fish a year, and employs 2,500 people in Scotland. In the decades since salmon farming was introduced, numbers of wild Atlantic salmon off British shores have declined by more than 70% , a depletion that should be a warning sign of significant environmental problems facing our rivers, coasts and seas which are only increasing as the oceans warm as a result of global heating. Simultaneously, industrial farming of Atlantic salmon in Britain, most of which is in Scotland, has been a commercial and consumer success. Salmon is ranked the most popular fish by British families – who consume 65,000 tonnes of it each year, drawn in by marketing material promoting it as nutrient-rich, protein packed and a good source of omega-3. Many are unaware that the salmon they are buying, with its pale colour and white fat lines, is the product of highly intensified industrial farming, not a wild fish that swims freely in the ocean. This week the Soil Association, an accreditation body, announced it was removing its certification of organic farmed salmon after 20 years. The association said an extensive review had found that environmental and welfare outcomes were not meeting its “high bar”, and there was a lack of evidence that this could change fast enough. Helen Browning, the CEO of the Soil Association, said: “When we started working on salmon 20 years ago, we had an aspiration for an aquaculture system that could deliver the principles of organic production in the sea. “We envisioned a multi-trophic, enriched environment which could provide the resources for a good life for salmon, with minimal negative impact on other species. However, progress along these lines has been negligible … the evidence suggests that welfare and environmental outcomes are not sufficient for us to continue.” Salmon farming begins with the stripping of eggs from female fish to be artificially fertilised and incubated in controlled freshwater hatcheries. Once hatched, the young fish are moved when big enough to larger tanks, and then pens, before being transferred again at 12-18 months into sea water cages, where they are fed fishmeal pellets and treated with drugs to prevent disease. Footage has emerged showing farmed salmon covered in blisters and sores – and in some images minus their heads – as a result of sea lice infestations, caused by high stocking densities. The use of chemicals to treat the lice, high mortality rates, and the environmental damage caused to wild salmon and coastal waters from disease and pollution are all reasons that a growing number of organisations are calling it out as inhumane and unsustainable. Chris Packham, the naturalist and broadcaster, says the industry is catastrophic for fish welfare and the environment. More than 120 chefs representing 26 countries across six continents have signed an open letter created by the charity WildFish, saying they would keep ocean farmed salmon off their menus unless changes were made to existing farming practices. Salmon farming, WildFish says, was and always will be antithetical to organic principles. It cites the use of harsh chemical pesticides and treatments such as formaldehyde to manage lice, pollution from the toxic chemicals and waste, high mortality rates and the unsustainable use as feed of wild fish, much of it sourced off the coast of west Africa, depleting the stocks there and straining food security for local populations. The Soil Association decision follows pressure from groups which argue its badge is greenwashing farmed salmon. WildFish has been asking the association to publish its salmon farm inspection reports for two years, via environmental information laws. The association has so far refused, despite being told by the first-tier tribunal to do so. But a two-year review by the Soil Association of its certified “organic” farms found concerns around suffering, and a high mortality rates on the sites, which were not significantly better than non-organic farms. In 2023, an unprecedented 17.4 m salmon died on salmon farms before harvesting.

events.title: Ecuador wants to monetize its biodiversity — while still drilling for oil
events.summary: Ecuador is pursuing green bonds, debt-for-nature swaps and biodiversity credits to channel more money into conservation. But the government also plans to expand oil exploration and develop critical-mineral resources, drawing opposition from Indigenous and environmental groups. Ecuador will host the U.N. biodiversity COP18 in 2028 and officials say they hope to issue the country’s first sovereign green bond in 2027. Ecuador, known for its " megadiverse " Galapagos Islands, Amazon rainforest, Andes and Pacific coast, wants to protect its natural landscapes for years to come — but it faces a tricky balancing act. As well as preserving its nature, the South American country also plans to capitalize on its critical minerals and continue to extract oil from parts of the Amazon — both of which have led to protests from Indigenous and environmental groups. One way Ecuador is planning to channel funds into its nature is via new financial tools, such as "debt-for-nature" swaps and its first sovereign green bond. It is also aiming to raise its environmental profile on the global stage by hosting the U.N.'s biodiversity summit , known as COP18, in 2028. Ecuador, which uses the U.S. dollar, is no stranger to green finance. In March, IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, and Ecuadorian lender Banco Bolivariano issued a $120 million biodiversity bond to back conservation projects. The government also completed two swaps in 2023 and 2024 — deals in which a country's debt is refinanced on better terms in exchange for commitments to spend the savings on conservation. Together, they freed up about $1.1 billion for conservation in the Amazon and Galapagos Islands . Juan Carlos Blum, Ecuador's minister of environment and energy, said the country hopes to issue sovereign green bonds for the first time in 2027, to raise finance to protect its coastal and mountainous regions and the people whose livelihoods depend on them. The government is looking to the European Union for advice on such instruments, he said. The bloc set green bond standards in 2024. For Blum, one of the challenges is public awareness. "A lot of us are not aware of how we depend on nature, how we depend on the biodiversity, how vulnerable we all are towards climate," he told CNBC by video call. Another challenge for Ecuador, as it looks to protect its biodiversity, is its reliance on oil. The country is a significant oil producer in Central and South America and in October, the government announced plans to open up new tenders for oil exploration in parts of the Amazon , according to local media reports. The news was reportedly met with criticism from Indigenous leaders , who strongly oppose the plans. "We are being careful on that balance between biodiversity and natural resources use, renewables or not renewables, and it's a delicate matter," Blum said. "That's my day-to-day reality, dealing with balancing this." About 80% of Ecuador's energy was generated from oil and oil products in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency, while about two-thirds of its electricity was produced using hydroelectric power. Cracking down on illegal mining is a focus for Blum, who told CNBC he was aware of the environmental impact of legal mining, but that illegal mining was a far bigger problem. At Ecuador's first Bio Summit held Nov. 4 to Nov. 6 in Quito — an event aimed at helping the country's natural assets "enter the global financial system" — a new way of monetizing nature was introduced. Marcelo Salame, the event's president, told CNBC he is working on a project to bring so-called biodiversity credits to the country for the first time, to "preserve and monetize" a 260-hectare, or 640-acre, area of the Prosperina forest owned by ESPOL University in the port city of Guayaquil. Salame said biodiversity is "multidimensional," with credits reflecting a whole ecosystem rather than carbon emissions alone. Biodiversity credits work in a similar way to the carbon credits that large companies buy to meet sustainability goals, but track a range of measures such as the number of species in a given area or tree canopy cover, with the money raised funneled back into nature protection. But whereas carbon credits can be used to offset emissions, biodiversity credits cannot. "It's all about funding verified nature outcomes and not, to date at least, compensating for damage," Martin Vaquié, co-founder of Berlin-based Bloomlabs, a company that tracks the biodiversity market, told CNBC. Jerry Toth, a conservationist and co-founder of Ecuador-based Third Millennium Alliance, a nonprofit that aims to protect the "last remnants" of Ecuador's Pacific Forest, told CNBC that carbon markets can reduce the ecological value of a forest to a single metric: how many tons of carbon it stores. "That can be potentially dangerous because then you have people that are optimizing for this one metric at the expense of all the other things," he said.

events.title: UAE Property: 'Should I waive the penalty if my tenant can no longer afford the rent?'
events.summary: Question: I own a one-bedroom apartment that I rent out. My tenant renewed only three months ago but has now lost his job and says he needs to leave the UAE . The tenancy contract says early termination requires two months' rent as a penalty. He has asked me to waive it because he has a family and says he genuinely cannot afford it. I'm sympathetic, but I'm also paying a mortgage and I'm worried the apartment could sit empty while I find another tenant. What would you do? Am I being foolish if I let him leave without enforcing the penalty? DH, Dubai Answer: There's the legal answer and then there's the answer I would give you after many years of dealing with landlords and tenants, and they aren't always exactly the same. Let's start with the contract. If you have an agreed early termination clause requiring two months' rent, that is the basis from which the two of you negotiate. A tenant losing their job doesn't automatically erase their contractual obligations. But of course, I wouldn't immediately turn this into a dispute . Ask the tenant when they realistically need to leave and whether they'll co-operate with viewings (presumably you will want to find an immediate replacement). Then, speak to a good local brokerage firm to establish how quickly the apartment could be re-let and at what level of rent. Suppose your existing tenant helps you secure a replacement who moves in immediately after he leaves. If you suffer little or no financial loss, insisting on the full two-month penalty may achieve very little other than making an already difficult situation for him worse. On the other hand, if the property is likely to sit vacant for six weeks and you'll incur cleaning, maintenance/preparation costs, or perhaps agency fees, it's therefore perfectly reasonable to negotiate compensation. If I had to be practical and you pressed me for my view, I would release him early provided he allows viewings , returns the apartment properly, settles utilities and rent up to the agreed handover date and perhaps pays a reduced termination amount if there's a genuine vacancy period. One piece of advice though: whatever you both decide ensure you put everything in writing. I've always believed the best landlord-and-tenant outcomes aren't necessarily the ones where somebody squeezes every last dirham out of the contract. They're the ones where both sides walk away feeling the agreement was fair. You have a mortgage to pay, so this isn't charity. But if you can replace the tenant quickly and help somebody through a genuinely difficult period without leaving yourself out of pocket, I'd call that sensible property management rather than weakness. Q: I own an apartment in Dubai that I bought as a long-term investment. My service charges have increased over the years, but the condition of the building seems to be going in the opposite direction. The gym has had broken equipment for months, there are regular problems with the lifts, the swimming pool has been closed several times and the common areas look tired. I don't mind paying reasonable service charges if the money is being spent properly, but as an individual owner I feel I have absolutely no influence. Can I refuse to pay until these issues are fixed, and how can I actually find out what I'm paying for? LM, Dubai A: Straight off the bat, I wouldn't refuse to pay. This puts you in a weak position and ultimately you will be falling foul of the law. Service charges in Dubai's jointly owned properties are regulated and the budgets are subject to Rera's approval. The charges can include security, cleaning, maintenance, utilities for common areas, insurance, management costs, master-community charges and contributions to any reserve funds. Your first step should therefore be to establish what the approved charge actually is. You can check this through the DLD Service Charge Index, Mollak or Dubai REST. DLD specifically states that management entities should not demand service charges before they have been approved by Rera. After you have thoroughly checked this out you can go ahead and separate the two issues of how much you're being charged and what standard of service you're receiving. A high service charge isn't automatically unreasonable if you're in a building with extensive facilities, cooling of common areas, several lifts, pools, landscaping and 24-hour security. But owners are entitled to question why facilities they are funding are not being fully maintained. Document the problems. Dates, photographs, emails and previous complaints are far more useful than simply saying the building is badly managed. Raise them formally with the management company first. If the standard of common-area maintenance remains unacceptable, DLD says owners can submit a complaint through Dubai REST using the Real Estate Violations System. From an investment perspective, I'd take this seriously. Poor building management doesn't just irritate residents, over time it can affect rents, tenant retention and of course resale values. Two identical apartments in neighbouring buildings can perform very differently simply because one building is well run and the other isn't. events.title: 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians stranded as US flight chaos grounds thousands of planes Adelaide woman Trish Crabb is stranded at JFK Airport in New York after thousands of flights were cancelled and delayed. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) A major air traffic control outage in the US has disrupted thousands of flights, leaving Australians stranded and warnings about global flow-on impacts, including international delays. Airlines are working to clear the backlog as US authorities investigate what caused the outage. Australians have been caught up in widespread flight disruptions across the United States after a communications outage forced aviation authorities to ground flights nationwide. More than 11,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, with passengers left stranded at airports across the country after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an unprecedented ground stop. The grounding has since been lifted, but airlines are warning it could take time to clear the backlog, with disruptions also affecting flights departing Australia for the US. Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia. Sydney Airport said flights to the US would now resume from Mascot after being temporarily grounded on Saturday morning, and urged passengers to contact their airlines. The disruption has affected travellers at major airports including New York's JFK, Los Angeles International Airport and San Diego. Adelaide traveller Trish Crabb snapped this photograph while in line at JFK airport in New York. She was among thousands of travellers caught up in US flight cancellations. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) Trish Crabb, from Adelaide, was among those caught up in the chaos after her flight from New York to Miami was grounded. She and her husband were due to fly out of JFK Airport when they discovered their Delta flight had been cancelled. The couple are holidaying in the US and had planned to drive from Miami to Fort Lauderdale to board a cruise. "My husband is going to try and find us a hotel room somewhere close by, and hopefully we will be able to get a flight out at some stage," she said. Despite the disruption, Ms Crabb said passengers appeared to be keeping their composure. "Everyone was very calm," she said, adding most people were taking the situation in their stride. Rivkah Brown, from Myrtleford in Victoria, was stranded at San Diego Airport after her Delta flight was cancelled. Rivkah Brown from Victoria was stranded at San Diego Airport following a cruise in the US. She's now boarding a bus to get to Las Vegas. ( Supplied: Rivkah Brown ) Ms Brown had just disembarked from a cruise and was stopping over in San Diego before travelling to Las Vegas, where she was due to meet her fiancé. She said she would now take a bus to Las Vegas instead, a journey of almost 10 hours. "It's disappointing but it is what it is," Ms Brown said. The FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop on Friday, local time, after communications problems affecting air traffic control centres across the United States. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centres, with technicians investigating the cause. What we know about the US flight groundstop Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage. The FAA said the decision was made because of "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety". US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said preliminary investigations pointed to a telecommunications outage, with no immediate indication of a deliberate attack. "There's no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," he said. The outage affected the 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft between airports across the country. At least 600 flights had been diverted, including aircraft sent back to their departure airports or redirected elsewhere. The order to ground all departing US flights was finally lifted after more than five hours. ( AP Photo: Tony Gutierrez ) About 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time on Friday. Planes already in the air were able to continue to their destinations, with authorities prioritising their safe landing. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a computer system failure at the FAA caused thousands of delays.

events.title: 'Plastic farmers' in Indonesia unaware of the dangers of burning waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Researchers investigate health impact of burning plastic waste in Indonesia Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Plastic waste was regularly burned in limestone kilns in Sumberejo, a village in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Ahmad Yani spent hours each day sifting through piles of rubbish, searching for recyclable materials to sell to help make ends meet. For decades, his family and other people in his village in East Java, in Indonesia, would buy truckloads of waste residue from factories recycling imported paper and cardboard. They would spread the waste on the ground, and separate plastics from paper and cardboard. The paper would be sold back to the recycling factories and most of the plastics to industries that needed fuel for furnaces. "It had become a source of livelihood for many low-income residents," Mr Yani said, adding he would make about 300,000 rupiah ($24) a month. Any plastics still left over would be used in his village to fire limestone kilns, to produce building materials to sell or use. Ahmad Yani says plastic waste from overseas has been coming to his village for decades. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Mr Yani said among the rubbish he noticed food sachets and cat and dog food packaging with Australian labels, as well as labels of countries in Europe. While burning plastic has helped support the family's livelihood, the smoke from their home and neighbouring households may be having a devastating impact on health. Mr Yani said some people he knew who had operated the limestone kilns had died from respiratory diseases and causes were never determined. He said the burning of plastics in his village was no longer happening. It stopped about a year ago. Several local media reported companies had stopped distributing waste to his community to sort, which had sparked anger among locals who lost their source of income. The ABC couldn't independently verify the reasons for the change. But health concerns for people who have been exposed to air pollution from burning plastics remain. Women sort through waste in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Researchers from the Climate and Health Centre at Brawijaya University were investigating the health effects of air pollution in East Java when they found locals were burning plastic waste. One of the researchers, Sekar Aqila Salsabilla, said pre-screening tests earlier this year on those in their study produced some worrying findings. She said at least 20 per cent of the more than 4,000 participants across six East Java villages were at high risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Sekar Aqila Salsabilla has been researching the health effects of air pollution in villages in East Java. ( Supplied: Sekar Aqila Salsabilla ) "When we first entered these communities, one of the most distressing findings was that many people were unaware of the dangers associated with burning plastic waste," said Ms Salsabilla, who, as part of a broader study, worked with more than 30 researchers, the majority of whom had medical backgrounds. People earning money from sorting waste, known as "plastic farmers", knew their health was "slowly declining" but did not understand the source of the problems, she said. "Despite the income they generate, many do not realise that the long-term health burden they may face is likely to be far greater than the money they earn from handling and burning this waste," Ms Salsabilla said. Environmental activists say Australian plastic waste was in this rubbish heap in East Java, Indonesia, in 2024. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Most plastic waste was no longer burned in people's homes but rather converted into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and burned in a designated facility, she said. "But I think this only relocates the problem rather than actually solving it," Ms Salsabilla said, adding the facility still required humans to sort the waste. Emissions from open waste burning, such as burning plastics, include a variety of air pollutants, some of which have particularly harmful effects on both the climate and health, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). "Exposure to these pollutants, whether short or long-term, can lead to adverse health effects such as coughing, skin irritation, respiratory diseases, and other negative outcomes," the WHO says on its website. Environmentalists say plastic waste from Australia is often found in East Java. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Ms Salsabilla said the waste imported to East Java was coming from places including Australia, the US and Europe.

events.title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
events.summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035 BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers. The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey. India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States. Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy. The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure . The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced. “If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.” The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan. Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products. “So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said. The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source. India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas. Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses. However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember. India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035. Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining. Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power. China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift Peoria police urge evacuations after reported bomb threat at Illinois plant Researchers at Berkeley estimate that beyond approximately 35 gigawatts of coal capacity already under construction, additional coal plants would not be economically necessary under the country's new clean energy goals. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets. Meeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers. India’s rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits.

events.title: Flights slowly resume after US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop
events.summary: Transportation secretary Sean Duffy says the airspace is now open and the problem has been identified Chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA Flights in the US have slowly started resuming after being grounded for several hours on Friday due to a major communications outage, but authorities have warned that a return to normal operations will take time. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop about four hours after it was declared on Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware , and throwing airports into sudden chaos. The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website . “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon .” Duffy said the federal government had “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”. At a White House briefing on Friday evening, Duffy said the trouble began at 3.36pm, when air traffic control centres experienced ​instability in radar and communications systems. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” he said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.” But the briefing on Friday evening with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”. A notice from the FAA had earlier said the ground stop was imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”. Duffy said more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued. Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”. “There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters. The flight grounding caused widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo. Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways. Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos. As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers on Friday evening, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said. Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations. “Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day. In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary. “There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.” According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US. The FAA said in a statement that they “thoroughly tested” their systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume. San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart. John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport. US airlines including United, Delta, Southwest and American Airlines announced they were resuming flights on Friday night after the ground stop was lifted.

events.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any connection. By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday. Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: PearlBone gets FDA clearance for world's largest orthopaedic market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts PearlBone from WA wins FDA approval for US orthopaedic market The PearlBone FDA approval follows years of testing, evaluation and development. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls ) A bone graft substitute made from Kimberley pearl shells has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Adminstration (FDA). The product is the first of its kind to repair bone fractures using nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl. Marine Biomedical says there is more to be done before the product can treat patients, but regulatory approval is an important first step. Mother-of-pearl harvested in Western Australia's north could soon be used to fill bone fractures for patients in the United States. WA biotech company Marine Biomedical has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its bone graft substitute, PearlBone. A manufacturing facility for PearlBone was built in Broome in 2022. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar ) The product is the first of its kind to be developed from nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl. The iridescent material has been used for ornamental items, jewellery and even buttons. But Marine Biomedical chief executive Rolee Kumar said it was also effective for bone repair and regeneration. PearlBone will be used to repair bone fractures for patients in the United States. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar ) "The material of what the mother-of-pearl is made out of, all of these are actually building blocks of our bone too," she said. "So in a way, it's not surprising when we do these studies we see PearlBone facilitates bone healing." The United States is the world's largest orthopaedics market, with the bone grafts and substitutes sector valued at $US1.1 billion ($1.5 billion). Ms Kumar said FDA clearance was an important first step in entering the US market, but there were more hurdles to be overcome before it could be sold. Rolee Kumar says PearlBone is as safe and effective as existing bone repair materials. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar ) "We've gone through a process where PearlBone was compared against another existing bone graft that's established itself in the market," she said. "We've been able to demonstrate PearlBone is as safe and efficacious as the predicate device ." She said the company also hoped to bring the product to Australian customers in future and expand into other treatments like dental work. 'Exciting' opportunity for pearl industry Marine Biomedical was established in 2021 through a partnership with local Broome pearling business Willie Creek Pearls and research expertise from the University of Western Australia (UWA). Paul Birch says shells are prepped at the farm before being transported to the manufacturing facility in Broome. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls ) Willie Creek chief executive Paul Birch said the collaboration was an exciting opportunity for the pearling industry. "And with more research, there might be other parts of the oyster that can be used for other biomedical technologies." The shells farmed by Willie Creek for pearl production undergo cleaning and preparations before being transported to the Marine Biomedical manufacturing facility in Broome. Mr Birch said there was an abundance of pearl shell available at the farm to meet current requirements, but this could change as the product demand increased. "So hopefully at one point in time, it might be something the entire industry is able to be involved in and supply to Marine Biomedical," he said. The shell is harvested at Willie Creek Pearls, off the Kimberley coast. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls ) UWA biomedical and health innovation director Kevin Pfleger said it was an exciting time for medical research in WA. The professor said it was common for products to gain approval in the United States market before returning to Australia. "One of the big reasons is because even though we're a very large country geographically, we've got a relatively small population," Professor Pfleger said. "So if we get approval in the US first, it means it's much more economically viable for us to then come back and market in Australia." Willie Creek Pearls, based on the outskirts of Broome in WA's north, will provide the product for PearlBone. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins ) Professor Pfleger said the clearance was an "inspiring" achievement for others in the industry. "The next point is obviously making sales, getting patients and benefiting from that and getting surgeons using it," he said. "But regulatory approval is critical.
