events.title: FAA lifts rare nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA on Friday lifted a rare nationwide ground stop that impacted more than 14,500 flights after a major outage affecting the US’ air communications system. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system,” and said the government didn’t suspect any nefarious causes, such as a terrorist or cyber attack. He said the issues were connected to old equipment that was overloaded, and that flights should start taking off again over the next day. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said, while trying to reassure travelers that the US remains “the safest system in the world.” The stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, caused widespread disruption and prompted shares in airlines to drop. American Airlines shares dropped more than 2% in after-hours trading, while United shares fell 1.6%. Those airlines are now navigating thousands of rebookings and frustrated passengers. This is only the third time the agency has ever issued such an order. The most recent was in January 2023; before that, air traffic was halted nationwide on Sept. 11, 2001. Duffy used a large portion of a press conference on Friday evening to blame the Republican-controlled Congress for withholding funds for air-traffic control repairs. He urged lawmakers to approve $50 billion to upgrade infrastructure through an emergency funding bill. “I’ve asked, the president’s asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Albanese, Bowen caught talking phones and 'dicks' in hot-mic gaffe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen caught on hot mic at COP31 climate summit A private exchange between Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen was inadvertently recorded at the COP31 summit in Türkiye. The prime minister's office said the pair were joking between meetings, but the Coalition has criticised the hot mic moment as "weird and gross". Mr Albanese has travelled to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit, while Mr Bowen remains in Türkiye. A conversation between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen about phone radiation and "dicks" has been caught on camera on the sidelines of a UN conference. The Coalition has criticised the hot mic moment as "weird and gross", accusing the pair of behaving like "14-year-old schoolboys". Mr Albanese's office said the pair was sharing a "joke" between meetings when the exchange was recorded by Australian media at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye. The comments were captured shortly before a business roundtable spruiking renewable energy transition investment opportunities in Australia began overnight on Friday. Anthony Albanese left Türkiye shortly after a business roundtable. ( AAP ) Cameras were rolling ahead of the event, during which time Mr Albanese and Mr Bowen were privately chatting to each other. Mr Albanese put his phone in his jacket pocket and — as he did so — told Mr Bowen he had heard it was better to store the device away from the heart because "it can interfere with your rhythm". Mr Bowen responded in a joking tone, asking if it was because the phone was "a little bit radioactive". The prime minister laughed, saying the idea "makes absolute sense". Mr Bowen then responded he was more conscious about putting his phone in his pants pocket. Mr Albanese asked, "Because of your dick?" The pair laughed and Mr Bowen agreed, adding it was "arguably more important than the heart". On Sunday, Liberal deputy leader Jane Hume said the gaffe undermined Labor's message about pitching Australia to the world on climate. "It's bad enough that these guys sent almost 200 bureaucrats to Türkiye at a cost of more than $2 million and spent $36,000 [sic] of your taxpayer money on a coffee cart so that Greta Thunberg could have a free latte, but they justified it on the basis they were 'selling Australia to the world', 'attracting investment from overseas'," she said. "Well, great salesmen you clowns are. "The only thing you've attracted to Australia is ridicule on the world stage." Hot-mic gaffe came ahead of roundtable The exchange, which did not appear to be overheard by anyone in the room but was captured by a news camera microphone preparing to record the opening remarks at the event, was later broadcast by Channel 7 after it was noticed in production. A spokesperson for Mr Albanese's office said, "They were having a joke in between meetings." Labor frontbencher Murray Watt agreed that the comments were made in jest. "This is really just about people having a joke," he said. Mr Watt laughed off a question about where he kept his own phone, and defended Australia's presence and performance at COP31. "I know there's been a lot of criticism from some quarters about every aspect of this COP, but the reality is participating in and in fact leading the discussions at COP is in Australia's national interest," he said. During the official proceedings of the business roundtable, the prime minister made a pitch to international investors to back Australia's clean energy transition. "If you're an investor, there's nowhere you'd rather be than Australia," he said. Mr Albanese said having abundant renewable resources, critical minerals and a stable investment environment meant Australia was well placed to capitalise on the multi-trillion-dollar industry. events.title: Trump doesn’t plan to raise Nvidia, spy issue during China trip: U.S. officials
events.summary: President Donald Trump does not plan to raise the issue of a suspected Chinese spy having an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming trip to China, senior U.S. officials said. Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The White House said that Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday. Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19. The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling "The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified. "In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there." Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement." "When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said. Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue." China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless. Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips. The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China. During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump. "I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said. "Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

events.title: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket
events.summary: SpaceX launched its 15th Starship test flight on Friday. In the test flight, Elon Musk's company tried but failed to recover both stages of the massive Starship rocket, with the booster splashing down in the Gulf of Mexico and exploding. Starship is key to SpaceX's plans to grow its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket. The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames. Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket. Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC. The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday. Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets. In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X. When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential." Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service. Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month . Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX .

events.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
events.summary: Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after a tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans , officials said Friday. The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current. "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
events.summary: Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short. Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas . The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top. As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers. SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The cause of that diversion remains unknown. “That certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” said Kate Tice, SpaceX’s director of quality management, but she noted the booster’s return was in line with “rigorous safety checks”. Early in the webcast, SpaceX simulated the return. The entire rocket was expected to be grabbed in the launch tower’s “chopstick” mechanical arms. Friday’s test did not rise to the double-catch mantle, which Elon Musk had described early in November as a “critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary”. Still, the flight is still poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage. Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster. The Starship, meanwhile, has continued to sail through space at over 26,000 km/h at an altitude of 270km. The launch went on as scheduled despite a nationwide ground stop that disrupted hundreds of flights. Flights to the west coast from Hawaii were temporarily paused, then resumed on Friday due to space debris from the launch, according to the island’s transportation agency. As in the past, Starship carried satellites for Starlink, SpaceX’s internet service wing, three of which were fitted with cameras to analyze the rocket’s heat shield. The data plays a role in determining if the spacecraft is ready to return. SpaceX chief executive Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability” as a vehicle, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars. Nasa has contracted SpaceX, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028. Musk has cast his reusable rocket as a buffer against the enormous costs associated with future space travel. SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws. In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time , although its engine failed during the ascent.

events.title: Questions remain after Nvidia CEO's departure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Despite Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, questions remain over the whole affair Jensen Huang was one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO. The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs. While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain. China's foreign ministry said allegations of spying in relation to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang (no relation) were "unsubstantiated" and "smears against China". ( Reuters: CTI ) When reports of an espionage plot against Mr Huang first emerged almost a week ago, top Republicans called on the tech executive to front Congress later this month. Senator Tim Scott reiterated those demands after Mr Huang's resignation, saying there were "serious concerns" to address. Separately the chairs of three House committees — the foreign affairs panel, the China select committee and the intelligence committee — wrote to Mr Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter requiring them to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? Mr Huang and Mr Teter have not publicly commented on the requests, but they could face subpoenas to compel their appearances. "There are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three committee chairs wrote in the letter. Mr Huang is also yet to comment publicly after reports emerged he allegedly had another two extra-marital affairs — both with Nvidia employees. His last statement was on Sunday, local time, when he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of over 40 years but did not name who he had been intimate with. In that statement, he said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security". Meanwhile, Nvidia and Mr Huang are facing a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders . Questions for the US administration Next to Mr Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been called on to testify in front of Congress on concerns he did not do enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China. In December 2025 Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to China in exchange for a cut of the sales, after Mr Huang argued that restrictions only accelerated Beijing's own AI development. That was despite concerns from both sides of Congress about China's access to the technology. Howard Lutnick is facing pressure over whether the US government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China. ( Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz ) Mr Lutnick has also been criticised for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist. In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held ⁠off adding more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the list. The US ⁠has not added to the list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. Previous reports said that Mr Lutnick's US Commerce Department had not blacklisted new Chinese companies for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Under-Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler has been called on to testify at a December 3 hearing as well. The Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. In America's pursuit to lead the AI race, Mr Huang had become a close ally of Mr Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him. He has visited the White House at least five times during Mr Trump's second term, is part of a council advising the president on science and technology, and accompanied Mr Trump on a trip to Beijing in May. The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $US25 million ($36.7 million) for Mr Trump's contentious White House ballroom project, while the president disclosed buying and selling Nvidia stock earlier this year. The New York Times reported Mr Trump was briefed on intelligence findings about a suspected espionage effort against Mr Huang about a year ago, and took no action.

events.title: Regional bands say it's now cheaper to do a gig in London than interstate
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Touring Australia no longer tenable for internationally-renowned local bands as regional airfares soar It now costs Arnhem Land band King Stingray more to fly to gigs interstate than to shows in the US. ( Supplied ) Managers of internationally-renowned Aussie bands say high airfares are pricing regional artists out of the market. It comes as the Productivity Commission this week revealed a widening gap between regional and metropolitan airfares. Yothu Yindi manager Alan James says travel costs will put emerging artists out of business before their careers have taken off. With the cost of regional airfares soaring, musicians and band managers say touring has become untenable for both famous bands and emerging artists from regional Australia. An interim Productivity Commission report released this week revealed a significant price gap between regional and metropolitan flight routes. It found long regional and remote flights cost 67 per cent more on average than major city routes, while short regional flights cost 173 per cent more per kilometre. Alan James says high airfares are pricing Yothu Yindi "out of the market" for live music. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Yothu Yindi manager Alan James said the cost of travel had forced the internationally-renowned band from Arnhem Land to turn down shows within Australia. "It's $5,200 return from Gove to Brisbane, it would be cheaper for us to go do a concert in London than it would be to do a concert in a capital city of Australia," he said. Yothu Yindi bassist Stuart Kellaway — who now manages fellow Arnhem Land rock band King Stingray — said the next generation band's recent flights to shows in the United States cost less than domestic flights. Yothu Yindi played the 2025 Garma Festival but had to turn down shows interstate. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) "We've had to turn down three or four shows in the past month or so because it just wasn't going to work financially with the airfare components," he said. Mr Kellaway the sky-high airfares were affecting the ability even of artists in the prime of their careers to make a living. "With streaming and everything else, gigs are one of the last, decent income streams for bands," he said. Limited options limiting opportunities Mr James said while all bands were impacted by the exorbitant airfares, for new artists in particular, the costs could make sustainable careers in the music industry impossible. "If you're an emerging group, you've got no shot, you're out of the business," he said. "It really means for musicians, if you're not based in a capital city, then you're not in the market anymore." King Stingray manager Stuart Kellaway (third from left) says bands based outside capital cities are "not in the market anymore". ( ABC / Matt Garrick ) Both Mr James and Mr Kellaway said they had noticed a decline in the number of airlines servicing Arnhem Land throughout the course of Yothu Yindi's career. Their observations align with the findings of the Productivity Commission's report, which noted competition in regional aviation was severely limited. Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients. Several airlines have reduced NT services recently, leaving flights between Darwin and capitals such as Sydney, Adelaide and Canberra serviced only by Qantas and its subsidiary Jetstar. In a statement, a Qantas spokesperson said rising costs had dramatically influenced the price of tickets in and out of the NT. "Aviation costs, including labour, airport charges and government air traffic control fees, are rising faster than the rate of inflation, while fuel costs also remain significantly higher," they said. "Great value fares can still be found on flights to and from the Northern Territory and we encourage customers to book ahead whenever possible to secure the best fare." events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO: Some prediction market traders bet Jensen Huang will make a comeback
events.summary: Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to Jensen Huang, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable. Some Kalshi traders bet Nvidia may rehire Jensen Huang as permanent CEO by 2028, even after his Nov 12 resignation. Ian Buck leads the market at 33%. Huang stepped down after reports of three affairs and admitted ties to Alice Huang, who is suspected by the US of spying for China. Supporters, including Shaun Maguire, Elon Musk and Donald Trump, praised him as vital to AI leadership. Nvidia faces big risks because it has no succession plan and 60 executives report to Huang. Shares rebounded after the shock exit, but Washington scrutiny and investor concern remain. SINGAPORE – Jensen Huang has stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive , but some traders on the prediction market Kalshi are betting that the chipmaker will name him its next permanent CEO before 2029. Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to one of the AI industry’s most influential leaders, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable. On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US but banned in Singapore, the implied odds of Nvidia naming Huang as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028 rose as high as 15% on the evening of Nov 13, before falling to around 7%. Nvidia executive Ian Buck is currently in the lead, with a 33% chance on Kalshi of becoming Nvidia’s next CEO. Buck is vice-president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia. He leads its multibillion-dollar data centre business, which supplies AI chips and software to major tech companies worldwide. Kalshi put the odds of Colette Kress getting the permanent job at 13%. Kress is Nvidia’s chief financial officer and was made interim CEO following Huang’s resignation on Nov 12. She is tied with Rene Haas, chief executive of British chip design company Arm Holdings. Other executives Kalshi traders are betting on include Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji, Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora, Nvidia executive vice-president Jay Puri, and AMD chairman and CEO Lisa Su. Puri oversees Nvidia’s global sales, business development and partnerships. Tech executives, investors and fans have voiced support for Huang, who stepped down following reports of three affairs. He has admitted to being involved with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based, Alibaba-backed data centre firm Megaspeed . She is suspected by the US of spying for China. “Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in an X post on Nov 8. He concluded that Nvidia’s Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”. About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post, noting: “I agree.” Maguire added on Nov 12 that Huang’s ousting “will leave a huge void, with the loss of a technical, aggressive, founder-CEO. “The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void.” Even US President Donald Trump called Huang before he stepped down, urging him to keep fighting for his job , according to The New York Times, quoting sources familiar with the call. After Huang announced his resignation, Trump wrote in a Nov 12 Truth Social post : “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – Tim Cook of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!” On prediction market Polymarket, trading implied a 6% chance that Nvidia would name Apple executive chairman Tim Cook as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028. There is also a 11% probability on Polymarket that Nvidia does not find a CEO by Dec 31, 2028. Regardless of who takes over, Nvidia’s stakes are high because so much of the AI industry relies on chips, delivered by a company that Huang co-founded, transformed and led for the past 30 years. A total of 60 executives across the firm report directly to him, and there is no succession plan. Huang’s departure therefore leaves Nvidia investors weighing several risks, Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson said in a Nov 13 note. Nvidia is “about to find out whether Huang’s grip on the company and flat organisational structure was effectively storing up trouble”, said Wilson. While a successor could keep Nvidia on the same course, Huang’s detailed knowledge of its products and his hands-on management style is unique and would be hard to replicate. Wilson also pointed to scrutiny in Washington, citing reported US Justice Department inquiries involving Megaspeed and Alice Huang, and a request by three House committee chairs for a closed-door briefing on Nov 18 over national security concerns. He expects Nvidia’s relationship with Washington to become more difficult, even with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s support. Investors, however, appear to think otherwise.

events.title: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
events.summary: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia but is at the beginning of growing calls from U.S. lawmakers to answer for what has transpired involving the company he co-founded. Huang, the enigmatic CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers are gearing up to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal. Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief Nvidia bulls mount uphill battle into earnings Nvidia earnings call drama: Will Jensen Huang talk 'Trump' and China chips after Xi summit? U.S. clears H200 chip sales to 10 China firms as Nvidia CEO looks for breakthrough Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers." And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.

events.title: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons' firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
events.summary: Cantor Fitzgerald’s reported Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found. That was the period when, according to Axios, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. The Wall Street firm, which Lutnick formerly chaired and is now run by his sons, maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives. Those relationships have come into sharper focus following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and revelations about Lutnick’s handling of national security concerns involving the chipmaker. There is no evidence that Cantor's business interests influenced Lutnick's decisions. In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC. The Wall Street firm liked what it heard. "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock. Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings. The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11. By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina. Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership. Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5. An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia. Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great." "His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC. There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions. "Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings. As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday. Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary. But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.

events.title: Amazon’s new Kindle Colorsoft is a premium e-reader with a premium price
events.summary: Amazon recently unveiled its refreshed Kindle lineup , introducing a new basic Kindle , Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new Kindle Colorsoft starts at $290, while the Signature Edition, which I’ve spent the past few weeks testing, costs $320. The base model comes with 16GB of storage, while the Signature Edition doubles that to 32GB and is available in graphite or a maroon-like Fig finish with an aluminum back. Amazon first brought color to its Kindle lineup in 2024 with the launch of the original Colorsoft. The latest model is lighter and thinner than its predecessor and features an edge-to-edge display. If you already own the first-generation Colorsoft, there’s little reason to upgrade. The core reading experience remains largely the same. Both models have a 7-inch color E-Ink display, 300ppi resolution for black-and-white content and 150ppi for color. However, if you’ve been eyeing a color e-reader, the new Colorsoft is worth considering if you can get past the hefty price tag. Unlike standard Kindles, which display everything in black and white, the Colorsoft brings your digital bookshelf to life with their original colors. This makes it a particularly appealing option for readers who enjoy comics, graphic novels, or cookbooks, where color makes a big difference. It’s also great for readers who like highlighting passages in different colors. It’s worth noting that colors on the Colorsoft are still relatively muted and not as vibrant as what you’d see on an iPad. Still, they add a welcome splash of color and make a noticeable difference compared to the black-and-white displays of standard Kindles. The Colorsoft lets you adjust the screen’s color temperature, so you can switch to a warmer, more yellow-toned display that’s easier on the eyes when reading at night. There’s also an auto-adjusting brightness option that comes in handy. When it comes to battery life, Amazon says that the Colorsoft can last up to eight weeks on a single charge, compared to up to 12 weeks for the Paperwhite. During my testing, I didn’t have to stress about charging the Colorsoft because like other Kindles, its battery lasts a relatively long time compared to other everyday electronics. One small but welcome improvement on the new Colorsoft is the repositioned power button. On the previous generation, it was on the bottom of the device next to the charging port, making it easy to accidentally press it when handling the Kindle. On the new model, Amazon has moved it to the top-right edge, where it’s less likely to get in the way. I quite like this change, and found the new location more intuitive when powering the device on and off. I enjoyed the premium feel of the aluminum back on the Signature Edition. Although Amazon provided a case with my review unit, I rarely used it, and the finish held up well. While the slimmer design isn’t a major change, I found the new Colorsoft quite comfortable to hold compared to older Kindle devices. For those who enjoy reading in the bath or by the pool, the Colorsoft is waterproof, so you don’t have to worry about accidental splashes or spills damaging the e-reader. One thing I appreciated about the Colorsoft was how infrequently the screen needed to refresh, which was something I noticed more often with the larger Kindle Scribe Colorsoft . I also didn’t experience any noticeable ghosting, where text from previous pages lingers on the screen, which is common on some e-readers. The Signature Edition supports a magnetic cover with built-in page-turn buttons that connects to the pogo pins on the back of the device, but I can’t speak to this experience because I didn’t have access to the case. The biggest drawback of the Colorsoft is its price. It’s a steep investment for a device that’s just used for reading. That said, if you really want a color display, the Colorsoft is definitely worth considering. For everyone else, it’s a nice upgrade, but far from a must-have. Many readers would be better off with the basic Kindle or Paperwhite, which start at $169.99 and $199.99, respectively. events.title: Even billionaires need human connections in AI age: Business Network International CEO
events.summary: Business Network International CEO Mary Kennedy Thompson says the world could see its first billionaire solopreneur within the next five years. SINGAPORE – While fears of AI-driven job losses persist, a new perspective on artificial intelligence is gaining ground: Workforce disruption is giving rise to more solo business owners, or solopreneurs, who will need human connections to succeed. The world could see its first billionaire solopreneur within the next five years, as AI tools take over functions such as accounting, finance, marketing and administration that once required a large organisation. But however brilliant such a one-person, billion-dollar operator may be, connections will always matter in business, said Mary Kennedy Thompson, chief executive of Business Network International (BNI), the world’s largest business referral and networking organisation. As AI continues to disrupt the workforce, this generation of solo business owners will need to master networking and find a community they can belong to, Thompson told The Straits Times in an interview. With the technology becoming more prevalent and powerful, the need for human connections becomes even more critical because people prefer to do business with those they know and trust – and face-to-face interactions build that trust, she said. Thompson said more firms from AI-related sectors have been increasingly expressing interest in joining the BNI network . As AI advances and people’s understanding of it improves, she believes BNI can help businesses establish credibility through human connections as AI makes it harder to distinguish genuine capabilities from convincing claims. “People are going to want proof points, and organisations like BNI that can provide those proof points and the human connection will grow faster.” Additionally, the organisation has observed a fall in the average age of its members over the past three to five years as more young people take the plunge into entrepreneurship. “Gen Zs are more entrepreneurial than millennials,” said Thompson. She noted that chapters consisting entirely of business owners aged 30 and below already exist in Singapore and the US, while the youngest member of the local network is a 21-year-old running an events management business. Creating a robust business referral network Founded in 1985, BNI is a membership-only organisation that helps business owners develop networks and share customer leads. Spanning 78 countries, its global footprint is organised into local chapters, each typically comprising around 35 business owners or professionals from different industries who meet weekly to share business needs and leads. In Singapore, BNI has grown from a network dominated by financial and property professionals in its first decade to more than 2,000 members from diverse industries today. Established in 2000, it now counts business development staff from several multinational companies among its members. No two professions within a chapter are the same, ensuring there is no competition within the group and that members can refer clients to one another’s businesses. Often, that results in collaboratio n , said Thompson. A chapter could include a property agent, a lawyer, a plumber and an electrician all helping one another with leads or even working together on the same project. “Every chapter meeting that we attend is a business development opportunity. That is to allow you to educate another business owner about who you are, what you do, how you value it and what businesses you’re looking out for,” she said. She noted that on average, a BNI member gets US$71 (S$91) in closed business for every US$1 spent on dues, with a one-year membership in Singapore costing around $1,700. “I don’t know any kind of marketing that has that kind of return on investment,” she added. “When you walk into a room, a lot of times what happens in networking is you and I are talking, we share greetings and pleasantries, but we didn’t get anything accomplished.” But if both parties understand the science of having a one-to-one conversation, a meaningful business lead could be developed in 30 minutes. That would be most beneficial for any business owner when developing a new connection, she noted. Over the last 12 months, the global BNI network generated more than 17 million referrals amounting to roughly US$27 billion in member-to-member business. Thompson herself has referred more than US$30,000 worth of business since the start of 2026. Beyond facilitating business development, BNI views its role as equipping entrepreneurs with the connection-building skills needed to scale their companies successfully. Thompson pointed to the weekly chapter meetings as regular practice for BNI members such that the honed skills become second nature in the real world. “It’s not just going to a meeting and talking.

events.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
events.summary: The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January. Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that state officials have warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage. Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience. Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times . The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that they'll be kicked out because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements. This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
events.summary: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.

The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. The FAA has not yet confirmed a reason for the stop. "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually. The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related. We'll update this story as more information becomes available.® Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment. Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

events.title: Nvidia stock suffers longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.7 trillion
events.summary: Nvidia shares plunged 13% this week, and just wrapped their sixth straight weekly decline. That's the longest losing streak since 2012. The chip giant has lost roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap since the slide began in early October. Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012. The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during the losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap and it pushed the company below Apple . Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor. Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair , this one with the company's vice president of health care. By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world. "With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote. Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout. In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets. Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term." "The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end lower as Nvidia uncertainty weighs on tech shares
events.summary: A ticker shows Nvidia trades as futures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange's NYSE American in New York City, on Nov 13. NEW YORK - The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed lower on Nov 13, as concerns about Nvidia pressured technology shares , while a reading on inflation failed to alter expectations for more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve. Nvidia’s shares fell 2% and recorded their sixth straight week of declines, their longest streak since October 2012, after CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday. He stepped down after revelations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for China . The Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Huang. The uncertainty about leadership at the chipmaker has raised concerns about the durability of the AI trade, given Nvidia’s primary role in the industry’s boom and its financial ties to a host of companies in the sector, which has been a pillar of the bull market in equities. “The tech trade, the AI trade, Nvidia is going to go through a period of volatility, and you’re going to see the bulls and bears kind of wrestle on where this narrative goes through the rest of the year ... there’s been a loss of confidence,” said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial in Troy, Michigan. “The market and investors are trying to navigate what does the AI theme look like when we have the absence of Jensen Huang, who was basically the AI champion and willing to use Nvidia’s balance sheet to fund a lot of this AI expansion. That’s gone.” Sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm elections last week also raised concerns about government regulations potentially slowing growth among AI-related companies. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 50.46 points, or 0.10%, to 52,347.55, the S&P 500 lost 30.73 points, or 0.40%, to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 229.82 points, or 0.91%, to 25,136.27. Despite the recent volatility, the major indexes recorded weekly gains, as the Nasdaq and S&P 500 both snapped a four-week streak of declines. For the week, the S&P 500 gained 2.51%, the Nasdaq rose 2.27% and the Dow climbed 2.07%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.4%, with Advanced Micro Devices dropping 8.8% and Broadcom down 4.8% as the biggest drags on the index. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius also ended lower, while data center-related firms IREN lost 6.7% and Applied Digital fell 5.8%. The losses come ahead of AI company Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO next week, which could test investor appetite for established AI heavyweights as money potentially shifts toward the new entrant. The S&P 500 technology index shed 1.7% and was the worst-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors. But Microsoft ended 0.2% higher, as it erased earlier declines after a global outage that included its Outlook and Teams products began to ease. Airlines dropped in the final minutes of trading with the NYSE Arca airline index closing down 1.4% after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop of all departing flights on Friday. The agency said this was “due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety” after it earlier reported serious air traffic control communications issues. On the economic front, the Labor Department said US producer prices were slightly cooler than expected in October, but still shot up 6.5% year over year, the largest annual gain since November 2022. The data kept expectations for a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed’s December meeting completely locked in, with markets pricing in a roughly 10% chance for an outsized 50-basis-point increase, according to CME FedWatch. Comments from multiple Fed officials earlier this week suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen. The sentiment for additional rate hikes was echoed by more Fed officials on Friday, including San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly, who said her “bias” is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, while Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said tighter monetary policy is coming because of high inflation. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.28-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange and by a 1.61-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 9 new 52-week highs and 1 new low, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 37 new highs and 340 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.38 billion shares, compared with the 18.52 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Airlines scramble to get flights in air after planes grounded across US — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US officials lift order grounding flights after thousands of travellers affected — as it happened Here is a summary of the day's key events: US officials have lifted a national ground stop order for all departing flights hours after thousands of travellers, including Australians, were impacted. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed an "old air traffic control system" for an outage that led to the ground stop. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says there is not yet any evidence suggesting a cyber attack was the cause. More than 7,000 flights were cancelled during the order. The halt is just the second ground stop issued by regulators since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. Choose what information you see below by using filters Thank you for sticking with us throughout our coverage of today's US air traffic control centre outage . We're ending our live updates here but, as always, you can keep up to date with the latest information on this story and other news via the ABC News website and mobile app . Until next time, have a fantastic afternoon! How Australians were caught in the mayhem of a nationwide US flights ground stop As we've been reporting to you throughout the day, Australians have found themselves among the thousands of people whose travels have been halted due to the US ground stop order. My ABC News colleague Kristy Sexton-McGrath has collated some of their stories in the link below. 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos 📷: US airspace, flights and airports come to a standstill Everything you need to know about the US air traffic ground stop In the hours after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued an immediate pause of departing flights across the country due to "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety" , air traffic ground to a halt. If you're looking to catch up on everything that happened following that order and the impact it had on national and international air traffic, my colleague Audrey Courty has covered it all in the link below: What we know about the US air traffic communications outage Safety investigators heading to earlier ship crash affected by air traffic outage In other news from the US today, more than 100 people were rescued after a tanker collided with a river cruise boat near the port of New Orleans . In the aftermath of that accident, the US's National Transport Safety Bureau (NTSB) announced it was launching an investigation and sending a team to Louisiana . While initially unrelated to today's nationwide halt on flights, both news stories have since merged. The NTSB has released a statement in the past 20 minutes saying the ground stop order has impacted its earlier plans. "Due to the residual delays from the nationwide ground stop, the NTSB will no longer send a board member and will instead send a team of investigators by ground to the scene of the vessel collision in New Orleans," it said in a statement on X. Passengers stuck on tarmac for more than 5 hours after cross-country flight Frustration is continuing to grow for travellers who are still impacted by the fallout of today's ground stop order. Among them is Ruth Coles , who jumped on an Alaska Airlines plane from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey and flew five hours across the country to Los Angeles . But, after her plane landed on the tarmac at Los Angeles International Airport , that is where she currently remains. She has told The Associated Press she was flying to visit her sister and attend a festival when she learnt about the ground stop order mid-flight. Passengers on her plane have been told they are waiting for a gate to open up, she said. "The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line," Coles said, but that was more than five hours ago . Coles said they have been given soft drinks and cookies and been allowed to use the restroom. Frustrated, she posted on X multiple times asking the airport for help and messaged Alaska Airlines support. The airline told her they were trying to park the flight in a remote area and provide bus transportation back to the terminal. FAA systems 'reliable' after earlier disruptions With flight services resuming across the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has released its own message to assure travellers the country is safe for air travel. It's worth pointing out that while thousands of planes were grounded and many more pulled out of the skies over the US, Donald Trump was mostly silent.

events.title: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance—2 habits that take 'a few seconds' can help you avoid similar traps
events.summary: Work AI is making a mess of how humans interact at work Psychology and Relationships Using AI chatbots mainly for companionship can lower feelings of wellbeing Work Some job seekers are refusing to do AI interviews, even in a tough market Psychology and Relationships I'm a psychologist who studies couples—to avoid feeling 'quietly resentful of each other,' make 1 simple change Earn Are you richer than you think? How to find out—and what to do if you are The biggest heist in cryptocurrency history began with small mistakes many internet users make. A hacking group tied to North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance. The operation was sophisticated, involving fake job interviews and malicious code. But it was also mundane. Although artificial intelligence played a role in the hack, this was not a cyberattack of the future, propelled by swarms of AI agents. Rather, it relied on humans who made some basic errors, like clicking a link because it appeared first on a search results page or trusting strangers at a fake company without taking a few seconds to look them up. We work at the Digital Inquiry Group , a nonprofit that researches how people evaluate online information and creates free, evidence-based curriculum that helps people decide what to trust. In over a decade of research, we've found that people frequently engage in online behavior that makes them more likely to get duped. Two simple strategies can help you better navigate today's information landscape, from traditional phishing to misleading social posts to AI fakes. Here's how. When searching online, the first result is not always the best or the safest The Binance heist began when one of the company's engineers downloaded compromised software. That engineer, according to the Reuters investigation of the hack , clicked on a sponsored search result that appeared higher on the results page and directed them to the malicious code. Our research at the Digital Inquiry Group suggests internet users frequently behave as if first is best. They click on the first thing they see. They incorrectly associate a higher placement with vetted content, ceding judgment to tech company algorithms. Students have gone so far as to tell us "Google is almost never wrong" or "AI is always right." Professional fact-checkers commonly practice click restraint . They understand that whether you're searching on the internet or querying a chatbot, first isn't always best. If you're researching an organization, the first link will often be to its own site, which is hardly likely to disclose anything that's wrong with it. So the next time you search for something online, be wary of links to sponsored content, the organization you're investigating, or to open platforms where anyone can post and information isn't verified, such as Quora or Reddit. Read the brief snippets beneath each link, and make a more informed choice about what to open. Always ask yourself: Who is behind this information? What makes them credible? Look for people and organizations that have direct expertise on the topic at hand, or have processes to ensure the accuracy of information, such as news outlets that employ editors and fact-checkers. 'The internet is a precarious place'—always get external verification Binance says it caught that first malicious download, replaced the device and changed passwords. But later, another engineer downloaded compromised code as part of what they thought was a job interview, which included a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fake company. It's tempting to think that the engineer should have seen something was off. But the internet is a precarious place because bad actors know how to make content feel legitimate. Binance says its employee was snared by a hacker posing as an HR rep who "shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust." When they encounter a piece of unfamiliar content, professional fact-checkers don't just read it closely — they read laterally . They open new browser tabs to see what other, credible sources have to say. Fact-checkers know that bad actors make themselves look good on their home turf, but that it's a lot harder to fake a good reputation across the internet. The next time you encounter something unfamiliar online, look for authoritative sources that can shed light on the person or organization. You might find a news article that confirms the claim you're looking into, or a report that identifies a supposedly neutral source as biased. In some cases, you may find nothing at all, which is a signal in itself: if you look up a company that reached out to you and find no external confirmation of its existence, that should be an immediate red flag. Had that first Binance engineer engaged in click restraint and verified the source of the software, they might have avoided the malicious download.
