Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters What, you didn't actually want to fact-check it yourself, did you? Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 16 hours ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 22 hours ago Alibaba's Qwen3.8 re-educated with a more Western worldview 1 day ago Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view 1 day ago A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs 1 day ago The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI. It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension , or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts , combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies , flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like. It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead. Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review. If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with. “We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin." Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system. According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something. Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation. A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then. To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline , potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. AI users are reportedly less likely to admit they don’t know something, even though use of AI has been found in studies to l essen brain activity , leading to poorer retention of facts and worse performance on tests. Is using more AI the solution to the problem? In an ideal world, we’d all just put the computers down and go touch grass, but we’re not in an ideal world: We’re living in the age of AI. LogicLens is free but requires sign-up and restricts nonpaying users to 15 analyses a day and 100 over the course of a month. A $4.99 monthly subscription removes those analysis caps.

events.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
events.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer. Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership, including: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.). Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.). Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine). Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.). Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.). Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda. Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership. The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios . Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen. Who's backing Schumer? Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week. Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King , along with Schumer himself. Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.). Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race. Senators who haven't picked a side Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate. Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership. Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate. Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate. The 2028 factor Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats. Ossoff and Booker , both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard. Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly , also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer. Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender. Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection . What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1. Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

events.title: Trump to rule on tariffs for Australian lamb after trade commissioners disagree
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Trump to rule on tariffs for Australian lamb after US trade commissioners disagree Some trade experts believe Donald Trump is likely to put new tariffs on Australian lamb as a result of the decision. ( Reuters: Leah Millis ) A US trade investigation has left the door open to putting tariffs on lamb imports. Australia argued against tariffs during the probe. US President Donald Trump will make the final decision, likely early next year. A US trade panel reviewing Australian lamb imports into the United States has been unable to agree on whether the American industry has been hurt by the imports. The rare tie-vote at the US International Trade Commission (USITC) means US President Donald Trump will ultimately decide whether to place tariffs or other trade restrictions on the Australian meat. "A tie vote … means the president can decide which vote (affirmative or negative) he chooses the 'winning' vote," Georgetown University's Jennifer Hillman, a former USITC commissioner, told the ABC. Australia has been warning the US that any new tariff would just push up prices for American lamb-eaters. Most of the lamb imported into the US comes from Australia and New Zealand. More than 100,000 tonnes of Australian lamb was exported to the US last year. It was valued at more than $1 billion. The next step in the process is a public "remedies hearing" to debate possible tariffs or other measures on December 1 . Commissioners will then produce a report for Mr Trump by January 11. "They will make recommendations to the president, but tariff decisions are always political decisions in part," said Alan Wolff, a former deputy director-general at the World Trade Organization. "In this administration, that's no different, except we know the president does, in fact, like tariffs. The USITC has been investigating the issue since July. The probe was requested by US trade ambassador Jamieson Greer, one of the key architects and strongest proponents of Mr Trump's tariffs policy. Australian lamb exports are already subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, along with many other Australian products. Republicans call for Australian lamb tariff probe Republicans write to Donald Trump's top trade officials to request an investigation into Australian lamb, as several members of Congress sponsor a bill for a 30 per cent tariff on Australian sheep products. Australia has been arguing against that tariff, saying it goes against the countries' free trade agreement. It has also argued against any prospective new tariff on lamb. Mr Trump has not publicly commented on the issue. But he recently angered US cattle farmers by publicly supporting an increase in beef imports to push down prices — a possible sign he could be persuaded by affordability arguments against tariffs on lamb. Australia's ambassador in Washington, Greg Moriarty, told a recent USITC hearing that Australian lamb was important to keeping prices low in the US. '"Any action to restrict lamb meat imports would only increase costs for US con­sumers, reduce product avail­ab­il­ity and risk revers­ing the steady growth in US demand for lamb to the det­ri­ment of the US industry," he told the trade commission. The American Sheep Industry Association described today's decision as "an important step toward securing trade relief for US sheep producers". The investigation followed years of campaigning by the sector, which argued "surging low-priced imports" from Australia and New Zealand were hurting the domestic industry. Dozens of Republicans in the US Congress backed their campaign. In a letter to trade officials in January, they argued foreign producers, "particularly Australia and New Zealand, have consistently taken advantage of our relaxed barriers and used them to undercut and infiltrate the US lamb market". events.title: This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board
events.summary: Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever. A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers. Drogue , which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now. The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.” Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors. In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms. To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious. After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said. As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it. The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s. Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said. To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28°F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then released, and dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats. The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said. To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said. There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said. Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean. In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers : find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

events.title: Senate Dems break 32-year drought on leadership challenges
events.summary: As House Democrats barrel toward a speakership coronation , Senate Dems are getting their first contested race for leader in over 30 years. Why it matters: Democrats have spent years tearing themselves apart over the party's direction — without forcing their leaders to win a head-to-head vote. Senate Democrats will get that fight this year for the first time since Tom Daschle vs. Chris Dodd in 1994 — courtesy of Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenging Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). But no one's challenging Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker. The last contested Democratic House leader race was in 2016, when Tim Ryan failed to beat Nancy Pelosi for minority leader. Between the lines: House Democrats are being bombarded with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, but the two most frequently floated alternatives — Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) — don't appear to want the job. Raskin told Axios that chairing the Judiciary Committee is his "dream job" and that he's "absolutely ... not a candidate for speaker in any way." "I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," Raskin added. Pressley has privately told colleagues she isn't interested, multiple House Democrats told Axios. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." The big picture: Since the last contested Democratic leadership election, Republicans have endured the rise of MAGA, former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell's fall from power and a revolving door of House GOP leaders. In 2018, Kevin McCarthy drubbed Jim Jordan 159–43 to become House minority leader. In 2022, McConnell had to beat Rick Scott after the Florida Republican challenged him for Senate GOP leader. In 2023, McCarthy needed 15 ballots to become speaker and was ousted later that year. Republicans burned through nominations on Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan before settling on Mike Johnson . In 2024, John Thune had to beat two challengers — Rick Scott and John Cornyn — to succeed McConnell as Senate GOP leader. In 2026, Jim Jordan ... well, you know what happened. It was Tuesday. The intrigue: Van Hollen told reporters in Denver on Friday he's stopped "pursuing" a 2028 presidential bid because the "size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call with the American people." Van Hollen is up to five public votes (himself included) ahead of the Dec. 1 secret ballot. Schumer's at 14. The winner will need 29. Over in the House, the real question at this point feels like whether any House Democrats will oppose Jeffries on the House floor on Jan. 3. Jeffries has enjoyed unanimous support from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022 and is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted," he told reporters yesterday. The bottom line: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill.

events.title: How the Microsoft outage impacted courts and governments
events.summary: Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication. Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance. Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received. Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work. That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump 's Kennedy Center takeover , saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination." In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well. Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally. The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting , "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems." U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms. The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage. What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project. She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed. While court deadlines can be pushed back, service disruption for individuals seeking urgent injunctive relief is more critical, she notes. "If the only way to communicate ... is through these servers, and the request wasn't reached, it can result in somebody having left the country or having moved money out of an account," Nia says. Reality check: Shay Cleary, a National Center for State Courts consultant who specializes in tech and cybersecurity, emphasizes that courts typically have manual back-up plans in place. "Many of the people who work in courts are dedicated public servants, and they can figure out how to do things right," he adds. With Congress back in session, Hill communications were also left in a holding pattern Thursday — with one staffer writing on X, "Hope nobody needs Congress for a little while, your Legislative Branch is currently paralyzed by the Outlook outage." Municipal governments in Austin , Texas, and Jacksonville , Florida, among several others , warned that their emails — and in some cases, phone systems — were impacted. What we're watching: A page providing updates on the suite of Microsoft tech tools said in a Friday morning post that it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress." That statement came some 22 hours after the page first said the company was investigating reports of issues with email access. The bottom line: The very tools that connect us digitally can also divide us when things go wrong — underscoring the importance of preparing old-school backup plans to fill the gaps. events.title: IMF says more progress needed on Lebanon's banking reforms
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has said Lebanon's bank restructuring law remains a key sticking point as Beirut seeks a new economic reform programme with the multilateral lender. The fund said progress was made in discussions during a November 11-13 visit to Lebanon and engagement was expected to continue. "However, further work is needed to reach an agreement on a strategy for an effective and durable restructuring of Lebanon’s banking sector, leading to a sound and resilient system," said Ernesto Ramirez Rigo, IMF mission chief to Lebanon. The IMF cited the implementation of the Bank Resolution Law and the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law - or the financial gap law - as "essential to restore financial stability and maximise deposits recovery" once they are adopted. Lebanon reached an initial staff-level agreement with the IMF in 2022 after the country's economy collapsed, although the government at the time was slow to implement the fund's recommendations. The country defaulted on its debt for the first time in March 2020, leading to hyperinflation, high unemployment, a surging poverty rate and depositors frozen out of their savings. Its financial collapse generated losses of roughly $70 billion, a figure used in official estimates since 2022, although that number is now expected to be higher. The fund said further talks are needed to maximise deposit repayments while ensuring consistency with the central bank's and the banking sector's liquidity positions, and public debt sustainability and the restoration of the central bank's solvency. The IMF also said it remained critical that the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law "upholds the hierarchy of claims in the allocation of losses, thereby maximising protection for depositors". Lebanon's Parliament passed a bank resolution law in August, although President Joseph Aoun appealed against it at the Constitutional Council over an amendment concerning the central bank's independence and power. The fund at the time said it would assess any changes to ensure they were consistent with international standards. "The mission looks forward to continuing the engagement with the authorities to make further progress on these fronts in the coming weeks and remains fully committed to supporting Lebanon in its efforts to design and implement a comprehensive economic reform programme, in line with the IMF’s policies and mandate," Mr Ramirez Rigo said.

events.title: Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. "The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC , external . "The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 1 day ago How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 1 day ago Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Huang. Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. They say Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection. A 25% tariff - a levy paid by US importers to the federal government - was imposed on those chips under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security. "Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said. events.title: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
events.summary: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use. True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce. events.title: Are you team car door or car bonnet? This town's history depends on your answer
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lightning Ridge opal history dispute plays out on car doors and bonnets Blow the layer of dust off Lightning Ridge and you will find a town as rich in colour as the precious black opal mined here. The stone’s dark undertone is the marriage of carbon and iron oxide, brought together over millennia beneath the earth’s surface. It brings colour to life in a way that no other precious stone can. It is an exceptionally rare find, with more than 90 per cent of the world’s supply located beneath this outback moonscape. Great fortunes have been made and lost here on Yuwaalaraay Country in Northern NSW, where stories have become facts and truth can be just as elusive as the black opal itself. Among the corrugated iron shacks and the long-abandoned mine shafts that pockmark this land, the past is everywhere. Exactly what that history is, however, depends on who's telling it. Barb Moritz is waiting for us in front of an old miner's cottage on the main street. Built in 1932, its warped pinewood beams and lopsided tin roof resemble an abstract painting. It's the headquarters of the Lightning Ridge Historical Society, and the seat from which Barb holds court. She emerges from the shadow of the verandah awning whirring with facts and directions, her dark eyes glowing. Barb cuts a strikingly vibrant figure amid a palette of rusted metal and aging wood. When she smiles, the afternoon sun catches her opal dental filling and it flashes with brilliant greens and blues. Introductions are swift before Barb leaps into her opening stanza, fine tuned over decades of leading tour groups. She points towards the local pool, opened by Dawn Fraser in 1990. The Opal Miners Hall of Fame is further out, just a few minutes' drive from the cottage. Then there's the Lightning Ridge Cemetery, or as Barb refers to it, the "dead end of town". She casts us a deadpan glance and pauses for effect. Barb is a long way from the cornfields of Iowa in the American mid-west, where she grew up. She still isn't quite sure if she chose to move to Lightning Ridge, or if the black opal lured her. "From the very beginning, I feel I was directed to opal," she says, her accent still thick. Barb arrived in Lightning Ridge in the summer of 1990. Three years later, she was working for the historical society. "I met the people who lived here, the old-timers who built this community," she says. It wasn't long before Barb was the society's secretary. Tucked away behind the old miner's cottage is an aging demountable filled to the brim with miners' ledgers and newspaper clippings dating back more than a century. It is the engine room of the historical society. And it's here, among the records, that Barb pieces together a version of Lightning Ridge's opal-mining evolution. In the late 1990s, this history was translated onto a conspicuous canvas unique to the town's identity, the "car door tours". Across the featureless landscape, car doors mark out four colour-coded routes (green, red, yellow and blue) to sites the society deems significant to the town's history. "People lock their car doors because they're afraid maybe one will go missing," Barb says with a glimmer in her eye. The doors have become much more than a tourist attraction for the droves of travellers and grey nomads who pass through. They are now part of the landscape. They're also used by locals and emergency services to help locate people living on claims that are well and truly off the beaten track. The population of Lightning Ridge is a bit of a mystery. Officially, it has about 2,000 residents. Unofficially, it's more like 5,000 because many people move to this outback town to disappear. We follow Barb's car as she navigates the dirt roads, tracing the green car door tour as it winds its way up to McDonald's Six-Mile opal field. Perched on an ironstone ridge above the town, facing the western horizon, it's a moonscape of colourless rock, sheet metal and dozens of deserted mine shafts. You can't miss the monument to Charles Nettleton. Protected by a wire fence, the jagged rectangular stone slab and its plaque look lovingly maintained, but resemble a tombstone. There is pride in Barb's eyes as she takes stock of the monument, pale yellow under the midday sun. It would not be here without her ability to move heaven and earth for her adopted home. "[Charles Nettleton] was the first professional opal miner who came to this country" Barb explains. "And we decided … we needed to have a monument — a historical reserve — to where he had sunk his first shafts for the syndicate of businessmen who hired him.

events.title: Microsoft says affected services fully recovered after more than 24 hours of global disruption
events.summary: The US tech company was not aware of any malicious activity and ruled out AI as the cause. Microsoft said Teams, Outlook and other services fully recovered after a global outage lasting more than 24 hours. The company blamed server issues and ruled out malicious activity. The outage hit governments, airlines, banks and businesses worldwide, blocking e-mails, calendars and meetings. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute. Experts warned the incident shows the risk of relying on one Big Tech provider. Microsoft has had more outages in 2025 and 2026, raising fresh doubts about its reliability. Microsoft on Nov 14 said that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications across businesses and governments for over 24 hours. “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company posted on social media platform X. Microsoft had said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out artificial intelligence as the cause. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending e-mails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings. It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the US, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. The outage, reports of which started climbing around 5.25pm GMT on Nov 12, according to Downdetector’s parent company Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services in 2026 . Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online – its cloud-based e-mail and scheduling hub – leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft’s workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Ookla. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels. “It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider’s e-mail and collaboration tools,” said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla. Microsoft shares closed flat at US$523.88 on Nov 13 . The stock has gained roughly 8% so far in 2026 . Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice-president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS. De Cicco estimated global insured losses at between US$300 million (S$386 million) and US$500 million – well below the US$400 million to US$1.5 billion toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than eight million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions. Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January 2026 and in October 2025 . In October , it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and industries worldwide. “The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage in 2026 ,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. “If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands.” Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations. A spokesperson for the British government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organisations such as the National Health Service (NHS) and London’s Metropolitan Police. Lack of access to e-mails and other services impacted the Metropolitan Police’s ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected. The NHS said its local services were turning to alternative measures such as IT systems or paper records. For businesses, the fallout was widespread. European exchange operator Euronext reported e-mail disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates.

events.title: Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule
events.summary: President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found . In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China. This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI. In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy. He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft. The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock. In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts. The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival. Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000. These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office. DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.” Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning The US – and the global economy – have been grappling with revelations that Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s former chief executive, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Reports have suggested this relationship allowed Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, to obtain billions of dollars worth of Nvidia’s chips, even as other companies struggled. Trump was twice briefed by US intelligence officials on their conclusions that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. He did not act on this assessment. Jensen Huang has been described as a close Trump ally and has met the president a number of times. Nvidia made a $25m contribution to Trump’s ballroom in October 2025, with Huang saying he was “delighted to be a part of it”.

events.title: Hassett expected to depart White House
events.summary: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett is expected to depart his role at the White House in the coming weeks, three people familiar with his plans told Semafor. Hassett has been inquiring about roles outside the administration since well before this month’s midterm elections, some of the people said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who could hold both jobs, and his counselor, David Zervos, are among those being eyed to replace him. Hassett’s plans haven’t been officially announced and, like much in the Trump administration, there’s always the chance they could change. The Treasury Department did not comment for this story. A White House official told Semafor that “there is no factual basis for this reporting,” adding that “Kevin Hassett is a key member of President [Donald] Trump’s economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump’s economic policies.” “Under President Trump, Americans have received more than $82 billion in individual tax relief, over 70 million children have been enrolled for a Trump Account, nearly 20 fair trade deals have been secured, poverty is at an all-time low and real wages for hardworking Americans have increased,” the official continued. “The Trump administration will continue delivering results for hardworking families.” Hassett later denied he planned to leave in a text message to CNBC. Trump tapped Hassett, who served in the first Trump administration, to return as his top economic adviser nearly two years ago. Since then, Hassett’s served as the face of everything from the economic fallout from the Iran war to the president’s campaign against former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell. Hassett, who was in the running to replace Powell, saw one of his top priorities advance in February, when the president signed an executive order that sought to expand access to retirement plans for workers whose employers don’t provide one. The order, first reported by Semafor , followed Hassett’s longtime advocacy for recreating the government’s Thrift Savings Plan for private-sector workers — but ultimately took a less ambitious approach, creating a website where workers can shop existing plans. Hassett’s expected departure, while not tied to Republicans’ lackluster midterm results, would be the latest in a series of staffing changes hitting the Trump administration in recent weeks. Hassett’s deputy, Ryan Baasch, left the White House at the end of September . More recently, Trump replaced his then-chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s strict immigration policies. Roles under Miller have been shifting in recent weeks, as Semafor reported . Multiple people inside and close to the administration say they expect further staffing changes and departures as the year comes to a close. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is currently in the crosshairs amid scrutiny over his handling of export controls on AI chips.

events.title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
events.summary: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics , governance , and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias , security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap. Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies. Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust. Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance. The benefits of microcredentials Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program. Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment. For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles. Translating standards into microcredentials Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards , most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle. The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust. To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert .

events.title: Homes with architectural designs that cost just $1 near completion
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts First Corrimal homes with $1 plans from NSW Pattern Book nearing completion Topic: Housing Construction Industry The four row homes in Corrimal will be the first in the state built using a Pattern Book design. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) A set of row homes in Corrimal will be the first of the NSW government's $1 pattern book designs to be completed. The government has sold more than 25,000 designs from the book, with 22 being built. The opposition says the low numbers show the scheme is a "failure", but builders say it is working. Construction costs might be soaring across the country but on a building site at Corrimal, north of Wollongong, no-one is complaining about the price that was paid for an architect's plans. Builder James Forrest and his team are putting the finishing touches on four new row homes, following designs purchased for just $1 from a pattern book launched by the NSW government in July 2025 . If he meets the November deadline, he will be the first in the state to complete a home under the scheme. Mr Forrest said using the design saved him an extraordinary amount of time, because it included planning controls and a 10-day complying development pathway. "All the rigours of the design work have been done already. It's just matching it to the site, and it's approved," he said. James Forrest aims to complete the project by the end of November. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) The Corrimal development used one of eight low-rise designs available for the nominal fee of $1 in the first six months of the scheme. The program was sold as a way to get more high-quality housing built faster and cheaper. So far, 25,000 designs have been purchased and 22 are being built. Harry Catterns says the designs can be adjusted to different sizes and configurations. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Architect Harry Catterns co-owns the company that designed the row homes. "We thought it would be a more helpful contribution to the housing mix if we could provide small house-like dwellings with their own front door, their own garden, rather than the typical apartment you might see on a site like this," he said. Mr Catterns said the design could be adjusted to one, two or three bedrooms and offered different bathroom configurations. All are two-storey, with balconies and sliding glass doors. The builder is hoping to have the homes ready for tenants, and owners, by Christmas. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Mr Forrest said he hoped to have three homes occupied by Christmas, and the fourth, larger home on the market shortly after. "These will be cheaper for buyers than ordinary builds for a number of reasons, but primarily because of its speed and cost-saving," he said. Mr Forrest estimated the Corrimal build was around $600,000 cheaper than an ordinary project. The Pattern Book now offers 17 designs after nine mid-rise options were added in November 2025. They cost up to $2,500 and do not have the same planning controls or fast-track as the low-rise designs. Tom Forrest says the scheme has been a "dud". ( ABC News: Sam Foster ) The Urban Taskforce's Tom Forrest said the mid-rise developments would still need final development approval from councils and faced the same planning timelines as a typical build. "Nobody is building and it hasn't improved the number of new dwellings brought to the market," he said. So far, the entire Housing Pattern Book program has translated to fewer than 60 applications, with 45 of them approved. The Housing Industry Association does not agree, with NSW chief executive Brad Armitage saying it was working for builders. "When you take those [economic] factors into consideration, so many approvals with this relatively new pattern book is actually quite strong," he said. Brad Armitage says the pattern book is a success. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) The NSW opposition has promised to overhaul the scheme with new designs and review planning controls if it is elected next March, describing it as a "failure". "We want to see a lot more builders like this one at Corrimal rolling out a lot more housing as part of the pattern book and clearly it's not working at the moment," Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said. "We need to make it much easier to actually build the pattern book designs. "It's just far too slow and far too restrictive." NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully defended the outcome. "We're seeing challenging economic conditions for new home building, higher interest rates, higher building costs, shortages of skilled labour," he said.

events.title: Nvidia approached Arm CEO Rene Haas to succeed Jensen Huang, report says
events.summary: Rene Haas is among several candidates being considered, and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings chief executive Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Nov 13, citing sources familiar with the matter. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs , including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an artificial intelligence industry he helped bankroll. Haas’ name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang’s exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice-president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He is among several candidates being considered and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia’s finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO. Nvidia’s board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” the board said in a statement. Prior to Huang’s resignation, a long-time Nvidia engineer had urged the board in an internal post to consider employee sentiment before taking any action, Wired reported late on Nov 12. The post has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, with several urging the board to find a way to bring Huang back, the technology news platform said, citing internal correspondence it reviewed. Nvidia has about 42,000 employees worldwide. Billionaire Elon Musk separately said on X that a petition was under way to reinstate Huang and that he would sign it. It was not immediately clear whether Musk was referring to the internal effort reported by Wired. Nvidia declined to comment on the Wired report as well as Musk’s post, while Arm also declined to comment. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Haas became Arm CEO in 2022, overseeing the company’s Nasdaq listing in 2023. Arm designs processor architectures and licenses them to other companies that develop chip designs. Historically, its strength has been in mobile phones and it is expanding into computers. Haas’ combination of familiarity with Nvidia and experience running a publicly traded chip company could make him an unusual fit for the role, said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities. “Rene is one of few external candidates who wouldn’t need to be brought up to speed on Nvidia,” Boloor said, adding that Haas’ understanding of the company’s culture alongside his experience running Arm was “a combination you don’t find very often”. Arm’s US-listed shares pared losses after the report and were down more than 5%. Nvidia’s shares were down over 3%. Some analysts expect the next CEO to break from Huang’s three-decade reign as the hands-on “chief conductor” who personally steered engineering road maps, geopolitical negotiations over China exports and massive investments across the AI ecosystem. A potential shift towards a more institutional leadership structure would come as Nvidia faces heightened regulatory scrutiny and growing consensus among US lawmakers to further restrict the company’s chip exports to China. Insiders and tech titans in the running Analysts view Kress as a steady financial authority, while veteran engineer Ian Buck is seen as a top candidate after leading development of CUDA, the software platform that powers Nvidia’s AI chips. Apart from Haas, external names discussed by analysts include AMD chief Lisa Su, who has navigated the key China market, and Micron chief Sanjay Mehrotra, whose memory chips power Nvidia servers. Other candidates cited by industry watchers include Marvell head Matt Murphy and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who oversaw the iPhone maker’s in-house silicon development. Former Apple chief Tim Cook was floated by US President Donald Trump , as Nvidia’s board evaluates whether to prioritise financial continuity, deep technical expertise, or experience running a global tech heavyweight. events.title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
events.summary: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. events.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
events.summary: Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world. Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced. Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries. From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America. The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues". In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels". The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade. "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday. Will emails affected by the outage ever arrive? Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery". In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away. Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up". The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email. When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent. Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time. Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues. "What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said. "The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. "You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit." The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online. Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time". He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said. In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services." How many people have been affected? More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed. Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.

events.title: Nvidia CEO’s exit marks pivotal moment for African AI
events.summary: Alexis’s view Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia could prove to be a turning point in the rollout of AI in Africa. The technology offers the potential to turbocharge economies across the continent, but chips form the backbone of this revolution. And, as our San Francisco Bureau Chief Reed Albergotti put it, “ Huang was Nvidia’s one-man, long-term moat .” Without Huang’s singular vision, there’s uncertainty. The questions swirling in the wake of his exit are a reminder that the development of African compute still relies on hardware and software supplied by US companies. Huang’s resignation raises questions, for example, about the US chipmaker’s relationship with Cassava Technologies: Nvidia last year became an investor in the pan-African digital infrastructure company, which it supplies with chips. The partnership is central to Cassava’s push to expand services in the more than 30 African countries in which it operates. Nvidia’s financial commitment and supply of hardware offered an opportunity for African companies to access the compute needed to train and run their own AI models. If Huang’s successor takes a different approach, the Cassava partnership may not be replicated elsewhere on the continent, limiting the access African firms have to cutting-edge technology. The implications extend to the public sector, too. Only last month, the World Bank named Nvidia and Cassava as partners in an initiative aimed at expanding digital access in Africa to improve services and create jobs. Any change in Nvidia’s strategy would, in the long term, have the biggest implications for South Africa. The continent’s largest economy is home to about 40% of its roughly 160 data centers. So next week’s visit by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to the US is well-timed. Ramaphosa, who will speak at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event , will be accompanied by a delegation that includes his ministers for finance, trade, and energy. He plans to meet tech executives, researchers, and investors during his trip, which will focus on AI infrastructure. Ramaphosa’s team has described it as an attempt to position South Africa as a “ competitive AI hub ” on the continent — but it’s shaping up to be a first peek at Silicon Valley after the departure of one of its central figures. Notable The proliferation of data centers across Africa is creating new pressure on the continent’s resources, reported Aaliyah Vayez for Al Jazeera.
