events.title: Nobody wants to run against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
events.summary: The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job. Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee. "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) has privately told colleagues she doesn't want the role despite an online movement seeking to draft her, according to multiple House Democrats who have spoken directly with her. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." "He's the only one running," Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios on Thursday when asked if she plans to vote for Jeffries as speaker. Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "I am really encouraging our leadership to make it easy for me to vote for the one person that's running. But as of right now, there's ... no one else that has put their name forward." "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only person running," said Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). Jeffries said in a NY1 interview : "Someone could always emerge in the next week or so, but right now there are no declared challengers, no indication that anyone may put themselves forward." The intrigue: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched his bid to replace Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Thursday night. Yes, but: The progressive grassroots have continued this week to swamp sitting and incoming House Democrats with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, according to lawmakers and aides. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) told Axios he has gotten an "avalanche of messages." Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said she is getting "hundreds" of calls "every day" urging her to oppose Jeffries. A senior House Democrat who is supporting Jeffries told Axios the callers into their office have suggested "like 10" different members as possible alternatives. Jeffries has pushed back on Axios' reporting that members are being flooded with calls, saying in his NY1 interview: "There's no indication that members of Congress have been overwhelmed by any calls." State of play: Jeffries has begun meeting with skeptics ahead of House Democrats' Nov. 18 leadership elections. He is expected to easily win the nomination for speaker, determined by a simple majority vote of the caucus. The real question is whether any House Democrats will oppose him on the House floor on Jan. 3 and deny him the unanimous support he has enjoyed from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022. "We're going to continue to talk to every single member of the House Democratic caucus, both current members and incoming members, about what we all can do together for the American people," Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Thursday. The Democratic leader said he is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted." Between the lines: Several Democratic House members and members-elect predicted that, given the grassroots pressure bearing down on progressives right now, at least a handful are likely to openly oppose him. What they're saying: Leonard told Axios he sat down with Jeffries on Wednesday and shared what he has heard from callers, including "that the Democratic establishment brand is in the toilet and that the leader's name is synonymous with the Democratic establishment." Ramirez said she has "begun conversations" with Jeffries and intends to "have more next week." Asked if Jeffries has met with the Jeffries-skeptic "Bloc" of incoming progressives, she said: "It is my understanding that that they're scheduling time to meet with them." Reps.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) and LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) said Jeffries met Wednesday with members of the North Carolina delegation, many of whom are holdouts in the speaker election. "We're still having conversations, we're still listening ... at the end of the day, we're going to all sit together, we're going to listen to everything and we're going to move forward like that," said Ojeda. The bottom line: "I mean, right now, I don't even know if there's anybody that's stepping up against him," Ojeda added.

events.title: My Dubai Salary: 'I said goodbye to two husbands to focus on my business'
events.summary: Madiha Abaida came to Dubai for a holiday. She ended up buying a property , opening a factory and never leaving. That was in 2018. She had been living in Monaco for a decade before that – a resident for tax reasons , as she puts it plainly – but after her marriage ended, she wanted a fresh start somewhere new. It was not straightforward, though. She launched a fashion brand in Dubai in 2020 and then the pandemic cancelled everything. So, she opened her own textile factory instead. She brought in staff, bought the machinery and worked 16-hour days. The fashion brand – originally conceived in Milan – became a Dubai operation born of necessity. Since then, she has pivoted again. Pink Madi, her beauty salon in Dubai, opened recently. Before that, she spent years building a real estate portfolio across the UAE and Spain's Golden Mile in Marbella, where she buys old homes, renovates them and sells them for $2 million to $3 million. She counts more than 25 properties in total. Today, she describes herself, without hesitation, as a millionaire . And she wants to go to Mars. What was your first job and first salary? When I was 16 or 17, I was selling Coca-Cola and noodles in order to study. People see me as a woman with power, but they don't know the price I paid. I was very hard-working from the beginning. I was a model first, when I was 17. And I studied to be a lawyer because my mother, she was married to a judge. I wanted to make my mother happy. But honestly, I never wanted to be a lawyer. I don't have this kind of personality. One day I said, “OK, I'm sorry – I need to do what I really believe I'm good at.” Then I started my fashion brand, and it was a big success in Milano. events.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
events.summary: The folly of just-in-time supply chains Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ). The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences. The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal. Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question. The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

events.title: Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds
events.summary: Gen Z is often cast as souring on AI, but they’re no more negative about the technology than their parents and grandparents. A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor, found that 73% of Gen Z adults haven’t made up their minds on AI, while half said they expect AI to harm society. That matches baby boomers (50%) and Gen Xers (48%), while millennials were the most upbeat, with 39% expecting harm. Companies and politicians are all eager to understand the generation’s stance on AI, given how much they drive tech trends and how AI and data centers played an outsize role in the US midterm election. The report also pointed to a paradox that seems to define young people’s relationship with AI: Many say it makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job — but 46% said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about the existential risk that dominates much of the AI safety discourse. And they are more conflicted about their own use: 30% of Gen Zers said they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s biggest mistake was getting too involved in DC
events.summary: Reed’s view Jensen Huang made a lot of mistakes, but the one that really brought him down was getting too involved in DC. The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone who’s great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it. That’s a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change. When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. It was irresistible for a lot of tech people (Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen also fell into this trap). For a while, it seemed like Huang was one of the few technologists to find success in DC. His friendship with the president helped advance his worldview — that America should export its technology around the world, even to China. But it was all a mirage. Political people understood this would never last, and it would end in hearings, investigations, and prosecutions. This has all come as a shocking surprise to many in the tech industry. Nvidia was aggressive in its policy positions in part because it had the backing of the president. It should have used that influence sparingly, and not just to get what it wanted but to make more allies on both sides of the political aisle. So far, the underlying allegations against Huang are unproven. The alleged spy who led to this mess may not even be a spy . And many in the tech industry are angry and want to fight back. That’s the wrong instinct. In the tech industry, the relentless will to win is perhaps the most redeeming quality of every operator. In DC, you can’t ever really win. You can only lose. The Nvidia scandal and the post-midterm tech industry peril are exactly the reason we came up with the idea for our convening, Silicon Valley & The World, which takes place next week in the heart of the industry. We’re bringing leaders in from around the globe to burst Silicon Valley’s bubble and make it a more worldly place. We have what I think is the best lineup of speakers ever assembled at a media industry convening and I hope Jensen Huang, who was supposed to speak, will reconsider. If you’d like to tune in, register for a virtual broadcast pass , or watch live on YouTube and at Semafor.com . Notable Palantir CEO Alex Karp, another CEO that developed close ties to Trump and Washington , told Politico Playbook that he is a “ progressive ” and a lifelong Democrat.

events.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
events.summary: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world F or politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices. Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya , promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action. That’s where things get tricky. Last month Burnham’s government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, dismaying climate activists. Soon there will have to be a decision on Rosebank, the much bigger proposed new oilfield northwest of Shetland. There are also signs that ministers are preparing to weaken the targets set for the car industry to shift to electric vehicles. And this week, the chancellor, John Healey, declared himself fully “behind building a third runway at Heathrow”. Small wonder that campaigners are talking of hypocrisy and the government’s “crumbling” credibility. What is Burnham to do? He has Healey in one ear, telling him that a thriving airport is an engine for economic growth, doubtless alongside the oil, gas and car industries. And in the other he has the climate scientists, reminding him that global carbon emissions are at record levels and the planet is getting hotter every year. What option does he have, except to keep putting off the moment of choice, buying himself time by saying, for example, that Rosebank is a “quasi-legal decision” that cannot be hurried? Naturally, there are advocates for each of the binary options, whether it’s green activists demanding he put the planet first, regardless of the impact on jobs or prices, or business leaders insisting it be the other way around. But he is in a different position from each of those warring sides – because he has to come up with something both can live with. The answer might just be an arresting blend of pragmatism and radicalism – both, and at the same time. Such an approach would begin with saying a couple of things campaigners might not want to hear. First, that the most reliable route to reducing the use of fossil fuels lies not with curtailing supply – blocking production – but with slashing demand. Or as Michael Jacobs, who served as the climate and energy adviser to Gordon Brown in Downing Street, told me this week: “We need to destroy the demand for oil and gas.” On that goal, there has been remarkable progress, whether measured in the shift to renewable sources of power, such as wind and solar, for the generation of electricity or the move to electric vehicles: last month just under one in two new cars registered in the UK were either fully electric or plug-in hybrids . The second message Burnham might deliver to a wary, green audience would be: symbols matter, but they should not obscure the thing they are meant to symbolise. In that context, and given that destroying demand is more important than curbing supply, he could argue that the green light he gave to Jackdaw should not be overplayed. That project is relatively small and has an expected lifespan of only about 10 years. Yes, it became a signifier, but the bigger picture is what matters. It would be much harder to make that argument for Rosebank, which is bigger than Jackdaw and set to last for 25 years, and harder still for Heathrow, not least because emissions from aviation are stubbornly difficult to reduce: you can’t shrink demand for aviation fuel, because, as of now, there are few readily available alternatives. So a third runway means a serious increase in the UK’s emissions of CO 2 . But what if Burnham felt he could not rebuff the growth lobby on Heathrow and Rosebank, especially if he also stands firm on his electric vehicle targets despite the howls of protest from UK carmakers? Is there a bone he could throw them, while not enraging the climate-concerned voters he needs to keep on side?

events.title: The global economy's Achilles' heels
events.summary: A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system . The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain. That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around). In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks. By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000. The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips. What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them." "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds. "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute. Reality check: Reducing vulnerabilities and building economic resilience isn't necessarily as simple as relocating a factory. "Some companies just change their suppliers or factory from a geopolitically distant country to a geopolitically closer country, and they think that they achieved resilience," said Jeongmin Seong, a co-author and McKinsey partner. "Even though you change the location of the final assembly, unless you eliminate the risk at this upstream level, you are still exposed." Between the lines: The steady march of globalization paid major dividends in recent decades in making goods more affordable and powering global growth. Now companies — and governments — are seeking to mitigate the vulnerabilities that system has created and that the last several years made plain to see.

All sites and data will be deleted on November 30. Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names. Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of. It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will. Mozilla told The Register : "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider." It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere. Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now. Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed rule amendments to make its executive and director compensation disclosure requirements more principles-based and materiality-driven, providing investors with clearer, more concise, and less complex disclosures. The proposal follows the Commission’s review of its executive and director compensation disclosure requirements, including a request for public comment and a roundtable discussion with representatives from public companies, investors, and other experts in this field. This proposal builds on Chairman Atkins’ efforts to reduce friction for companies looking to join and remain in our public markets. The proposal would refocus these disclosures—last comprehensively reformed in 2006—on material information and improve investors’ ability to track equity awards through their lifecycle. The proposed amendments aim to reduce compliance burdens for registrants where there is not commensurate benefit for investors and would provide registrants with more flexibility to present their disclosures in a way that is consistent with how compensation programs are constructed today and better represents the intention of their boards of directors and compensation committees. “Today, the Commission proposed amendments to its executive compensation disclosure requirements contained in Item 402 of Regulation S-K. These amendments reflect a comprehensive reform of Item 402 that, together with other previously proposed actions, are central tenets of my agenda and focus on transforming the SEC’s public company disclosure regime to one rooted in materiality,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement . “With the benefit of input from more than 80 comment letters received from investors, companies, and advisors in connection with the SEC’s roundtable on executive compensation in July 2025, today’s proposal aims to elicit more informative disclosure rooted in materiality.” The proposed amendments to Item 402 of Regulation S-K would permit registrants to tailor disclosure in a way that provides greater transparency regarding the registrant’s compensation practices and is more efficient for investors to read and understand. In support of these goals, the proposed changes would, among other things: Revise the named executive officers to encompass the principal executive officer and principal financial officer—the positions whose compensation are generally most material for investors due to their roles in managing a registrant’s most consequential matters—thereby reducing the number of named executive officers from typically five or more individuals under the current rule to two in most circumstances. Modify the primary executive compensation tabular disclosure requirements into three new tables (Earned Compensation Table, Granted Compensation Table, and Status of Equity Awards Table) with accompanying narratives that would replace the primary four tables required under the current rule. The proposed changes would retain material information required under the current tabular disclosure framework but would seek to streamline and clarify the presentation. Raise the minimum aggregate reporting threshold for perquisites from $10,000 to $150,000 and introduce a new de minimis tracking exclusion. The proposed amendments would retain disclosure of material perquisites for investors while reducing compliance burdens for registrants. Revise the Commission’s interpretive guidance regarding perquisites to give registrants more flexibility to make the determination of whether a benefit is a perquisite, so long as the determination is reasonable and made in good faith. Make the Compensation Discussion and Analysis (CD&A) requirement more principles-based, require registrants to address only three topics in the CD&A, and eliminate the list of 15 example topics contained in the current rule. The proposed changes would streamline the presentation of information, reduce complexity and repetition, and focus more clearly on material information. Simplify the pay-versus-performance disclosure requirement by reducing required performance measures and replacing the complex “Compensation Actually Paid” calculation with the total compensation earned amount from the proposed Earned Compensation Table. The proposed changes would continue to satisfy the statutory mandate of the Dodd-Frank Act while simplifying disclosure requirements. Limit the population used in the determination of “median employee” under the pay ratio rule to U.S. full-time employees and reduce the required frequency of the determination to every five years. Eliminate required check boxes from the cover pages of annual reports and certain potentially redundant disclosure requirements regarding the application of a registrant’s clawback policy that overly burden registrants without eliciting material information for investors. The underlying mechanics of a registrant’s clawback process would remain unchanged. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days following publication of the proposing release in the Federal Register. events.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
events.summary: Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say. Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump , dated February 2025. The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise. However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs. Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible. "Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said . The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session. Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication . The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity. "The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said. "An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources." The threats Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings. The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger." Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire. Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country. "To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare. "Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them." Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate. Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming. Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low. Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible. In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station. The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks. At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome. Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®

events.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
events.summary: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. events.title: Ford throws open the doors to its new Vault, unveiling 125 rare historic vehicles
events.summary: Ford is throwing open the doors of its historic vehicle collection at the new Vault in Romulus, Michigan ROMULUS, Mich. -- Ford will open the doors to its new Vault this weekend to some lucky gearheads and fans of history. The 123-year-old carmaker on Saturday will allow select members of the public and employees into the Ford Vault to take a gander at everything from rare concept cars and Hollywood Mustangs to historic police cruisers and even a 1938 ambulance. Tickets were snapped up quickly, but Ford Motor Co. said there will be future showings. “You don’t create an experience like this and a space like this and then hide it away,” said Ted Ryan, Ford’s Archives and Heritage Brand Manager. “We’re going to find a way to make it available to the car community in Michigan as soon as we can.” Ford’s collection of historic vehicles once was housed at its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters and other locations. Its vast new home, the Vault, is situated inside a former Amazon fulfillment center in Romulus, another Detroit suburb, and measures 79,000 square feet (7,339 square meters). “I can tell you, after working here for a couple weeks, I'm averaging about 20,000 steps a day,” said Ryan. The Vault brings together 125 of the Heritage Fleet's historically significant vehicles, including race cars, design concepts and vehicles tied to pop culture. “Here, we can actually have a purpose-built space for the cars,” Ford Archives Manager Ciera Casteel said. “That's our legacy. That's what we do here. That is what this company is.” Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged — A 2005 Mustang GT proof-of-concept that paved the way for the Shelby GT350. Engineers nicknamed it “Johnny Cash” (inspired by his song “One Piece at a Time,” about an autoworker who cobbles together a car out of mismatched parts). “It's like Frankenstein. Things have been bolted onto Johnny over the years. This is the first time he's ever been displayed,” Ryan said. — The first three cars to cross the finish line at Le Mans in 1966, a race immortalized in the 2019 Matt Damon/Christian Bale film, “Ford v Ferrari.” — A 1910 right-hand-drive Model T that was built in the U.K. and remained there until 2025, when it was added to the Heritage Fleet. — A 1973 Mustang convertible used in "The Mary Tyler Moore Show.” The vehicle was sold in 1974, and remained in private ownership until Ford bought it last year. events.title: Jaguar Land Rover reports £451m quarterly loss after cutting 4,000 jobs
events.summary: JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China. Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions. JLR said it expected the vast majority of the job cuts to be achieved via voluntary redundancies, with 3,000 already confirmed. Most of those people will leave at the end of November. JLR said it had scraped into profit from its operations if it ignored the restructuring costs, but it was hurt by falling sales in China and the Middle East. Many European carmakers are struggling as they face competition from Chinese rivals at the same time as they invest in electric car production. PB Balaji, JLR’s chief executive, said on Friday the “onslaught of competition” from China meant the UK and EU should stop plans for new post-Brexit trade barriers on each other. The automotive industry is lobbying the UK and EU intensely to delay the implementation of “rules of origin” on 1 January, which threaten to impose 10% tariffs on UK-EU electric cars that use batteries from Asia. The EU is also considering “made in Europe” rules that would lock UK-made cars out of subsidies. “Now is the time for actually fostering this entire electrical ecosystem,” Balaji said. “It’s so important for us that we all hold hands, stick together and ensure that we get the system to evolve into the world of electrics.” He added: “We just need time to ensure all these plans start coming into fruition.” The company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, previously sought to target China for growth, only to write off billions in investments in 2019 as a new wave of Chinese carmakers led to massive overcapacity in the country. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning JLR, which was last year hit by a devastating hack , is targeting growth in the US, where it is in the process of agreeing a deal for the Chrysler owner, Stellantis, to manufacture Land Rovers for the first time. JLR has started to produce electric Land Rovers, beginning with its flagship Range Rover, built in Solihull in the West Midlands. Electric versions of its cheaper, higher-selling Range Rover Sport, Defender and Defender Sport will follow. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters HPE aims for the market with faster, more cost-effective HPC storage to combat rising costs Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor 1 day ago AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM 3 days ago AMD's Epyc X-chips are back after a three-year hiatus 3 days ago A closer look at Verano, AMD's first step toward a Zen-based superchip to rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin 3 days ago Oak Ridge labs gets hybrid quantum-HPC system to test qubit error correction 7 days ago HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems. The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack. The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks. For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives. HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads. One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives , as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported. HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need. “When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions. The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027. HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control. Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow. The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June.

events.title: Inside the aftermath of the Logan Circle shooting
events.summary: It took just minutes for a gunman to shoot six people and upend one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Thursday morning's violence left one person dead in a Logan Circle gym and five others injured nearby. The gunman later shot himself, police said. The massive police response shut down streets, sent nearly a dozen schools into lockdown and forced residents to shelter in place. By evening, the streets around VIDA Fitness, where the shooting began, were quiet. Several nearby businesses remained closed, with police tape blocking off storefronts and officers standing watch. Councilmember Brooke Pinto held a vigil . People left flowers and notes outside of the VIDA . "Logan Circle is still a place for love," read one. "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many," read another. But life also carried on: A delivery van unloaded Christmas trees at Whole Foods, and 14th Street bars put out signs advertising happy hour. Flowers and handwritten notes line the outside of VIDA Fitness. Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios One note reads: "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many." Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios What we know: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness. The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said. Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold. The timeline: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed. Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline. Police announced a sixth shooting victim — a woman with nonfatal injuries — on Friday morning, per the Washington Post . The victims: Stuart was pronounced dead inside VIDA. Police say the gunman then returned to his apartment, where he fired at people below from an upper-level private balcony. Two men and two women were hospitalized, one of whom suffered serious injuries. The standoff: Lambert barricaded himself in his apartment, where he broke a gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire inside the apartment, per police. Flames were visible outside the building, but sprinklers helped contain the blaze. Police recovered gasoline and other flammable materials. Police negotiators heard a gunshot while speaking with Lambert by phone, after which he stopped responding. Officers forced entry and found him suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The weapons: Investigators recovered a handgun, shotgun and rifle from Lambert's apartment. Carroll said the suspect used all three firearms, none of which were registered in D.C. People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Behind the scenes: Lambert had been fighting his condo association over alleged leaks and mold, per court records. He filed a lawsuit against the group in March 2025. Months later, he told now- Washington Sun reporter Michael Brice-Saddler that he'd spent nearly $200,000 on legal and engineering fees. In those interviews, Lambert said he knew Stuart's daily gym routine. What we don't know: Police have not determined whether Lambert knew the five surviving victims or deliberately targeted them. The precise timeline and extent of the suspected planning also remain under investigation. Context: The shooting prompted a massive response from local and federal authorities, including MPD, D.C. Fire and EMS, U.S. Park Police, Metro Transit Police and other federal law enforcement agencies. Asked whether the show of force was due to the shooting's proximity to the White House, roughly a mile away, Carroll said it was because police were responding to an active shooter. "The expectation is folks will go there to try to stop the loss of life," he said. Mayor Bowser confirmed the White House had been briefed. President Trump has surged federal law enforcement in D.C. through his Safe and Beautiful Task Force . In a speech before the midterms last week, Trump declared D.C. "one of the safest cities in the country." Asked about Trump's role in reducing crime during Thursday's morning briefing, Bowser pushed back: "I praise MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors." Editors note: This story has been updated to add details about a sixth shooting victim.

events.title: UK-EU deal will ‘dissolve’ £60m a year of costs for plant trade, says Angela Eagle
events.summary: Signing of agreement to smooth movement of food, plants and animals next week will not recoup huge sums firms were forced to spend The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said. Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November , Angela Eagle said she hoped paperwork headaches for importers would “disappear” after the changes, although the move would not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls. “If we get the ink dry on 20 November, which I very much hope we will … all of that uncertainty, the extra cost, the paperwork and the potential problems if things get stuck at borders would all disappear,” Eagle told the Guardian during a visit to a plant nursery in Kent. “The cost, that £60m, can just dissolve and people’s potential to both export back into the EU and get their imports in … gets easier and more predictable.” The UK’s departure from the bloc triggered the introduction of border checks on imports and exports of plants, food and animal products, from sausages and cheese to trees and leather goods. Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit, according to analysis by the National Farmers’ Union, with egg, chicken and potato producers badly affected. The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed between the two sides in May , is due to be signed at next week’s summit. It will permit the removal of the vast majority of physical checks and most of the accompanying certificates and paperwork. This will save businesses in the horticulture sector the current cost of trading with Europe , including plant health inspection fees, phytosanitary certificates, document and ID checks, port fees, agents’ fees, additional labour costs and extra haulage costs. These costs total £60m a year, according to calculations by the industry body the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), but do not include late delivery penalties or sales lost because of port delays or damage to goods. These savings should put “downward pressure on food prices”, Eagle said, although she would not confirm the deal would lower the cost of food in the UK. The promise of the deal was welcomed by Provender Nurseries, one of the UK’s largest wholesale nurseries, which sells thousands of plants, trees and shrubs to local authorities, parks and landscapers from its base at Swanley in Kent. However, the company has already spent at least £500,000 on building a post-Brexit control post on its eight-hectare (20-acre) site, which will become obsolete once the deal is implemented. Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, said the business constructed the “sealed building and bought four electric forklifts to operate in it” to allow inspections of lorry loads of valuable trees and shrubs imported from the continent. The company decided to build the site to reduce the “delays and damage” it had experienced when smaller loads were inspected at government-run border control posts such as Sevington . “It cost a lot for a barn, but it gave us security as a business,” said McKenna. Despite this, McKenna hopes the SPS deal will convince some of Provender’s European suppliers, previously deterred by the paperwork and potential pitfalls of post-Brexit trade with the UK, to restart exports. “We need to see the small print on the agreement,” he said. “It could have been sooner, but we are pleased that it is happening.” The deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028, meaning businesses such as Provender will still be subject to the current border arrangements for more than a year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In the meantime, Fran Barnes, the chief executive of the HTA, called for “some easements as a transition arrangement that are pragmatic” to help horticulture businesses, such as fewer or no checks on imports of lower-risk products. Eagle conceded the implementation date was later than the mid-2027 targeted when the former prime minister Keir Starmer announced his EU “reset” deal in May 2025. Starmer’s replacement by Andy Burnham led to a “pause” in negotiations with Brussels, said Eagle, with the upcoming November summit pushed back from July. The original target was “always a very, very ambitious timescale,” she said. “That extra time has meant we could deal in a more coherent way with some of the knottier, thornier issues on things like pesticides.” The UK has continued to use some pesticides and fungicides that are banned in the EU . This has prompted industry concerns that British potatoes grown in 2027, treated with pesticides banned in the EU, could need to be thrown away if the resulting frozen chips went on sale after the deal’s implementation.

events.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
events.summary: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. events.title: Jensen Huang and the End of the Founder Fairy Tale
events.summary: It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy. I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing. What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides. Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this? I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube .) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat. As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would . And to a large extent he did. Until this week. Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm. Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy. Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt: Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories. WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively. Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling. You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck. That’s right. It was really about telling the story. Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China. Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips. This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Rivals offer sympathy for stranded admins – and a reminder that putting all your eggs in one basket has consequences Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about 3 hours ago Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum 5 hours ago FAA lifts ground stop after hours-long delays snag travelers 14 hours ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 16 hours ago This year’s bug count just passed 100K 16 hours ago Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study. Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope. The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on. At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked. Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems. Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today. "This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs. "When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped." Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure." Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services." This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable ." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal. And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax.

events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’ More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. November 12, 2026: Democrats launch investigation into Nvidia; Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick summoned to testify before Senate Banking Committee In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X. November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia. November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors.

events.title: Inside energy’s next chapter at Adipec 2026, powered by $67bn in deals
events.summary: Following a year of supply disruptions and heightened geopolitical uncertainty, the $67 billion (Dh246 billion) in agreements signed at Adipec 2026 underscore the energy sector’s proactive approach to tackling questions of security and resilience in the face of growing demand. Taken together, the agreements spanned gas supply, infrastructure, logistics, industrial capacity and digitalisation, reflecting an industry focused on strengthening resilience across the entire energy value chain. The world’s biggest energy show closed out the week with more than 50,000 deals over four days, a 26.4 per cent increase on 2025. In total, Adipec 2026 brought more than 240,000 attendees and 2,260 exhibiting companies representing 170 countries to Abu Dhabi to showcase solutions, discuss opportunities and forge partnerships. Collectively, the agreements announced in Abu Dhabi pointed to a new phase for the energy industry, one defined by investment in resilience, infrastructure, intelligence and cross-border partnerships rather than supply growth alone. Record energy sector participation More than 40 government ministers and policymakers attended, including representatives from Germany, Canada, Egypt, Austria, Japan, Kazakhstan and Nigeria, underscoring the show’s role as a global platform for energy dialogue and investment. They were among the 1,800 speakers spanning governance, energy, technology, finance and more. “The breadth of international participation, from energy, advanced technology and investment sectors, the record exhibition scale and billions of dollars in agreements advanced this week are particularly significant against the backdrop of this year’s extraordinary challenges,” said Abdulmunim Saif Al Kindy, chairman of Adipec 2026. “They demonstrate what Adipec is here to do: connect energy, technology and capital to turn ambition into action. They also reinforce Abu Dhabi’s position as a trusted global centre for the energy industry and the UAE’s commitment to working with partners around the world to strengthen energy security and unlock long-term economic growth,” he added. Over more than 40 years, Adipec has become the annual gathering of the energy industry. Deals are made here, capital is mobilised, new technologies are introduced, and projects are accelerated. As Karim Badawi, Egypt’s Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, said, "The world needs more energy, and to be able to unlock and deliver this energy, it can only be done through collaboration and partnership.” He was speaking alongside ministers from Romania, Azerbaijan and Venezuela at a session titled Beyond borders: can national energy strategies deliver a connected global system? Tackling complex challenges for future security The energy sector must overcome a complex array of challenges. On the one hand, demand is rising as populations grow and new pressures come from artificial intelligence and industrial development. On the other hand, energy-transition imperatives require that production expands to renewables and alternative fuels while leveraging traditional energy sources to avoid supply deficits. Most industry leaders (93 per cent) expect demand growth to require several energy sources, according to the Adipec Global Energy Report 2026 , which surveyed more than 1,800 executives in ten markets. Investment needs span the entire value chain, from oil and gas to renewables and nuclear power at the upstream end, to logistics solutions that get energy to consumers in the form of terminals, grids, pipelines and storage. The International Energy Agency estimates that 3,000GW - the equivalent of a year’s worth of energy for more than 2 billion homes - of advanced-stage renewable and storage projects are waiting for grid connections. Digital infrastructure, such as AI and data centres, is adding to demand as technologies move from experimentation to wide-scale deployment. The range of partnerships announced at Adipec this year demonstrates how complex the energy business has become. But they also reveal how the sector is responding and the broad directions ahead. Preparedness is now the biggest priority, as UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Adnoc Group chief executive Dr Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber said in an address on the event’s first day. He said ensuring energy security was now the top question for “every family, every farmer, every industry and every business owner”, and reiterated that the solution would come from teamwork among the sector’s leaders, many of whom were present at the event. “The choices we make today will determine the energy landscape a decade from now,” he said. "Let’s apply the lessons we have learnt. Let’s build capacity and everything that supports it. Let’s forge partnerships that hold when it matters. And if you want a partner you can count on, you are in the right room, in the right city, in the right country. Because when it counts the most, you can count on the UAE.” Turning ambition into action Agreements announced in Abu Dhabi show how the industry is translating resilience from ambition into action. Among the major deals last week, the investment company XRG agreed to acquire Anglo-Dutch energy group Shell’s stake in Australia’s North West Shelf LNG project for $1.5 billion as it seeks to expand its international gas portfolio while strengthening energy links with Asia-Pacific markets. Separately, the Abu Dhabi-based industrial zone Ta’ziz reached financial close on $1.39 billion (Dh5.1 billion) for two projects in Ruwais: a logistics gateway terminal and an ammonia facility capable of producing one million tonnes of the alternative fuel a year. Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) took a final investment decision on the Ruwais Diyab unconventional gas project, aimed at producing and supplying the UAE with 345 million standard cubic feet of raw gas a day from 2029. Project announcements at the show also reflected cooperation across national borders and industrial sectors. Indonesia’s Special Task Force for Upstream Oil and Gas (SKK Migas) also announced several agreements, including partnerships with PT Pertamina, Halliburton Worldwide, and Tara Industries. They covered drilling services, offshore vessel support and establishing a new surveying and mapping company in Abu Dhabi to serve the subsea energy cable sector.
