events.title: Uber confirms hackers stole thousands of drivers’ license information in data breach
events.summary: Uber is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California , the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion confirmed its data was also stolen in the Fireworks hack. “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch, deferring our questions to Fireworks. Uber did not say how many customers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. When reached by email, a spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident. According to data breach notices seen by TechCrunch, the stolen data includes driver’s licenses of 2,567 individuals in Massachusetts, 3,430 people across South Carolina, and 1,873 residents of Rhode Island. A filing with Illinois showed that some state residents had their driver’s license information stolen, but that the number of affected people was pending. Uber also notified drivers who live in California, but did not say how many had their information stolen. The number is expected to rise as more data breach notifications roll in. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft. This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data. events.title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
events.summary: It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed. He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy! In the aftermath, Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same. In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang. These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS. That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999 , which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today. That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA . This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing. Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America , the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers. Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996 . The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day. Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break. Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money . I think I was wrong. What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady . Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening. Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated. That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it. In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

events.title: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams
events.summary: In the last few months, Fireflies , Wispr Flow , and Granola have all released competing capabilities in the dictation and meeting note-taking space. The newest entrant in that category is voice AI giant ElevenLabs , which this week released an experimental app called ElevenAI that combines meeting note-taking, dictation, and agent integration. Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion , is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual. ElevenAI packs all the features typically found in other apps in the category. It can take meeting notes across your meetings and notify other participants that the conversation is being recorded. Users can query data across meetings and get live assistance during a chat, helping them recall a key detail from older conversations. ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes. Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription. ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case , and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript. events.title: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
events.summary: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran , according to three sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters : The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran. Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said. Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment. State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official. Instead, the president has sided with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to continue the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran, while seeing if a deal is possible. "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday. "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period." The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel. His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so. In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds. On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran. A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think the current situation demands immediate military action against Iran.

events.title: DR Congo president enacts referendum law
events.summary: DR Congo’s president has signed a law allowing the constitution to be changed or replaced through a referendum, a move opponents warn could pave the way for him to seek a third term in the mineral-rich country. Félix Tshisekedi, in power since 2019, is due to complete his second and final term under the current constitution in just over two years. He said in May he was not seeking constitutional changes to stay in power, but would accept a third term if the Congolese people wanted it. The country was ruled by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko for three decades until his overthrow in 1997. After years of war, its 2006 constitution introduced safeguards against a return to dictatorship, including presidential term limits. But Tshisekedi’s predecessor, Joseph Kabila, still stayed in office for two years after his final term expired. Opposition leaders have joined forces to resist any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s rule, organizing protests at home and seeking support from European governments. They argue that a referendum cannot override the constitution’s ban on changing presidential term limits. — Ruben Nyanguila

Driving the news: " Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC Friday morning. "You ... have to ask them about their internal processes," he added. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: Ghana sets out $10B investment plan
events.summary: Ghana aims to invest $10 billion over four years to expand domestic production and reduce its dependence on raw commodity exports, as the West African country seeks to turn its recovery from a debt crisis into employment growth and higher incomes. Presenting the budget, the finance minister told lawmakers “too little value” was added domestically. As part of the push to shift the economy, Africa’s largest gold producer wants to phase out exports of unprocessed minerals by 2030. Much of the skilled employment linked to its mineral wealth currently takes place abroad, the finance ministry says. The government is targeting economic growth of 8% by 2030 and the budget has allocated $2.6 billion to support agriculture, energy, and manufacturing over the next year. Ghana completed an IMF bailout program this year and now plans to repay about $3 billion in domestic and international debt ahead of schedule. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive
events.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement. Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow. The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled “Stand with Jensen,” and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company. The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him . Notable Several names have been floated for who could replace Huang, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, or even, on President Donald Trump’s suggestion , former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

events.title: Hydropower generation in the Southwest fell to record lows this summer
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923, Power Plant Operating Data Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey. Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam , respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge , a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows. However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook , November 2026 We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region's generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011. events.title: Nvidia lost its founding CEO. Can it keep its momentum?
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business. Nvidia’s founder Jensen Huang resigned after a scandal, but analysts say the chipmaker’s AI business should stay strong in the near term. The article says tech companies often do best when founders are replaced by leaders with deep technical and product skills, not mainly finance or sales experience. Apple, Microsoft and Intel show that successor choice can shape long-term success, while Nvidia now needs a leader to plan for rivals and the next AI shift. Advice to Nvidia’s board: choose a techie. As the chip giant’s directors seek a replacement to Jensen Huang , the history of successions at Silicon Valley companies suggests that the odds of long-term success are better with a person steeped in technology and product development rather than finance, sales or marketing. Replacing a founder is a defining moment for any company, whether it has been planned for years or is a sudden departure; whether the company is thriving or faltering. For Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and former chief executive officer, the fall came remarkably quickly. He resigned on N ov 12 after the disclosure of affairs with a woman identified by US intelligence as a Chinese spy and with an executive who reported to him. Nvidia’s business as the leading chip supplier to artificial intelligence data centres is flourishing. Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business, despite a big stock-market reaction – the company’s shares have fallen 14% in the past five days. But the best tech leaders steer their companies towards opportunity. At Nvidia, founded in 1993, Huang recognised more than a decade ago that chips used mainly for image-processing in computer games could be repurposed as the hardware engines for AI software. It was a huge bet for the small company – and paid off. “You can coast on the founder’s work for years with good execution,” said Steve Blank, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and investor, who is an adjunct professor at Stanford University. “But you can lack the founder’s vision to see over the horizon and identify what’s next. That’s why the best successors have a lot of technical acumen as well as business acumen.” Over the years, the results for tech companies replacing founding executives have been decidedly mixed. In 1985, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs was forced out after clashing with his CEO, John Sculley, who had come from Pepsico. Under Sculley, Apple enjoyed years of rising profits. But the company eventually struggled to compete against lower-cost personal computers based on Microsoft’s Windows software and Intel’s microprocessors. Scully left Apple in 1993. Three years later, with Apple’s survival uncertain, Jobs returned and became CEO. A renowned product team leader, he led a corporate renaissance, introducing new digital devices including the iPod and the iPhone that transformed the product categories of music players and cellphones. In 2011, shortly before he died, Jobs named Tim Cook as his successor. Cook has a degree in industrial engineering as well as a master’s in business administration (MBA). While some analysts said Apple lost some of its innovative spark, today the company is valued at US$5.16 trillion (S$6.64 trillion), the most valuable in the world. In September, Cook became executive chair and John Ternus, a mechanical engineer and product development executive, became the company’s CEO. Intel did not fare so well. While Andrew Grove did not found the chipmaker, he was among its first employees and led the company for nearly two decades. Grove emigrated from Hungary, learnt English and earned an undergraduate degree and a doctorate in chemical engineering. Grove led Intel’s drive to dominate the market for microprocessor chips, the electronic brains of personal computers. He became the face of Intel and one of the architects of the personal computer industry, named Time magazine’s Man Of The Year in 1997. Grove’s immediate successor in 1998, Craig Barrett, was also a technologist. But later successors were less so – and Intel’s fortunes declined precipitously. As part of efforts to help revive American chip manufacturing, the US government said in 2025 that it would invest nearly US$9 billion in Intel for a stake of just under 10%. Some of the biggest tech companies have learnt that technical expertise at the top is indispensable. Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, stepped aside as CEO in 2000 and handed the job to his long-time business partner, Steve Ballmer. Ballmer was known as a brilliant sales and business development executive, and a tireless, hands-on manager. During his years as CEO, from 2000 to 2014, Microsoft’s sales and profits rose steadily. But Ballmer’s lack of tech expertise contributed to an erosion of Microsoft’s reputation as an industry leader.

"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said . The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change." Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it. Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms." Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put. The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027. Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite. Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well . events.title: Microsoft says Outlook and other 365 services have been fully restored
events.summary: Microsoft on Friday said it had fully restored the services of its Outlook email and other apps in its 365 suite, following a two-day outage that paralysed millions of users globally. "We've confirmed that the services across the previously affected environments have fully recovered and the backlog of email messages has been processed, thus this issue is remediated," the company said in a final update on its service health status website. Disruptions to Microsoft's services began on Thursday, disrupting users, businesses and governments across the globe. It affected Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI service. Microsoft also offered an explanation - and a subsequent apology - for why the problem took so long to resolve. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue… — Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026 “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration … We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” the statement read. Partial restoration began on Friday, with users in parts of the Asia Pacific, North America and Europe among the first to get their access back. At the time, Microsoft said it was "seeing improvements in key customer scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing". In the UAE, users began receiving emails again in their Outlook accounts starting at about 5.20pm local time on Friday, on desktop and mobile versions of the app. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack as a trigger for the disruption. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” Microsoft said. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” it added. The company promised to give a more detailed explanation about what had happened and carry out a robust investigation once its review was finished. “We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” the company said. Analysts told The National that a continuing outage of Microsoft’s collaboration tools would have a “cascading” effect on businesses, with the financial impact increasing with its duration.

events.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
events.summary: Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won't substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government. Spencer Platt/Getty Images New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses . What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see. That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide. Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them. Scott Gries/Getty Images How the plan will work New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all. While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices. In this respect, the stores offer a “ public option ” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives , like public schools and city hospitals. Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable. At his May announcement , Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” A fresh form of intervention Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program , known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets. This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “ the submerged state .” Bringing the state into the open Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate. Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Grou

events.title: UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer
events.summary: Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’ The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis. Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows. It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes. Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims. Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said. A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August , up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence. The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year. Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable. We continue to deliver strong, profitable growth, particularly in the capital-light areas of general insurance and wealth.”

events.title: Global oil supply returns to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, says IEA
events.summary: Supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October as market shows ‘tentative signs of rebalancing’ The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said. Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”. The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported. It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes. The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April. However, this week prices fell to their lowest level since late August, at $89.66, after the US president, Donald Trump, told reporters that the war with Iran was “ effectively over ”. Brent crude was trading at about $95 a barrel on Friday. There are still concerns around continued attacks on oil tankers in the Middle East, and this week reports emerged that senior Iranian officials believe the US could be planning further military strikes . However, the IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m barrels a day in the final three months of the year, 1.7m higher than forecast demand. The agency had previously expected a deficit in the fourth quarter. The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict. The IEA said its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Opec+ oil cartel said this week that it had pumped 41m barrels a day of crude in October, up from about 2m in September and at 97% of its prewar volumes. Global oil demand is also expected to fall by 2.68m barrels a day this year to 103.2m a day, the IEA reported. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feed stocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency”.

events.title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
events.summary: Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high. Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover. Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers. The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices. The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate. Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say. Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month ( see the chart above ), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft. A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens. "The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states. Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too. The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning . Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states. With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA predicts the global market will return to a surplus this quarter. Yes, but: Insurance and shipping costs are elevated, and that puts upward pressure on prices. "Both Iran and the Houthis have demonstrated that they can severely restrict oil flows from the region using a range of attacks and tactics. This is something that will have to be priced in," Torbjorn Soltvedt, a senior Verisk analyst, tells me via email. And there's no guarantee that higher tanker transit and increased shipments through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz won't be curtailed by fresh attacks. Zoom in: Goldman Sachs estimates that the tanker market's "adaptation to Mideast shipping risks" accounts for most of the $20-per-barrel year-over-year increase in average costs for shipping oil. These freight rates reflect vessel availability, insurance, fuel cost, logistics, travel distances and more. What we're watching: It's unclear how much more oil can keep leaving the region in the near term, as intermittent attacks keep happening. "The current recovery may be close to the limit of what the existing logistics system can sustain," HSBC's Kim Fustier said in a recent note. The bottom line: "We would not equate [oil] exports with normality," Fustier writes. She cited substantial volumes of well production that remain curtailed, lower refined product shipments, and "and the cost of sustaining exports." events.title: Oil market to return to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, IEA says
events.summary: The global oil market is to return to a surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war, despite supplies remaining tight, the International Energy Agency has said. Global oil supplies have outpaced demand for the first time since the conflict broke out in late February. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as exports from the Gulf recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based IEA said in its monthly market report on Friday. Inventories climbed by 2.3 million bpd to 105.4 million bpd last month, raising output by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million bpd since August, the IEA said. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, hit 18.4 million bpd in October, which was 26 per cent below prewar levels as attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz continued. That narrowed the year-on-year output decline to 2.9 million bpd, compared with an average loss of eight million bpd loss from March to September, the agency added. The higher export rates also prompted the IEA to "significantly" raise its expectations for global oil supply for the remainder of 2026, with fourth-quarter estimates now 3.3 million bpd higher. The oil market is "straightening out" and "showing tentative signs of rebalancing", the IEA said. But the agency acknowledged that global oil demand continues to be weighed down by high prices and disruptions to exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas from the Gulf, which largely remain at about half of prewar levels. The agency forecasts that global oil demand in 2026 will fall by 2.7 million bpd to 102.3 million bpd, a slight decrease from its October projections . Demand is to recover by two million bpd in 2027, it added. While LPG, ethane and naphtha will account for about 80 per cent of the expected increase next year as supply chains normalise, transport fuels will see a modest gain, "as high prices accelerate electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet", the IEA said. The "severe tightness" in supply is still particularly pronounced for diesel, which has soared to record levels, especially in the US. Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country’s diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East, the IEA said. "At the same time, Atlantic Basin refineries, particularly in the United States, are running hard to capture high margins, while improved crude availability in Asia and fresh Chinese product export quotas could support higher refinery throughput rates in the region," it said. "Notably, the accelerated release of IEA emergency diesel stocks over the coming months will provide a critical bridge across the supply gap until the global refinery system and product output recover." The oil market is gradually recovering from the effects of the Iran war, which is now in its ninth month. While the US has signalled that it does not plan to carry out further military action against Tehran, a resolution to the conflict remains unclear. Oil prices have been volatile throughout the war, but have markedly declined over the past weeks. At 5.02pm UAE time on Friday, Brent was up 0.35 per cent at $96.16 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate shed 0.18 per cent to $88.58 a barrel. The IEA's supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a more substantial build in 2027. "As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery," the agency said.

events.title: Microsoft’s latest email outage turned into a full-blown global cloud crisis
events.summary: Microsoft is slowly recovering from its daylong outage after much of the company’s systems were hit by a cascading software issue. The problems, which started Thursday, were initially flagged as affecting the company’s services in the U.S. and the Americas, but quickly spread around the world, as engineers struggled to recover downed servers. What began as an Outlook email and Teams video conferencing outage soon developed into a full-blown meltdown affecting the company’s cloud services for both consumer and business email, files, and documents. The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools and Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features. Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers. Microsoft hasn’t yet said what caused the issues, only saying the outage involved “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable.” The company said it continues to investigate the cause. The outage affected a broad range of industries, including TechCrunch’s own email. We’ve reached out to Microsoft for comment about the incident. As of Friday morning on the U.S. East Coast, Microsoft’s Outlook email service had begun to recover and some emails have been trickling in. The recovery comes after engineers initially could not find the cause of the issue that was causing servers in Microsoft’s data centers to fail. Doug Madory, the director of internet analysis at Kentik, a company that monitors internet traffic worldwide, said in a post on Bluesky that traffic was returning to Microsoft’s services after about 18 hours of downtime. Microsoft said in its latest status update on Friday that there was “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident,” and later noted that there was “not related to cyber or AI / agents.” That may be some solace for the millions who went without their email and online services yesterday, but the company is likely to face questions about its inability to swiftly recover from an outage of its own making. A Microsoft spokesperson did not respond to our questions asking if the company has the technical means to detect malicious activity, such as logs, or if Microsoft has a way to check what happened. “We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents, and platform, in a statement on Friday. “Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.” The last major incident affecting Microsoft services was in September , when a dayslong outage hit Microsoft’s cloud services. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service. events.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong? —Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers. Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think . Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China. events.title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
events.summary: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts . Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. “Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson , chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic. The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries. events.title: FTC to block $3.5B veterinary merger
events.summary: The Scoop The FTC is flexing its regulatory muscle again. The antitrust regulator is planning to file suit to block a $3.5 billion veterinary deal later today, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to prevent a private equity-owned company from acquiring a smaller rival. The regulator plans to cite increased costs for pet owners and veterinary clinics as part of the suit to block CD&R and TPG-owned Covetrus from acquiring MWI Veterinary Supply, the people said. Covetrus and MWI are both national suppliers of medical supplies and products. The Commission believes that the combination would result in a highly concentrated market, the people said. Neither Covetrus nor MWI returned a request for comment. Rohan’s view Under Andrew Ferguson, the FTC, unlike the Justice Department, has managed to focus on its regulatory mission — even if it has allowed many mergers to pass uncontested. It has used its enforcement tools to execute President Donald Trump’s agenda, which has recently centered on affordability. It is that focus, Washington insiders say, that has now given Ferguson a degree of latitude to pursue cases and merger enforcement that he desires. The FTC is also planning to block a $5 billion merger of two uniform and office equipment suppliers, Semafor reported . The FTC plans to set a last-rites meeting — a precursor to that formal suit — in the coming days, other people familiar with the matter said. Notable Merger investigations neared a record low in 2025 , according to the DAMITT database maintained by law firm Dechert.

events.title: South Africa’s Ramaphosa takes AI pitch to Musk's turf
events.summary: The News South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to land in California this weekend for a week-long push to court billions in American AI infrastructure investment. The roadshow will throw him into the backyard of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, whose regulatory clash with Pretoria is at the center of a widening diplomatic rift with Washington. Ramaphosa is likely to face questions about domestic ownership rules which Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has slammed as “openly racist” and cited as the reason his Starlink satellite-internet venture does not operate in Africa’s biggest economy. The working visit , which kicks off on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World summit , unfolds against a deepening diplomatic row as Washington steps up pressure against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices. South Africa was recently also removed from the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program. US Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III warned in recent weeks that South Africa’s mandatory local equity ownership transfers under Black Economic Empowerment laws, a policy designed to address dispossessions caused by South Africa’s racist past, are holding back “billions with a B” in American capital. Ramaphosa, whose itinerary includes meetings with Google, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks, and Microsoft, is bringing eight cabinet ministers, including his finance, trade, energy, and communications chiefs — in a bid to capture a slice of America’s $650 billion AI capital expenditure this year. Speaking to the press ahead of the trip, Ramaphosa’s spokesman Vincent Magwenya said South Africa aims to court American capital while firmly “safeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection, and responsible AI governance.” The BEE controversy Under South Africa’s BEE rules, companies in regulated sectors like telecoms and mining must hand at least 30% of their local ownership to Black people to secure operating licenses — a redress policy that prompted Bozell to say that “time for dialogue has ended” after South Africa failed to meet US demands for regulatory reforms, and executive condemnation of inflammatory political rhetoric. The stand-off has triggered US visa restrictions on unspecified South African officials deemed responsible for “government sponsored discrimination,” led Washington to pull PEPFAR funding to the country, which poured $8 billion into treating the world’s largest HIV/AIDS caseload over two decades, as well as the AGOA ejection. Tiisetso’s view Ramaphosa’s flight to California deliberately skips a potentially frosty reception in Washington. The itinerary, which starts off at Semafor’s inaugural Silicon Valley & The World summit, tells you everything you need to know about Pretroia’s game plan. It is a bold geopolitical arbitrage, an attempt by Pretoria to wall off diplomatic tensions to chase a slice of billions of dollars in AI spending. Pretoria has reasons to believe US boardrooms can look past Washington’s hostility. To start with, boardrooms seem to have a high tolerance for political noise when the economics make sense, if what has been happening in the background is anything to go by. The value of trade between these two countries rose in 2025, industrial giants such aluminum producer Alcoa and transportation behemoth Wabtec keep writing checks despite tariffs, visa curbs, and Bozell’s warning that billions in investment are frozen over South African domestic policies. Next week, we will find out if commerce can keep outrunning politics. Room for Disagreement Sakeliga, a pro-business lobby group, took South Africa’s telecoms regulator to court, arguing that forcing companies to hand over 30% of their local equity to obtain a license acts as a hard barrier to entry that shuts out global players like Starlink . Notable SpaceX has floated a $110 million local infrastructure commitment alongside hundreds of millions rand in free satellite broadband for rural schools as an alternative to handing over its local equity to Black South Africans.

events.title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years. Intel, Microsoft, and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from the company’s leadership crisis. As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel. “Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch. Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen. The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.” Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis , Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list . Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away. According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.” Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips . Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.” And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s. “These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said. events.title: Jensen Huang didn’t show confidence in his successor, report says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who has now replaced him as interim CEO, as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation earlier in the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing an anonymous source. Huang made the comment during a meeting with Nvidia’s finance team about the company’s plans to provide guarantees worth billions of dollars to data center operators that couldn’t afford to buy its chips up front, according to the report. He reportedly also said Kress was a person who couldn’t help him steer strategy or decision-making. Kress has been with Nvidia for over 13 years now , after serving as SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology and Operations Finance. The report said she has questioned Nvidia’s program-focused, credit-based deals involving Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, and wanted to know how to decide which deals are beneficial, how to value guarantees, and determine returns. Earlier in the year, she had scaled back on Nvidia’s commitment for OpenAI’s ambitious Ohio data center project. The company was in talks to provide $250 billion in credit to OpenAI but ended up committing $105 billion . Huang resigned Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs , including one with the company’s VP for healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The company is also investigating a possible Chinese espionage plot . After Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported that he was having a third affair with another employee . Nvidia is currently searching for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, who had the top job for over 33 years. events.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
events.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing. 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves. In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings. Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire. AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence. Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters AI doubts trigger market turbulence The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly. Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple , Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day. In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy . On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still. Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts. In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion. "We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money." Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction' Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction." "We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie." In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates. Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share. Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head. "Is this the best timing?" he asked. While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion. Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030. "If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued." Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects. "Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize." Signs to watch, not reasons to flee With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing. This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

events.title: Commonwealth Fusion’s CEO sees UAE primed for new energy tech
events.summary: The Scene When Massachusetts-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems looked for companies that could produce large metal components and complex machinery for its prototype, it landed on the oil and gas industry. CEO Bob Mumgaard said the hydrocarbons industry shares many of the same skills and tools that fusion developers need to achieve a breakthrough and eventually take a share of the energy mix. The UAE is well positioned to use its expertise in oil and gas to adopt fusion technology, Mumgaard said, especially after it has developed a track record of building nuclear power plants and its embrace of AI. “They understand what energy leadership and first mover advantage, advanced technologies can bring to their society, their place in the world,” he said. Abu Dhabi’s government-owned fusion fund, Plynth Energy, acquired a minority stake worth more than $100 million in Commonwealth this year, according to Axios. The US company raised $1 billion in July, bringing its total funding to $4 billion, which Mumgaard said would be enough to build the prototype and prepare for a larger, utility-scale plant in the early 2030s. Next decade Scientists have long predicted that the fusion breakthrough is a decade away. The prospect of unlimited, clean, and safe power is tantalizing, and it now appears that mastery of the reaction that essentially powers the stars is within reach. Commonwealth’s Massachusetts prototype uses powerful magnets and hydrogen isotopes (deuterium and tritium) to produce a reaction that’s hotter than the sun’s core. The machine is about 80% complete, Mumgaard said, and is due to start up in 2027. Its goal is to show that it can release more energy than it takes in. The company then plans to build a 400-megawatt plant in Virginia and has secured Google and Italian energy company Eni as buyers, Mumgaard said. Global adoption at scale is still decades away, but Mumgaard said the US-Iran conflict is also making the case for accelerating research and deployment. “Fusion is one of the most secure, resilient energy systems because it doesn’t need pipelines or ships, and it doesn’t have emissions,” he said.
