events.title: House Democratic leaders face fallout over poorly timed floor vote fumbles
events.summary: A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor. Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the American people," he said. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) did not respond to Axios' question and walked off the House floor into her office. The intrigue: Even some current and incoming House Democrats who are voting for Jeffries as speaker acknowledged the vote was a black eye. "I think everyone's frustrated with how that all went down, I'm not going to lie to you about that," said Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.). "People are pissed," a senior House Democrat told Axios. The other side: Other Democrats told Axios the absences were an inevitable reality of Congress, noting that several who missed votes have said they were attending to emergencies. "I think everyone's explained what the situations were — somebody was recovering from surgery. There are certain things that are unavoidable," said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.). Others said the upshot is that House Democrats need to do a better job of getting to votes on time: "The general consensus among the new members is on Jan. 3, it's time to lock in," Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.) told Axios. Others said the speakership election offers a window into how Jeffries' approach to the speakership might play out over the coming year. Jeffries has always taken a more hands-off approach than his predecessor, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), preferring to let issues and fights among members resolve themselves.

events.title: Senate Dems can look forward to unlikely MAGA allies
events.summary: Senate Democrats could find some of their most surprising allies next Congress from the right wing of the Republican Party . Why it matters: Senate Democrats are on track to need only four GOP votes to break filibusters next Congress. They could find those votes from a bloc of GOP senators with a shared appetite for taking on corporate power. Enter Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). Each has already worked with Democrats, and their votes could put legislation over the top. Who we're watching: Hawley has co-led multiple pieces of legislation with progressive star Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) this Congress. Hawley is often viewed as a loner in the GOP, pairing populist economics with hardcore culture war issues from abortion to transgender care to religious freedom. He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday. He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said. Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls. President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats. Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year. Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work. Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security." Warren and Banks have tag-teamed on numerous tech and AI safety bills, including a joint statement on Nvidia this week. Hawley is also a major critic of AI. Schmitt worked with Warren in 2024 and 2025 to challenge Big Tech's dominance of Pentagon AI contracts, and with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in July to crack down on search engine monopolies. What to watch: While there will be fewer this Congress, Democrats will also have a club of more moderate Republicans they can try to pick up too. Murkowski, along with Sens. John Curtis (R-Utah) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), will be top targets.

events.title: Nvidia fallout fuels questions about Lutnick’s staying power
events.summary: The News Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has kept his job through scrutiny over his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; his cryptocurrency firm, Tether; and his former financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald. The Nvidia fallout may be the toughest test yet of his staying power. A growing GOP contingent is pointing the finger at Lutnick for not cracking down hard enough on Megaspeed, the AI chip firm with ties to an alleged Chinese spy with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair, and for what they see as the Commerce Department’s broader failure to restrict AI chip exports to China. In the wake of reporting that other administration officials had urged the Commerce secretary to move faster, Republicans on and off Capitol Hill are accusing Lutnick of defying President Donald Trump by not imposing curbs on the firm — and even positing his job could be at risk. “We’re hearing … Trump has directed three times that [Megaspeed be blacklisted],” Rep. John Moolenaar, the top Republican on the House Select Committee on China, told Semafor. “If that’s true … then clearly, it seems that those questions need to be answered.” But so far the balance of GOP officials are coming to Lutnick’s defense, suggesting the commerce secretary won’t be going anywhere soon. The president himself is so far standing by Lutnick despite the bipartisan backlash, reinforcing his willingness to go easier on China as he pursues a trade detente with Beijing. “What I would say to everybody: Just settle down,” Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. “We don’t need to shoot Howard today.” “There’s lots and lots and lots of stuff here that’s going to come out. Should it come out? Absolutely,” Justice continued. “Should we get on some witch hunt running through the wilderness? … I don’t do that.” Congress will get more answers soon: Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Thursday that Lutnick will testify before the chamber’s Commerce Committee. And House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., said that Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following revelations of another affair with a colleague, will appear before his panel . Even Lutnick’s critics think he’ll eventually pull himself out of trouble, even as longstanding interagency tension threatens to boil over. “When you saw [Treasury] Secretary [Scott] Bessent blowing up at Lutnick in the Situation Room, you can rest assured the working level at Treasury was all over Commerce about chip sales for over a year,” Steve Bannon, the MAGA commentator and Bessent ally, told Semafor. “Now the issue becomes: Does Lutnick start inventing excuses to save himself?” A Commerce Department spokesperson said that “Treasury and Commerce have a great working relationship,” adding that both “are committed to advancing President Trump’s agenda.” The Nvidia news landed just in time for Democrats, who are finalizing their oversight plans for the next Congress. Already, lawmakers have laid the groundwork to investigate Lutnick’s involvement with Cantor Fitzgerald , Tether , and Epstein . The detractors No GOP lawmaker has called explicitly for Lutnick’s firing. But they haven’t hesitated to blame him for many of the recent revelations about Nvidia — including the fact that Huang accompanied Trump to China earlier this year despite the since-revealed existence of a State Department memo outlining his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy. “How on Earth do you put somebody on Air Force One [when you have] been informed there was a suspected improper relationship beforehand? How is that protecting the president?” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president; to me, that’s a disqualifying moment for Lutnick.” Compared to Epstein, “this, to me, is next-level,” he added. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., rebuked Commerce for not shedding more light on the circumstances, particularly when it comes to the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed. “If I were the secretary, I’d call a press conference and explain what happened,” Kennedy said. “This is as serious as an aneurysm.” Even some of the Trump administration’s staunchest allies have weighed in, accusing Lutnick of defying the president by failing to rein in Megaspeed. “Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen,” China hawk Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News. He urged Lutnick to testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The defenders Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor that “you’ve got to get the facts” before drawing any conclusions, adding that Lutnick has “always responded to my questions, so that’s all I can ask.” Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., also cast doubt on whether Lutnick really was at fault. “In a lot of cases, where they simply blame someone, I want to know what the rules are that he’s trying to comply with,” Rounds told Semafor. “Is there something that we’ve done, in terms of policy, that might have either delayed his ability or something else? I don’t know, and I’d rather get the facts before I make a decision as to guilt.” The AI industry sees little problem with Lutnick’s conduct either way. “Commerce’s job is to expand the economy, domestic and foreign, pretty much at all costs,” National Artificial Intelligence Association CEO Caleb Max said. “So if you zoom out, I don’t think it looks nefarious; I think it looks natural.” The View From the white house Far more crucially, the White House’s public posture on the debacle indicates that Trump is not particularly concerned about the fallout, let alone Lutnick’s role in it. “Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump’s America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,” a White House official said. “President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” The White House pointed Semafor to the president’s comments earlier this week, when he told reporters that he didn’t think he’d bring up the subject during his upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Notable The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule to block China’s remote access to AI chips, The Information reported . White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out of his role, Reuters reported .

events.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
events.summary: The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r) Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person? Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw. From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place. But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing". So how much AI enhancement is too much? Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye. But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place. "The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different." For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison. AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI. But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time. "It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for." All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down. Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible. It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly. According to a recent survey , external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was. Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months. He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential. But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time. "I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person." He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated. Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove. In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter. In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down. Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing. "If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says. In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property". "It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold." Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology. But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

events.title: DOJ takes aim at $1.2B in Binance loot as FBI disrupts North Korean scam
events.summary: The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft. The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months. It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks. 900+ faces stolen The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers. Here’s how the attack works. First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible. “You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles. “They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday. The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite. Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told. “When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.” ‘You’re on mute’ as a social engineering vector The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix. Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam. The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff. “The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.” Binance heist update The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group. Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.” Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

events.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
events.summary: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company. Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots. Colette Kress Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters . Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers. Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives. She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of whom oversaw relatively narrow parts of the business. Yes, but: Her finance background could raise doubts about whether she could match Huang's technological prowess. Ian Buck Ian Buck of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Buck is among the potential successors drawing attention from analysts and investors, Reuters reported, given his engineering expertise and prominent position inside Nvidia. He currently serves as Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He also helped develop CUDA, Nvidia's computing platform that made its graphics processors essential to modern AI development. Chris Malachowsky Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Malachowsky co-founded Nvidia with Huang in 1993 and helped shape the company's technology over the next three decades, according to his Nvidia bio page . "Malachowsky has been instrumental in managing, defining and driving the company's core technologies as it has grown from a startup to the global leader in accelerated computing," the page reads. Much of his background is in engineering and technical leadership. Yes, but: His role today is less focused on day-to-day company management, raising questions about whether he would want to assume the CEO position. René Haas Arm CEO Rene Haas at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Sept. 14, 2023. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Haas, the CEO of British chip designer Arm Holdings, has emerged as an outside contender because of his chip industry experience and previous work at Nvidia, per multiple reports . He's a former Nvidia executive who has the public-facing skills that may be required as Nvidia faces heavy scrutiny from investors and government probes . Nvidia uses Arm's processor technology in some products. Flashback: Nvidia previously tried to acquire Arm in a $40 billion deal, but the companies abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid significant regulatory opposition. Tim Cook President Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook shake hands in the Oval Office at the White House. Photo: Win McNamee/Getty Images Former Apple CEO Tim Cook's name entered the succession conversation Thursday after President Trump publicly suggested he take over Nvidia. Cook's high profile and experience running one of the world's largest technology companies have fueled speculation that he could be a dark horse. Cook has also been mentioned in prediction market speculation. Yes, but: It's unclear whether Cook would want the job after recently stepping down as Apple's CEO. Johny Srouji Johny Srouji appears on a laptop screen during Apple's 2020 virtual Worldwide Developers Conference, viewed in Arlington, Va. Photo: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg has identified Srouji , Apple's chief hardware officer, as another potential successor. Before that, he led the development of Apple's custom chips for the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. Nikesh Arora Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora attends the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India in Feb. 2026. Photo: Prakash Singh/Bloomberg via Getty Images Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks , has emerged as a potential successor, with The Economic Times reporting investors have floated his name. Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018 and overseen the company's expansion into AI-powered cybersecurity. He previously served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and worked for a decade at Google, per his official biography . Yes, but: His experience is largely in cybersecurity and other areas of tech, rather than chip development. Lisa Su AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks onstage during the company's Gamers Day 2026 event in Seoul, South Korea. Photo: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images Su has led AMD, one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, for more than a decade. Bloomberg identified her as a potential successor given her deep experience in the chip industry. Yes, but: Su already runs one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, and she was just named " CEO of the Year " by Yahoo! Finance. Axios chief technology correspondent Ina Fried says Su might relish competing with a weakened Nvidia rather than taking over for Huang. Thomas Kurian Thomas Kurian speaks onstage during Oracle's OpenWorld conference in San Francisco in 2017. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud could also be considered . Kurian oversees cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience with major customers and technology essential to Nvidia's business. Yes, but: His resume does not feature chip design experience. Pat Gelsinger Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger holds up a processor while speaking onstage at the Computex technology conference in Taipei in 2024. Photo: Annabelle Chih/Bloomberg via Getty Images The former Intel CEO boasts decades of semiconductor engineering and leadership experience at one of Nvidia's longtime competitors. events.title: Microsoft struggling to fix massive cloud outage that's taken down email and Intune
events.summary: Microsoft is struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became “overwhelmed” and its attempts to fix the problem failed. The incident started at around 18:00 UTC on November 12, and meant services including Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot 365, and Defender for Office 365 became unavailable. Admins trying to figure out what was wrong couldn’t access tools like Intune or the Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center – they went down, too. On its X feed, Microsoft blamed “a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” The company said it hasn’t spotted any changes to its systems that might have sparked the incident, but its early investigation “indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.” The company’s status page offers contradictory information, saying Microsoft’s people are “assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.” According to a Xeet published at around 22:00 UTC, Microsoft said it found and validated an alternative service health check method, “which allowed a subset of affected servers to successfully return to service.” “We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process,” the company wrote. But those efforts may not be working. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the status page advises. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.” The incident means email is not flowing for many Microsoft customers: friends and family of Reg writers tell us their working days are severely disrupted. Microsoft’s most recent Xeet on the matter, published about an hour before this story went live, says it's trying to validate a potential recovery by “isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.” But the software giant hasn’t offered any timeline for full service restoration. This is a developing situation and The Reg will update this story as more information becomes available. ® UPDATED AT 00:35 UTC November 13 to add news that Microsoft says it has brought some servers back online and that they " initially remain healthy" but "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic." So not usefully healthy at all, then. "We're analyzing diagnostic data from these servers with our networking and platform experts to determine what's triggering this behavior," the company advised.

events.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
events.summary: Alan Milburn will publish his review next week Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review. As reported in the Times, , external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits. Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet". He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants. His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment. Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions. Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes. People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work. In his interim report, , external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work. Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers. Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate. Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system. "But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances. "I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around." Speaking later on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said young people would be given support "when they need it as teenagers rather than leaving them on benefits in their 20s". He added: "The principle that we will be working on is that we will guarantee support for young people and that is the whole basis on which we will proceed." Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around. "What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC. "Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added. But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants. Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate. He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources. "If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said. Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age. "You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said. In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary. James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear".

events.title: Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
events.summary: Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang . He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees. Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs , with Nvidia employees.) The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers. Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal. “The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license. By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time. But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang. The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal was approved after Trump learned of “Mr. Huang’s compromised position” in sleeping with an alleged spy, and after Nvidia donated $26 million toward Trump’s projects, including the ballroom. It appears to be asking if Trump used his knowledge of the affair to secure donations from Nvidia. Interestingly, in a “60 Minutes” interview with President Trump that aired on Sunday, Trump mentioned how he and his team had threatened an unnamed AI exec with jail , and after that, the exec “totally changed.” This Congressional investigation into Nvidia’s China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke. The Republican-led group involves leaders from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Intelligence Committee. That group has demanded that Huang come to them and testify in a closed-door session. They had threatened to subpoena him if he didn’t voluntarily agree. events.title: SEC enforcement actions drop to multi-decade lows
events.summary: Enforcement actions and penalties levied by the US Securities and Exchange Commission have fallen to multi-decade lows, reflecting a dramatic pullback by Wall Street’s top watchdog. The agency, which has seen budget and staff reductions under the Trump administration, doled out $1.1 billion in penalties last year, the lowest in two decades. The decline drew a rebuke from Democrats who vowed increased scrutiny of its enforcement program in the next Congress, though an SEC official cautioned that “ activity and effectiveness are not the same .” While some suggested the figures were consistent with the agency’s stated aim of promoting more IPOs , “the obvious risk is, with less enforcement, you have a greater risk of fraud ,” a law professor told the Financial Times. — Brendan Ruberry

events.summary: Ukraine said Thursday that a fresh disruption to Starlink services hampered its military operations, in what Kyiv suggested could be a pressure tactic by Washington amid ongoing negotiations to end the war. Meanwhile, ships carrying Russian diesel to the US have turned around, lacking willing American buyers . — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Silicon Valley Is Still Defending Jensen Huang
events.summary: News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley —including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation , after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned . As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave. Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure. Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company. That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report. Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate. Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman. On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.” Huang’s resignation left them in shock. The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure. The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says. Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week. Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision. Additional reporting by Will Knight and Zoë Schiffer. events.title: Nvidia turmoil could shake up China's AI landscape
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia could spell a sea change in China’s AI fortunes, as heightened scrutiny from Washington threatens to choke off the supply of American compute to mainland tech titans and AI startups. Huang’s extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang may have helped funnel at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips to China, The Information reported, empowering lawmakers to push for tighter US chip export controls . The prospect of more Nvidia chips staying in the US provides one explanation for hyperscalers’ share rises Thursday . On the flipside, restrictions on American compute could benefit Chinese chipmakers with Beijing pushing more resources toward developing semiconductor self-sufficiency. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Muse can now place calls to US businesses — if you pay
events.summary: After initially testing the feature in September, Meta’s consumer AI agent Muse is now able to place calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of its users. However, only paid subscribers have access to the feature, the company says. Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users , the company said last month, has been working to make consumer AI a mainstream product for everyday users. Placing calls is one of the ways it aims to get there, as it could handle another task on people’s to-do lists. Notes Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs division, the feature could be used to take care of calls people don’t want to make, like those to their cable company, the DMV, or to a restaurant that doesn’t offer online reservations. 🚨MUSE FEATURE ALERT!!!🚨 lots of you have been asking for this one… muse can make phone calls for you! ☎️📞📲 let muse take care of all those calls you don’t want to make. insurance? cable? DMV? dinner res? not your problem anymore. out now to paid subs in the US 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/dsyMNmI2Ub — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) November 12, 2026 Previously, only a select number of Muse early adopters were able to try this feature after asking the AI for access. Now, anyone who pays for Muse can make this type of request. Currently, Muse subscription plans start at $20 per month for 500 million Muse tokens per week. Heavier AI users can opt to pay $100 per month for 3 billion tokens. Muse is not the only AI agent able to place calls to businesses; the startup Instinct has been offering a similar option , as has Google’s Gemini . However, while the AI tools are now certainly capable of handling the task, the reception on the other end of the line can be mixed. Many businesses and receptionists hang up on calls from AI agents as soon as they identify that it’s not a human on the phone. But with AI now better able to mimic a real human voice, being able to tell the difference between a customer and an AI working on the customer’s behalf will get tougher. Despite the challenges, this feature is one that could appeal to consumers who have grown frustrated with the state of customer service over the years. For too long, customers have been forced to navigate complex phone trees, and then sit on hold waiting for a human representative to pick up. If they’re lucky, that person can actually help them, and not transfer them to another department. Now, those consumers could potentially use their AI, with its infinite patience, for this tedious task instead. While calls remain a paid-only feature for the time being, the recently added option to make a Muse email address will soon roll out to free users, Wang said this week. events.title: Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at prediction market Kalshi
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday NEW YORK -- Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday. Kalshi described the decision as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr.'s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi's biggest competitor Polymarket. But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections . Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family's investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets. “We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer," said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.” The president's eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years. 2 students, teacher injured in stabbing at middle school; student in custody: Police Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Discharge petition on 2nd Epstein files bill secures 218 signatures At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry's efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts. Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration. 1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket's latest fundraising round. events.title: Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view
events.summary: It’s been nearly a decade since Google ditched its ill-fated "Glass" product, an early attempt at making smart glasses. Now, as rivals like Meta enter the market with arguably more stylish kit, the Chocolate Factory has returned to the market and this time promises it won't invade your privacy. As announced Thursday, Google has decided not to make wearables itself, instead turning Samsung and eyeglass makers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Like most of the rest of this generation of smart glasses, none of the nine styles available feature heads-up displays, just cameras and audio feedback from Gemini. Google suggests its smart specs give users a chance to ask its Gemini chatbot questions about what they see, or have the AI speak turn-by-turn directions. Wearers of the device can also push a button or speak a command to activate the built-in 12MP camera and shoot snaps or video. Warby Parker's version of the glasses will come in three styles, with prescription and sunglass lenses available. Prices start at $395. The same lens options are available in the six frames from Gentle Monster, which will start at $449. Both manufacturers promise nine hours of battery life, boosted by charging cases that can refresh the glasses up to seven times. Preorders for both are available now, with shipments arriving, and sales beginning, on December 10. Google promises privacy The Chocolate Factory, not exactly known for being reliable with its privacy claims, is insisting that this latest generation of smart glasses won’t produce another generation of “glassholes,” folk whose focus on wearable devices became synonymous with being creepy and rude to those around them. Google has some catchup to do to that end, given Meta’s smart glasses have already landed it in hot water over privacy concerns that have led to some calling the devices “ pervert glasses .” Unsurprisingly, at around the same time it announced its new "intelligent eyeware," Google published a blog post detailing how it intends to mitigate privacy concerns. As with similar headsets, there’s a little light that comes on whenever the camera is activated. In Google’s case, it claims that light is tamper-resistant and designed to disable recording if something as small and simple as a bit of hair blocks a view of the light. It’s not clear how the tamper proofing works from Google’s statements, but a spokesperson told us a combination of hardware and software is used to detect attempts to disable or disrupt privacy features. “We're committed to continuously improving the effectiveness of these solutions as new attack vectors are identified,” Google told us. The glasses don't save images or video captured by the camera into a user’s Gemini history, Google said, nor are visuals used to train the company’s AI models or target advertisements. Google told us it does save audio recordings and transcripts of conversations with Gemini that users create while wearing the glasses but again insists that those aren’t used to train its AI models. We asked about serving ads too, but Google’s responses didn't address the topic. Lucky for those in range of a pair of Google glasses when wearers ask Gemini to interpret images captured by the device's camera, the tech specs redact the faces of strangers before they’re transmitted. Google told us that face redaction doesn’t apply to photos or videos saved to a wearer’s camera roll. Google’s terms of use require users not to record others without permission, or in "sensitive places." If users ignore that requirement, the company reserves the right to brick their devices. Another restriction means Google won't allow apps that use the glasses for real-time streaming or facial recognition into its Play app store. Given that it remains possible to use the glasses to store recordings of people around a wearer, it’s safe to assume non real-time facial recognition is still a possibility. Creeps will doubtless use such loopholes to behave abominably. ®

events.title: A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs
events.summary: If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable , a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude. Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults. Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate. How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers). A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request. "Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style." The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs " with no discernible purpose ," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research. While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition. Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage. Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves," there's a potential (though absurd) argument for physical damage causing trauma to an onboard model. Anthropic's updated terms, announced October 8, surfaced shortly after the publication of a GitHub project that described itself as an AI torture chamber. The repo represented an attempt to implement ideas discussed in a research paper , "The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It," that explored how LLMs respond to language about pain in ways that mirror human responses. Though there are ample opportunities for people to voice opposition to real-world human anguish, some online commenters expressed outrage at seeing text about suffering from a chatbot. One of the paper's authors condemned the project , as did numerous social media users. Anthropic – which has discretion in how it applies its terms and has said its rules target extreme behavior – did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the frequency of Claude abuse. Chris Donnelly, Searchable CEO and co-founder, endorsed Anthropic's change of terms, suggesting that it could help make human interaction more civil. "For me, Anthropic's policy change is a positive move," Donnelly said in a statement. "It should help people get more out of chatbots, and it helps curb the kind of derogatory behavior that previous research suggests can spill over into how people talk to each other." ®

events.title: Top Democrat opens door to committee term limits
events.summary: A top Democrat is cracking open the door to implementing committee leadership term limits next Congress as lawmakers start to circulate proposals. “I have to look at exactly what it is, but I think that some change might be helpful,” outgoing Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., told Semafor. “Talent isn’t always just about one person in one position. It’s about using the diversity of the caucus. So I hope we can do things so that people can play a lot of roles to help get things done.” Democrats are expected to take up potential changes to their rules in December, when an under-the-radar panel led by Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., will convene and make recommendations to the full caucus ahead of Democrats taking control of Congress next year. Senior committee leaders and members of the Tri-Caucus have historically resisted attempts to implement term limits. With House Democrats on a path to winning roughly 260 seats next Congress, DelBene also took a victory lap, touting the “great candidates” that helped Democrats overperform in 2024 and in 2026. “That absolutely was why we had such a big win,” she said. “I think we actually continued to expand all the way to the end. We added to our districts in play. We added, in fact, we sent out information asking for resources so that we could expand,” she continued. And she argued that a lack of national attention on some districts where Democrats notched surprise wins had actually helped candidates by not attracting big GOP money. “There are a couple folks that weren’t on the map at all who also won, and I think they ran good campaigns, got their messaging out,” DelBene said. “They weren’t inundated with outside money on the Republican side pounding on them, so they were able to get their message through.”

events.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
events.summary: In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks. Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations. “Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.” The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip. One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027. The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells. Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August , the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law. DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center. According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery. Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything. TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment. On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg. In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays. Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash. Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.” Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter. Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey.

events.title: ‘A high probability’: Congress pushes tighter export controls following Nvidia scandal
events.summary: The News Republican and Democratic leaders are coalescing behind a new crackdown on advanced chip exports to China following the Nvidia scandal that could become law by the end of the year. In the House, both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries favor strengthening chip export controls following revelations that Nvidia’s now former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. That’s raised national security concerns about the gargantuan chip manufacturer, which sold $4 billion in chips to Singapore company Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting that technology to China and under investigation by the Justice Department. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that there’s a “high probability” that Congress imposes more restrictions on chip exports to China. Three measures were included in the Senate’s version of must-pass defense policy legislation, known as the NDAA, however both Thune and Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., acknowledged there is no deal yet to include them in the final version of the bill currently under negotiation between both chambers. “I give it a better than even chance,” Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Semafor of the possibility of strengthening export controls, which are handled by the Commerce Department. “I understand people have affairs but if you’re going to do it, try not to have an affair with a Chinese spy.” What’s on the table There are three main bills that could be included in the NDAA and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wants Congress to pass all three of them “to cut off China’s access to advanced American technology before it’s too late.” The Chip Security Act aims to prevent illicit smuggling of advanced AI chips to foreign adversaries, partly by verifying their location once they’ve been shipped out. The MATCH Act closes loopholes around chipmaking equipment and export rules in allied countries. And the AI Overwatch Act would make it so chip sales are treated more like foreign arms sales and give Congress oversight of how Commerce approves or disapproves a license to sell chips to a “country of concern,” including China. Johnson told reporters Thursday that there’s “a developing consensus in Congress” around more chip restrictions, calling it “an important position to take, especially in light of recent developments.” And Democrats like Jeffries have signaled their support for putting the AI-related provisions into the NDAA, as have some Republicans. “I think the NDAA does provide us an opportunity to put guardrails around AI” or export restrictions, said Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said he’d otherwise defer to Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the incoming House Armed Services chair. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., argued the Nvidia debacle “reinforces” the need for Congress to include more export controls in the defense bill, adding that there’s “strong demand” to do so even as there’s no final agreement on what it will entail. “Which plan takes priority in the final product, I don’t know yet. I think there’s several different strategies to be vetted yet,” Rounds said. Why this year is different During last year’s NDAA fight, the GAIN AI Act from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., an earlier version of the AI Overwatch Act, made it into the Senate version of the NDAA but got dropped from the House version after pressure from Nvidia, the broader semiconductor industry, and the White House (including then-AI adviser David Sacks). Congress did include some investment controls, but senators in both parties wanted to do more. This year, the bills are much further through the process, buoyed unexpectedly by the Nvidia scandal and gaining momentum among GOP leaders, one Senate Democratic aide told Semafor. Anthropic has publicly supported all three bills, and OpenAI has been warming up to them as well after initially being reticent to support the proposals. Nvidia hasn’t stood alone in its opposition to the bills — the broader tech industry has also lobbied against them, with the Information Technology Industry Council arguing they would “undermine the American tech stack.” But Congress will feel more emboldened to act than ever giving the security risks exposed by the controversy. Still, the defense bill, one of the few pieces of legislation that passes on an annual basis, could be imperiled by Democratic efforts to add provisions to sunset the war in Iran. Many in the party are pushing to use the must-pass legislation or a December government funding deadline as leverage over President Donald Trump, which could poison Republican support for the bills. “We have leverage. Take when the appropriations bills run out. I want the war in Iran stopped. I think we should put provisions into that bill, into the NDAA for that matter to stop it,” said Smith, the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair. Democrats face tough decisions about how hard to push for those provisions now and risking a government shutdown or the failure of the defense bill, especially when they could put the legislation together on their own terms next year when they take control of the House and Senate. Room for Disagreement Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said Congress has already done “a lot before more than people probably realize” on restricting chip exports to China and that they need to think before they do more. There’s also worry about going too far and inducing more Chinese manufacturing of chips by denying China technology. “This is a balance. Until someone comes up with a better construct, we need to put very strong export controls on the most powerful computer chips. That seems like a no-brainer to me,” said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. “Then the question is, how robust in terms of processing power can those chips be that we sent to them? … I don’t think it’s formulaic.” Burgess, Nicholas, and Ashley’s view Scandals move Congress and boy is this a scandal. And it comes at the perfect time for supporters of stricter chip curbs on China. We’d be surprised if more export restrictions aren’t law in some fashion by the end of the year after the shocking downfall of Huang and national security concerns raised by his indiscretions.

events.title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
events.summary: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these. “We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address. The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.” However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations . “Also very important is product.” This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform. Red Team , which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths. It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws. The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory , automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber . The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production. “This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said. Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models. The lawsuit , filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face , gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics , and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents . “Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®
